Nearly impossible? How Fairphone built the ethical, repairable Fairphone Gen 6+

Ars Technica Long form September 04, 2026

Fairphone’s CTO explains how and why the Dutch company builds a different kind of smartphone.

Smartphone longevity didn’t used to matter. In the past, before you could wear out or break a phone, there was always some shiny new thing to buy. Today, we expect our smartphones to go the distance, but they’ve also become less repairable and, in many cases, more fragile. Fairphone, a Dutch smartphone maker that has just entered the US market, thinks about phones differently.

The new $650 Fairphone Gen 6+ is designed both for longevity and easy repairability. There are trade-offs to this approach if you’re used to the standard glass and aluminum sandwiches filled with glue, gaskets, and teeny-tiny screws. But the drawbacks could be worth it for the right buyer. Fairphone CTO Chandler Hatton told Ars that Fairphone’s goal is to provide a compelling mobile experience while also enabling the user to “fully own” their device. At the end of the day, this is what a lot of people say they want in a smartphone.

These days, Google, Samsung, and Apple support phones with software updates for the better part of a decade, but will the hardware last that long? And what happens when it needs a repair? You may be out of luck or out a lot of money, but Fairphone prioritizes the self-repair experience.

“We’re doing something that was long thought to be nearly impossible,” said Hatton. “Which is delivering high-performing modular smartphones that can last for a very long time.”

Fairphone designs devices to be sustainable, focusing on avoiding conflict minerals, using recycled materials, and paying workers a living wage. Fairphone says it doesn’t want to sell you a bunch of phones, just one that you can keep using even if something breaks.

“Our goal is that every single person that purchases a Fairphone uses it for at least five years, and we track that as a KPI [Key Performance Indicator],” said Hatton.

The standard way to design a modern smartphone is to cram as much as you can into an aluminum and glass sandwich, with the expectation that it will be assembled once in a factory and never opened by the buyer. Devices rely on glue and awkwardly placed screws to accomplish this, making the internals a little like metal spaghetti.

The Gen 6+ is designed so that anyone can replace parts, reducing e-waste and potentially saving consumers a lot of money. If you’ve had, say, a Samsung Galaxy phone for a couple of years and need to replace the screen or USB port, the cost might be higher than just buying a new phone.

“There is an incentive in terms of planned obsolescence to replace your device,” said Hatton. “On the one hand, it’s a good way to keep selling devices, but that’s simply not the proposition that we have.”

That means designing the phone differently—it’s not just a matter of skipping the glue. Inside, the Fairphone Gen 6+ is clean and orderly. It starts with a pair of T5 Torx screws exposed on the back of the phone. After removing those, the back cover slides off. With the same driver, you can extract the battery, camera modules, USB-C port, display, and more. In all, the phone supports user replacement of 12 different parts with just that one (included) screwdriver. One drawback is that the modular approach makes the phone a millimeter or two thicker than most glued-together phones.

The battery stares you in the face once the back panel is opened. You’ll have to remove a few more screws to get it out, but quick swapping isn’t the goal here—this is about longevity.

“We know that after about three years, it will be wise to replace your battery with a new one,” said Hatton. “Batteries aren’t meant to last forever, but your phone on the whole can last a lot longer than a battery.”

While the Fairphone is designed to be disassembled, what about the long haul? The Fairphone 6+ is mostly plastic rather than metal like a Pixel or iPhone. The phone still manages to feel solid, though, thanks to its internal metal frame, and the company has worked to ensure the device doesn’t become progressively less sturdy as you tinker with it.

“When we’re in our product development cycle, we introduce tests that are specifically dedicated to disassembly and reassembly,” said Hatton. “So we’re looking in part at the robustness.”

Robots work the assembly line, but humans are less predictable. Hatton pointed to tests that examine, for example, what happens when someone over-tightens screws while servicing their device. Does it warp the casing? Damage any nearby components?

Hatton said it takes her 15 minutes to fully disassemble a Fairphone Gen 6+, but she did have a hand in designing it. That said, it shouldn’t take a novice much longer. After a couple of minutes perusing Fairphone’s documentation, I was able to take the phone apart and remove all of the user-serviceable components in about 20 minutes. Everything went back together without issue and still works perfectly, with no new gaps or wobble.

The process is pretty intuitive, with most of the parts held in with flat board-to-board cable connectors. Just pop them off with a spudger or your fingernail, and the component lifts right out. There are a good number of screws to remove to get all the way down to the metal frame and screen, but again, they all use the same T5 Torx bit.

Glass backs are common on smartphones because they’re good for radio performance, and they add significant rigidity to the design. But they’re also easy to crack and difficult to remove (they’re almost always glued in place). Naturally, the only glass on the Fairphone 6+ is covering the 6.31-inch 1116 x 2484 OLED display, which is fully replaceable. This is probably the most challenging component to swap, but even this isn’t too bad. The screen is held in place by a handful of screws and has a generously long ribbon cable attachment, making a swap much less frustrating than your typical smartphone.

The OLED is about what you would expect for this price range—the resolution is more than sufficient, and the colors are great. The brightness is good enough to be legible outdoors, but at a mere 1,300 nits peak brightness, it’s harder to see than the displays you get on phones like the Pixel or Galaxy S26 that are a few hundred more expensive. Good luck replacing those displays on your own if you get a crack, though.

Smartphones have become more powerful over the years, but their designs have also been streamlined. Headphone jacks and microSD card slots are now rare, and even the SIM card slot is quickly fading away. OEMs often cite the space constraints when dropping these features.

“There’s a reason that most phone manufacturers prefer slightly larger footprints—because you can fit more stuff in there,” Hatton said. “So yes, it is legitimate if phone manufacturers are saying, ‘Hey, we dropped this feature to save space inside the device.’”

The Fairphone retains some of these elements, but not because there’s a surplus of space, Hatton said. The Fairphone 6+ still has a microSD slot and physical SIM card because people want them. These features don’t come free, though. In addition to the space constraints, adding more components adds to the price and complicates supply chains. That’s another reason some OEMs have removed features.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ plays to picky smartphone and DIY enthusiasts, but there’s still no headphone jack. Hatton notes that the team hears from a small but vocal cadre about headphone jacks every time it starts planning a new device, but it hasn’t made sense to include one in recent phones.

“In terms of how to actually get [a headphone jack] into the device, it is quite difficult,” Hatton said. “It’s a relatively large hardware component, but it’s not just the component itself. It’s also where it needs to be. You know, you’re not going to put the headphone jack in the middle of the back of the phone. You also need to make sure it attaches to the right things on the inside, and because we’re Fairphone, you need to make sure it’s repairable. So when we look at that total picture, we assess the needs of our customers to fulfill some other wishes at the expense of the headphone jack.”

Looking at spec sheets side-by-side, the Fairphone also lacks something that many of today’s phones have: IP6X water resistance. An upshot of making non-repairable phones that are chock-full of glue is that they’re relatively easy to seal against water intrusion. With an IP6X rating, a phone can be fully submerged in water for up to 30 minutes, at least in theory.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ is only rated as IP55, which will protect it from splashes. That could be enough, though. “Our phones are designed for what people need on a day-to-day basis,” said Hatton. “How often is it that people would like to take their hardware underwater? I think the answer there is less often than some manufacturers would have you think.”

While it might be comforting to think you could drop your phone in a pool, that’s still risky. OEMs don’t warranty the water-resistance of their phones, and if you’ve made any repairs, it’s possible the sealing of that difficult-to-open device was compromised. Hatton notes that it wouldn’t be impossible to make a repairable phone that’s also IP6X, but you’d have to design around that in numerous ways.

“There are a number of things that you need to weigh against a higher IP rating,” Hatton said. “You can achieve it in a very small form factor with higher costs, or you can achieve it with a larger form factor—you could increase the Z dimension and perhaps also the other dimensions, and that way you could create all sorts of gaskets and other things. But we assess the whole landscape and say, ‘Hey, the customer doesn’t want a phone that’s a brick.’ They also don’t want a phone that’s incredibly expensive. So within those boundaries, what IP rating meets their needs?”

It’s a trade-off, but it’s one that many people would probably make in the name of repairability if given the choice.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ is similar to the Gen 6 that launched in Europe last year, but there are a few notable changes. The new phone has a slightly upgraded Snapdragon chip, and it has more memory than the last Fairphone at a time when AI has driven up costs considerably.

“We decided to increase the RAM to 12 gigabytes,” said Hatton. “This is something that I think is a little bit unique, given the current circumstances in the consumer electronics industry. But the reason that we did is that it really underscores the value proposition of longevity that we’d like our customers to enjoy when they purchase the Gen 6+.”

Google, meanwhile, is catching some well-deserved flak for regressing from 16GB to 12GB of RAM in its latest Pixel phones, which start at $900. Samsung is also sticking with 12GB of RAM in its $2,000 foldables. And all those phones devote a lot of memory to AI services that not everyone cares about. The Fairphone has the Gemini app installed like all Google-certified Android devices, but the company has yet to create any on-device AI services of its own. That’s on Fairphone’s radar, but the team is taking a measured approach.

“We have not immediately jumped onto the bandwagon of creating AI features without really understanding what the use scenario is and what the customer really wants,” said Hatton. “We see that people are quite interested in understanding how their data is used and having control over their data and privacy. That means that as we continue to use more AI in all sorts of different settings, we’ll continue to work on AI features for our devices that focus on these aspects that are important.”

Fairphone has been offering devices with generous support windows for years. The Fairphone 3, which launched in 2019, just reached end-of-life a few weeks ago. The Gen 6+ will be supported through 2033 with software updates and replacement parts.

Hatton says that multiple factors go into determining the length of support. The availability of hardware in the supply chain is part of it, but it becomes impossible to update devices once vendors like Qualcomm stop supporting the underlying firmware. Seven or eight years is the functional limit for any smartphone due to vendor support, so it’s impressive to see Fairphone in the same range as the likes of Google and Samsung. It really can’t do more than it’s already doing here.

At $650, the Fairphone feels like a good deal in 2026. Maybe a year or two ago, the device wouldn’t have seemed as competitive, but with price increases and RAM regressions becoming standard, Fairphone comes out looking much stronger with the Gen 6+. It has a solid mid-range Snapdragon chip, ample storage (with a microSD card slot), and 12GB of RAM, which is still flagship territory.

There’s also something to be said for knowing that your phone is repairable if something goes wrong, and when the time comes to replace the battery, you can do it yourself in a few minutes. Fairphone is committed to keeping all these parts in stock for the duration of the phone’s support window, which runs through 2033.

The Fairphone may not be everyone’s style, but I like the utilitarian vibe. My design complaints are fairly limited and minor: the volume buttons are too low, and the power button (with fingerprint sensor) is too hard to find by feel.

The modular design allows for a little fun in the form of accessory back panels. You can swap them just by removing the two external screws. There’s a finger loop back (below), a card holder, and a lanyard that works with any of the backs. Hatton notes that the accessories also invite users to open up the phone to see how easy it is, something Fairphone recommends people get familiar with even if they don’t have any accessories to swap—it’s like knowing where the spare tire is in your trunk.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ runs a minimally customized build of Android 16, so it’s a bit behind the latest and greatest. Thankfully, Google doesn’t limit as many features to the latest builds of Android anymore. It has almost no bundled software outside of the standard Google apps, which is nice to see, but if you’re hoping for a phone that’s crawling with snazzy software features, this is not it.

One of Fairphone’s few software customizations is called Moments, which you can toggle with the brightly colored side switch. Moments can help limit distractions by hiding most of your apps behind a minimalist UI. It’s just a full-screen app overlay rather than a completely custom home experience, though. If you don’t fancy the digital well-being approach to mobile tech, you can remap that switch. Using it as a flashlight toggle is nifty, for example.

The camera may be the biggest compromise if you switch from a Google or Samsung phone. The hardware is typical for the mid-range, with a 50 MP Sony 700C joined by a 13 MP OmniVision OV13B10. That third lens on the back is actually a window for a time-of-flight sensor that helps with focus. With ample light, both rear sensors produce good images, and the primary even does fine in some more challenging conditions.

Capture speeds are long, though, making it hard to get clear images of moving subjects. Colors look a bit flat, too, and autofocus speed seems on the slow side. There’s a 32 MP selfie camera, which looks a touch dimmer than most devices in this price range.

With support increasing for making electronics more repairable, other companies may need to start moving in Fairphone’s direction. In Europe, regulators are preparing to require removable batteries, and more US states are enacting right-to-repair laws. The Fairphone CTO stresses that other OEMs have what they need to make phones more repairable.

“We’re producing our phones on the same production lines as our competitors, and often with many of the same components,” said Hatton. “It’s actually quite a small industry when you’re in it, and there is very little room for one of our competitors to say it’s impossible when on the next production line over it is happening.”

The Fairphone Gen 6+ is available directly from Fairphone, as well as on Amazon. It’s unlocked and works on both AT&T and T-Mobile.

Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 21:31:40 GMT

New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England.

The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development.

A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under 16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work.

Education unions said the ideas were welcome but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years.

Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards.

The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the new V-levels which colleges are teaching from autumn 2026, and T-levels.

The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell argued the new vocational GCSEs would give young people a "stronger connection" to careers, while the prime minister said it was a change from a "one size fits all" education system.

VCSEs, a new style of vocational qualification unique to Wales, will be taught in schools and colleges from September 2027.

Learners in Wales can choose from 15 VCSE subjects including Animal Care​, Nature Restoration​ and Motor Vehicle Maintenance​.

Vocational subjects at 16 currently make up 7% of the entries for qualifications in England and it is up to each school how many subjects with hands-on learning they offer.

Wright Robinson College in Gorton, East Manchester, already offers 10 practical or vocational subjects for study in Year 10.

Daisy, in Year 11, is taking business studies as a BTec Level 2 which she said is giving her "practical experience" and building her confidence to progress to an A-level in the subject.

This is the kind of subject that may be replaced by one of the new vocational GCSEs.

Many of these existing tech awards have their standards set by the examining organisations, not the regulator. The standards for the new VGCSEs will be national.

Sarjo, also Year 11, already knows she wants to be a flight attendant so she is taking hospitality and catering as a BTec Level 2 alongside GCSEs.

She said she "learns faster" in the practical subject and most teenagers want to do something they enjoy alongside core academic subjects.

Martin Haworth, executive headteacher at Wright Robinson College, said any new qualifications had to "add value" to what was already on offer and labelling them as GCSEs might help with credibility.

He said schools would need to recruit specialist staff if the courses and exams were going to be "robust", and it would cost schools money to convert existing classrooms for practical learning.

New analysis of school funding by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies shows the budget per pupil is growing faster than expected, by 9% in real terms between 2025-26 and 2028-29.

This is partly because of various government top-ups to the budget and falling pupil numbers in some areas.

Economist Luke Sibieta said asking schools to offer more vocational routes would be a "big change" on top of the significant reforms to support for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities.

He said there was a "big question mark" over whether there were enough people to teach technical and vocational subjects, with further education colleges already struggling to recruit.

The Association of Colleges (AoC) suggested schools worked with them because they could offer "industry standard facilities" and qualified staff.

David Hughes, from the AoC, said this would help ensure learning was "authentically different to school and properly employment focused".

Daniel Kebede, from the National Education Union, said "sustained investment and resources" was needed to make a success of the new qualifications.

While Pepe Di'Iasio, of the Association of School and College Leaders, described the government's plans as "well intentioned" but without making sure schools had the staffing and resources would not remove barriers to young people.

He welcomed the national push for work experience and said with placements "extremely difficult" to secure more support was needed from employers.

The existing statutory career guidelines for secondary schools in England already require "meaningful" work experience for 14 to 16-year-olds.

Employers are now being asked to contact their local careers hub to offer placements.

Laura Trott MP, who is the Conservative Party's shadow Education Secretary said she was concerned the changes risked losing the progress England had made in improving standards, and "ripping up the system" could mean "sabotaging young people's futures".

"Better schools will continue to protect rigorous subjects but disadvantaged children will be steered towards easier routes, lowering expectations for the very pupils who need high standards most", she said.

UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 21:16:00 GMT

A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.

Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.

Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.

But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.

Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.

As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.

But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.

Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair.

"I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day.

"I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting.

"I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened.

"I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."

Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her.

"I'm learning that things can get better," she said.

"I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."

Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.

He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.

David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021, said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health.

"Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids.

"I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."

A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.

Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics.

"The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said.

"The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives.

"We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."

Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.

He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear.

"We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death.

"Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life.

"I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."

Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023.

"He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said.

"Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."

Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness.

"Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living.

"That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him.

"When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."

Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis.

"Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said.

"The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart.

"It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."

The hearing continues.

Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 21:01:55 GMT

The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling.

Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work.

This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items.

The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable".

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms.

"Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off."

The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year.

Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.

Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.

The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".

For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.

Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.

The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair".

"The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said.

"Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."

However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided".

"Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said.

"We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."

Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.

The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.

The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 21:01:16 GMT

Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination".

The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled.

Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction.

The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges".

The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds.

Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton.

Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands.

Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street.

Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different.

"And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.

"But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently."

Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement.

The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area.

A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned.

A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games".

He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour.

"It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games."

He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area".

FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league".

He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed."

A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined.

The rules have been relaxed this season with all Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcohol to supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials.

The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently and fans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games.

Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 21:01:06 GMT

Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK.

The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA.

The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down.

That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it to manufacture coating for frying pans until 2012.

Sam and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result.

"When we opened the results... it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale.

"I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said.

Forever chemicals are a group of substances, also known as PFAS, that are resistant to water and oil and are in thousands of everyday products, such as clothing and cookwear.

But because they do not break down easily they have raised health concerns. PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 because it was classed by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as a Group 1 carcinogen, which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer.

The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have been testing the area close to the AGC Chemicals factory since 2024 to determine if it has been contaminated.

They found PFOA at elevated levels in the soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have now been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land, while residents within 1km of the factory have been advised to peel any fruit or vegetables grown in their gardens.

Those investigations concluded the PFOA was likely to have come from the factory having been carried in the air.

Residents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals".

Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues.

Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday.

Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category.

"I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't."

Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family.

"One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said.

Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now."

Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick.

"To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population."

The UK does not have any recommendations about acceptable PFAS levels in people, although the US and Germany do.

Of the 49 residents tested, 70% had readings that could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects, according to these countries' guidelines.

Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis.

Having elevated forever chemicals in their blood is not a guarantee residents will develop these conditions, but US and German authorities have suggested anyone with elevated levels should be offered further health screening.

More than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contamination

Sarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land.

She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally".

The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country.

Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits for a total of $671m (£526m). Both companies have always denied any wrongdoing.

The factory in Thornton-Cleveleys first start operating in the 1950s, when ICI manufactured coating for non-stick frying pans using PFOA. AGC Chemicals took over the factory in 1999 and continued using PFOA until 2012, when it switched to a replacement chemical called EEA-NH4, which was also found in the blood of 10 residents tested.

A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals said the site manufactured chemicals long before the company was established. "Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps," they said.

Earlier this month, AGC Chemicals said the factory would close later this year after deciding there was no "viable solution to keep the site operating in the context of a volatile and competitive market".

Dr Steve Hajioff, a specialist in public health, who was not involved in the Thornton-Cleveleys blood testing, said PFOA levels could have been even higher in the past, given the factory stopped using the substance in 2012 and it does break down over time.

He said the levels measured in Thornton-Cleveleys are associated with elevated risks of serious health condition, but added: "If you increase the risk of something really rare, like kidney cancer or testicular cancer, by 30%, then the chances of an individual getting affected are still pretty low."

Moore said she was representing residents in the community who were pregnant and worried about their children, as well as those who have families who were refusing to visit their homes over concerns about the risks.

"What we're looking at in Thornton-Cleveleys at the moment might be seen as something of an outlier. My worry is that it's the tip of the iceberg, it's just the beginning," she added.

The researchers said further blood testing should be done in the wider community to understand the scale of the issue.

A previous report into PFAS in Jersey recommended that residents with elevated levels should be offered treatment, including cholesterol-lowering medications and blood letting - a treatment where blood is gradually withdrawn from a vein, allowing the body to naturally replenish it.

Wyre Borough Council, which is overseeing the investigation into the site, said: "We recognise that PFAS is an emerging area of scientific research and will continue to press for updated advice and guidance from expert health agencies on behalf of our communities as further evidence becomes available."

Essex cricketer Das charged with two counts of rape

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 20:32:31 GMT

Robin Das last appeared for Essex in a One-Day Cup match against Middlesex on 21 July

Essex cricketer Robin Das has been charged with two counts of rape.

The 24-year-old will appear at Inner London Crown Court on Friday, 9 October after he was charged on 23 July.

Das was arrested on 27 August last year following reports of a woman being raped in Brixton in March 2024.

The Metropolitan Police said in a statement: "Robin Das of Queens Road, Waltham Forest, was charged on 23 July 2026 with two counts of rape.

"The charges follow his arrest on 27 August 2025 following reports of a woman being raped in Brixton on 30 March 2024. The woman continues to be supported by specialist officers."

Das, a top-order batter, has made 60 appearances for Essex and last appeared for the club in a One-Day Cup match against Middlesex on 21 July, his only senior appearance in the 2026 season.

Essex have confirmed that he has been suspended since his arrest, two days after his last appearance for the club.

Essex said in a statement: "Essex County Cricket Club can confirm that a male member of the playing staff, currently under contract with the club, recently appeared in court in relation to an incident that took place outside club activities.

"Throughout, the club has remained in contact with the ECB, PCA, the Cricket Regulator and the player with regard to the matter, which included an immediate and ongoing suspension. The club will continue to follow all appropriate legal processes and guidance.

"As a club we have strict safeguarding and HR procedures in place, and all employees of Essex County Cricket Club are required to meet the highest standards of professional conduct at all times.

"As legal proceedings are in progress, the club are unable to make any further comment at this time."

Das made his debut for Essex in 2020 and has made nine first-class appearances for the county, along with playing 29 games in 50-over cricket and 24 matches in T20s during his career. Two of the T20 appearances were for Dhaka Dominators in the Bangladesh Premier League.

Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 19:10:22 GMT

The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios.

Common Bond emailed customers announcing its locations, all of which are currently in London, were closed "until further notice".

The firm describes itself as a wellness collective and charges £2,400 for 12 months of unlimited classes. It also runs Reformcore and Triyoga brands and said in August last year it had ten sites.

Its website is no longer publicly accessible. The BBC has contacted Common Bond for comment.

The email sent to customers on Wednesday seen by the BBC said: "We're sorry to let you know that all Common Bond studios are closed until further notice.

"We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and disruption this may cause . We understand this is frustrating, and we appreciate your patience while we work through this."

Instructors have told the BBC they were told last week they would not be paid on time and that they only found out about the studios closures from the Wednesday email.

One instructor said she and her colleagues were told their pay would be delayed on the day it was due on 14 August.

She said: "In good faith, I continued to teach my classes without any news on when or if payment would be made. I have heard absolutely nothing since."

It is not clear how many instructors and customers have been hit by the sudden decision to shut the studios down.

Companies House filings for Common Bond show the company was incorporated in June last year, so has it has not yet published any accounts.

The most recent filings show a director, Ben Allen, left the role last month.

Gaspar Lipszyc, listed as a Belgian national living in Spain, is the only currently shown director of the company.

Barrecore is a brand specialising in barre, a fitness discipline that combines pilates, ballet, and yoga.

Barre is a low impact exercise and its popularity has soared in recent years as famous names including Pippa Middleton have praised its benefits.

Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 18:51:12 GMT

Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.

In a victim-impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".

Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions".

Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York, where he has faced three trials over rape and abuse allegations. He was convicted in a seperate sex-crime case in Los Angeles.

This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was first convicted and sentenced in 2020, but New York's highest court overturned the conviction in 2024, along with another involving actress Jessica Mann. The court ruled that Weinstein did not get a fair trial.

He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.

Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.

Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace in 2017 after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades.

The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.

In the 2020 trial, Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. Haley was a production assistant on the Project Runway television series at the time.

On charges related to Mann, juries could not reach a verdict, and he was found not guilty in another charge involving model Kaja Sokola.

After testifying in the retrial last year, Haley told the BBC she felt compelled to take the stand.

"I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she said.

Weinstein is still awaiting sentencing in the California, where he was convicted in 2022 of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013.

An appeals court ordered he be re-sentenced in the case after the New York convictions were overturned.

Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and said he believes he will be proven innocent.

Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 18:15:31 GMT

President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Iran will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, he told the UN General Assembly: "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying."

Pezeshkian also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using a key Gulf waterway.

"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said.

There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.

"The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.

He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February.

He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab.

"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said.

Also on Wednesday, an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor, the Agence France-Presse news agency reported, citing Omani and Indian authorities.

The attack was condemned by India's foreign ministry, which called for unimpeded passage through the Strait to be restored.

In February, Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.

It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected.

In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".

Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality".

"[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said.

But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force."

Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal.

"It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said.

He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons.

"We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology."

Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions".

On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.

But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

Home secretary hits out at 'unacceptable' migrant landings

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 17:18:49 GMT

The Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted.

Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday.

Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe.

Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought.

Migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats.

Before Monday, no small boats had been officially recorded as arriving in the UK without an escort since 6 September 2025.

Uncontrolled landings of migrants in the UK, as seen on Monday and Tuesday, are so rare that the incident in 2025 was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023.

Mahmood said the beach landings were "not acceptable".

She said: "Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many.

"That is why I have ordered an urgent review by the Border Security Command into how this happened, and what must be done to ensure it doesn't happen again."

She said that new tactics adopted by people smugglers, including launching small boats from much further west in France, were "a reminder of two things".

The home secretary said: "Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings.

"Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat."

Early on Wednesday, migrants were brought to Dover after embarking on a crossing from a village near Bayeux in Normandy to Gosport in Hampshire, spending more than 33 hours at sea.

Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, called it "a day of despair" for the Labour government.

He said: "Our border security has descended into chaos with illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats."

Philp said: "This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants' boats in French waters, instead they are escorting them here."

"What's more, there have been two uncontrolled migrant landings in a week. It is a complete free for all – the Labour government have no idea who is coming into the country.

"The only way to stop Channel crossings is to deport anyone who arrives illegally to their home country or a safe third country. That's the only way we can end this madness."

Earlier, a government spokesperson said: "Border Security Command officers alongside Kent Police have been responding to an incident in Dover.

"Twenty-one individuals have already been detained under a swift enforcement response.

"There is a thorough investigation ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Officials said those who had been detained had been taken to Western Jet Foil for processing.

The uncontrolled arrivals come after Border Security Command suggested they were a thing of the past, because of new surveillance technology and improved resources.

Earlier this year, Reform UK set out a proposal to call in the Royal Navy to help intercept migrants, but it was rejected.

On Tuesday, 154 migrants arrived in three boats, of which one was an uncontrolled landing.

It takes the total of migrants to have arrived in the UK this year to 17,784.

The total so far this year is down 44.7% compared with figures for 22 September 2025, at which point 32,188 migrants had arrived that year.

UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 17:01:11 GMT

The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.

The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".

It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.

It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".

The squadron will protect British satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the MoD said.

In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy £1.4bn a day.

"Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said.

"We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."

Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said the threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".

A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head of the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week".

The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".

Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites.

Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space.

However, Washington has already accused both Russia and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.

In May, the RAF tracked a series of "dangerous manoeuvres" by five Russian satellites moving close to two Finnish commercial satellites. The RAF's Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth said in June that a Russian satellite constellation had caused disruptions to GPS signals across Europe and Canada.

The UK has a handful of military satellites in orbit for surveillance and military communications. But it works closely with the US Space Force - which has many more.

In a separate speech at the space conference, ACM Smyth added that "unfortunately we are seeing more and more irresponsible and provocative actions from our adversaries".

ACM Smyth warned that without satellites, some of the technologies people take for granted would be lost and would make every sector "less efficient, less prosperous and less secure".

"Sat-nav systems would fail, congestion on our roads would be severe and our emergency services would take longer to help those in need," he said, adding that satellites are also needed to monitor the weather and the effects of climate change.

Is Burnham right to blame Russia for spreading online disinformation?

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:35:11 GMT

After Prime Minister Andy Burnham put Russia-linked disinformation campaigns under the spotlight, BBC Verify has been examining how these attempts to influence people's opinions work.

We have tracked – and debunked – numerous online disinformation campaigns produced by Russia-linked groups that have attempted to shift public opinion on issues like the war with Ukraine, influence elections in the US and Germany, damage social cohesion and undermine trust in authorities or institutions.

In his UN speech, Burnham said there was an "insidious campaign" being carried out by the Russian government to target people in the UK.

Last year, a series of fake videos featuring British public sector workers appeared online.

Among them was a 999 call operator in Preston named Aaron, who told BBC Verify he was shocked to find out his voice had been cloned with AI to create a fake video of him talking about the 2025 Polish presidential election.

Those videos are part of a major Russian-linked disinformation campaign known as Matryoshka, which BBC Verify and other research groups have been tracking.

AI is used to create fake videos - sometimes dozens a day - which impersonate journalists and major news organisations like the BBC to push disinformation about Ukraine and Western countries onto people's social media feeds. But Aaron's case indicates ordinary British citizens could also be a target.

In the run-up to the 2024 US presidential election, BBC Verify reported how there was a shift in focus from Ukraine to post fabricated videos about the US election. We are once again seeing early evidence of similar misleading videos ahead of November's US midterm elections.

BBC Verify has previously exposed a large-scale disinformation campaign run by a former US police officer now based in Russia. With the help of AI, the operation created hundreds of fake local news websites in the UK, US, France and other Western countries with the aim of spreading completely made-up stories.

One of these was a fake news website called the London Crier which falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a bargain price.

It was seen by hundreds of thousands of users on X and shared by an official Russian embassy account.

We also found that a fake AI-narrated video on YouTube was the source of the bogus story. The platform removed it after we reported it.

And in 2023, BBC Verify found a major propaganda operation involving bogus accounts on TikTok, which posted misleading videos in multiple languages - including English - generating millions of views, with the aim of influencing the views of users in several European countries about the war in Ukraine.

TikTok removed more than 12,000 fake accounts involved in the operation, saying its investigation indicated that the accounts originated from Russia.

Another campaign was discovered during the 2019 UK general election campaign when a trove of confidential documents about a possible trade deal between the UK and US was posted by an anonymous user on the platform Reddit and later used by the Labour Party in its campaign.

While the documents appeared to be genuine, Reddit later confirmed in a statement the leak "was part of a campaign that has been reported as originating from Russia".

But there are questions about how widespread or effective some of these disinformation campaigns are in reality.

While many of them appear to be extensive and organised, it is hard to determine how widely they have spread or how significant a role they have played in actually influencing people.

Russia is also not alone in using industrial-scale disinformation campaigns which spread false information to further its own geopolitical aims, as other authoritarian governments like China, North Korea and Iran are also major players in online disinformation.

BBC Verify has previously reported on a number of X accounts posting in support of Scottish independence, but whose location information indicated they originated from Iran.

And, at the height of the Coronavirus pandemic, the BBC discovered a network of more than 1,200 faked or hijacked accounts on Facebook, Twitter and YouTube that posted pro-Chinese government and anti-US messages.

There is evidence to suggest Western governments also engage in disinformation campaigns, although the scale of their operations are not always clear.

An investigation by Reuters in 2024 revealed that during the Covid pandemic, the US military ran a covert anti-vaccine influence operation to discredit China's Sinovac jab.

And Meta has previously removed an influence campaign originating from France that targeted a number of countries in Africa.

AI has also exacerbated the spread of disinformation, as images can now be more easily faked and videos misleadingly edited using text prompts.

Text generation has also improved and can create plausible, authoritative and coherent sounding fake news reports.

BBC Verify saw evidence of this during US-Israel war with Iran. While in the early weeks of the Russia-Ukraine conflict most of the disinformation published online consisted of old or misleading videos and inaccurate claims, we have seen a deluge of AI-generated images and videos since the Iran war began back in February of this year.

Carl Miller, an author and founder of the Centre for the Analysis of Social Media at Demos, told BBC Verify that state-run influence operations "amplify and exploit existing grievances and fissures - making it really hard to work out exactly what sort of effect they might have".

"Influence operations are quite fragile things, usually, and we need to find ways of making them much more likely to fail if they target us," he added.

Award-winning singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka has revealed he has suffered a stroke and faces a "long, tough journey ahead" to recover.

The 39-year-old from London, who won the Mercury Prize in 2020 and has been nominated for five Brit Awards, said in an Instagram post that the stroke occurred "a few months ago" and was caused "by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure".

He added that "the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done", but told fans he will "look forward to seeing you all soon".

Kiwanuka simultaneously announced the release of his fifth album, titled Fudge, which was recorded before the stroke.

"I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said.

"I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure.

"It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.

"I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better.

"It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now."

He thanked "all the incredible NHS staff and every single medical professional who has helped care for me and continue to help and encourage me in my recovery", and his friends and family for their support.

"This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I've faced and I'll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes. Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road."

US singer Miguel wrote: "Man, take your time healing, you are needed brother."

Radiohead guitarist Ed O'Brien posted: "Sending love to you Michael."

Kiwanuka first made his mark 15 years ago, being named the BBC's Sound of 2012, and has established himself as one of Britain's most acclaimed singers and songwriters.

Fudge was originally scheduled to come out last year. Before it was postponed, an early review in Mojo Magazine described it as an "intimate" and "brooding" album, influence by Neil Young's On The Beach.

Millions of lettuces ruined by UK aphid outbreak

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:08:49 GMT

Millions of lettuces are set to be wasted as farmers are grappling with a record outbreak of aphids that has devastated the end of their growing season.

Growers are facing losses of £10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable, according to the British Leafy Salads Association (BLSA).

The organisation says that warm and dry weather has produced "ideal conditions" for the bugs, with as much as 30% of the UK crop between now and the end of October set to be wasted.

Homegrown lettuce dominates the market in the summer and early autumn weeks before a transition that sees more imports filling shop shelves.

But imported lettuces are now likely to be on the shelves in the UK a couple of weeks earlier than usual.

Farms in many parts of England - the Midlands, East Anglia, the south-east, south and north-west - have been impacted by the outbreak.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, BLSA spokesman Dieter Lloyd described the issue as "serious", while not affecting all of the UK crop.

He said people have been eating salads from UK products "all summer" but added: "The issue though is serious, the aphids bloom in June and again in August/September."

"What we're talking about here is the loss of the crop over the course of the last couple of weeks and the couple of weeks ahead."

He said that "this is not all of the heads in the UK, but it's a significant percentage of it" and producers are "looking at not using 30 million heads of lettuce at the cost of £10m to the growers".

Over the course of the season, UK growers produce around half a billion heads of lettuce.

Asked if weather is a factor that has contributed to the issues, Lloyd said that short-term weather patterns and regional variations do have an impact.

"We had a problem with aphids last year, we've had a mild winter which traditionally might affect the aphid populations and then they do like warm weather."

The National Farmers' Union said that they are looking to support growers and researchers amid the outbreak.

Martin Emmett, the organisation's horticulture chairman, said: "This summer's warm and dry weather created a number of challenges for growers and the effects are still being felt, with rising levels of pests and disease now adding further pressure to farming businesses following an already difficult period.

"While growers are working hard to tackle record high numbers of aphids, the NFU is supporting the work of grower groups, plant breeders and researchers."
