A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.

"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."

Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.

"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."

Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.

After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.

Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.

Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.

The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.

He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.

Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.

"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.

"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.

"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.

"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."

Antonelli climbs out of his Mercedes after crashing in first practice for the 2024 Italian Grand Prix at Monza

Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.

At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.

He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.

Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.

"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.

"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.

"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'

"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."

Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.

"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.

"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.

"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.

"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."

Antonelli crowd-surfs with joyful home fans after winning the Italian Grand Prix earlier this month

Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.

"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.

"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."

Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.

Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.

All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?

"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.

"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."

His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".

"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.

"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."

There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.

"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.

"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.

"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."

The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.

Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"

He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.

Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.

"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."

All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.

Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.

"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.

"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

Man Utd still £1bn in debt with £63.5m spent on new stadium

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 14:10:21 GMT

Manchester United are currently 12th in the Premier League

Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for the team's new stadium.

Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, the club have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.

This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24.

However, while United have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased.

Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, net finance costs alone have now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005.

Manchester United's new stadium will be the centrepiece of a wider Old Trafford regeneration

In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125m (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club have not explained what they have done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.

It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximately 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.

This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first-team squad this summer.

United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than promoted Ipswich.

However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches because of injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.

While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts.

"We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada.

"This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

"While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.

"With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."

United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, who currently sit second bottom of the table with one point from three games.

Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m.

"This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first-team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

Orkney island welcomes first baby in more than three decades

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 13:17:09 GMT

A baby has been born on Orkney's most northerly island for the first time in more than three decades.

Parents Jorge Suarez and Alice Traill Ford welcomed baby Duncan Wilder Thorstein Traill Suarez Ford in North Ronaldsay last week.

Islanders toasted the birth with a dram of whisky to celebrate the first newborn in the remote location since Thomas Brookman in August 1992.

The family, who split their time between Costa Rica and Orkney and travelled more than 5,000 miles for the birth, said Duncan was born in a much-loved place.

"North Ronaldsay has always been a very special place for me and I felt alive and free here every summer when I came up as a little girl," Alice told BBC Scotland News.

"My intuition was telling me this was the right place for us so we spoke to the NHS to see if it would be possible.

"We have this beautiful family home steeped in our history and ancestry so to be surrounded by that felt a very special introduction for him to come to Earth."

North Ronaldsay is Orkney's northernmost island and is only accessible from Kirkwall on the main island via a 20-minute plane journey or a ferry, which takes two hours and 40 minutes.

The island is famous for its seaweed-eating sheep, which are mostly confined to the shore by a 13-mile-long drystone wall that encircles the island.

Baby Duncan was born in Holland House, which was built by Alice's ancestors - the Traill family - who bought the island in 1727.

The house has been passed down through generations and is still owned by her family.

Alice's grandfather, Duncan, was the former Laird of North Ronaldsay and provided the inspiration for her son's name.

"I didn't know I was going to name him after Duncan when we arrived but I was sitting on the sofa and right in front of me was a collage of his pictures with my grandmother, so he has been very present with us," Alice said.

"He was an incredible man, very kind and really strong and I felt like there would be no better name than his to carry on and continue his legacy in the world."

Historically when the Laird was on the island, a flag was flown at Holland House to inform the residents.

So when baby Duncan was born at 04:05 on 15 September, Alice and Jorge followed the tradition to share the news.

"Over the years we have found a lot of magical four-leaf clovers here and have kept them in a book," Alice said.

"We stuck a four-leaf clover to a glass bottle, glued a Groatie Buckie to the lid then filled it with whisky and gave it to each of the islanders.

"We raised the flag and everybody opened their whisky and shared a dram - a celebratory drink - together."

A Groatie Buckie is a small, pale pink and white shell found on beaches across Orkney, which in local tradition brings good luck and fortune to the keeper.

The family will return to Costa Rica in November, where the couple run a school.

But Alice is certain her children will have the same opportunity to spend time in North Ronaldsay as she did growing up.

"Duncan will absolutely be back every year," she said.

"One of the things I want to give my children is the gift my mother gave us, bringing us to this island every summer, letting us run wild, explore the island and feel the connection to the community."

UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 12:52:53 GMT

The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.

In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".

"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."

Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.

He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.

During Trump's first face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US president criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it.

Burnham replied: "Yep."

He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution".

Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well.

"What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."

The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York, and an official readout from that meeting said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal.

The "review" is not expected to constitute a formal process operating to a specific timeframe.

Government sources are insisting that Burnham and Streeting's comments do not represent a major shift from the previous position, which was that any deal would require American support.

However Streeting's comments were notable for their explicit acknowledgement that without changes the deal is not going to attract Trump's support.

Prior to the pause in April, the UK and Mauritius had signed an agreement in May 2025 and a final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty of the islands had not passed Parliament.

Under the terms of the deal agreed in 2025, Britain would hand sovereignty over the archipelago to Mauritius but lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, which the UK government said would be a net overall cost of £3.4bn.

However, Sir Keir, who was then prime minister, came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to £35bn, adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.

Trump, who originally backed the deal, has been a frequent critic of the move, previously branding it a "a blight on our great ally" and an "act of total weakness".

Reacting to the review, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to "just scrap this terrible deal".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."

In 2019, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) gave an advisory opinion that Britain's separation of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius was unlawful and stated the UK must end its administration as rapidly as possible.

While non-binding, the ICJ advisory opinion - which was endorsed by the United Nations General Assembly - emboldened Mauritian assertions of sovereignty and led to the UK opening negotiations in 2022.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday that no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal.

Describing the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", he said work was underway to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with".

Dolly Parton's manager accuses her nephew of 'threats and intimidation'

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 12:22:53 GMT

Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.

The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.

The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.

In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.

In a statement to TMZ, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people.

"Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said.

"A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."

Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life.

Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.

In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".

They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."

The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.

The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.

In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.

Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."

The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.

In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police.

"All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.

In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."

But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".

The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.

She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.

The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.

Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August.

Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.

Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.

Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.

In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.

In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death.

"She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement.

"Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."

The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

Police examine video of anti-migrant activist slashing dinghy with knife

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 11:47:17 GMT

Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel.

The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area. They were then transferred to a UK Border Force vessel and taken to Dover for processing.

Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.

The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and starting to slash at the side of the migrant boat.

There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille Liberté.

As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Thomas shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."

Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat.

"Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat."

It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat.

"We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Thomas told his followers.

Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting".

There is no evidence that any boats that have been used by migrants to cross the English Channel have ever been taken back to France for reuse.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said: "We are aware of a video circulating online relating to damage being caused to a boat in the English Channel on the afternoon of 22 September, and we are conducting inquiries into the matter."

Autumn equinox 2026: When was it and what happens now?

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 11:11:19 GMT

Astronomical autumn has officially started after the equinox took place in the early hours of Wednesday.

It happened at 01:06 BST on 23 September, according to Royal Museums Greenwich.

It is a precise moment in time when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and neither hemisphere is tilted towards or away from the Sun, meaning day and night are roughly equal in length across the world.

While the equinox itself cannot be seen, the day has cultural and spiritual significance for some people. Gatherings took place at sites including Stonehenge and Glastonbury Tor (pictured above), where people came together to mark the occasion and watch the Sun rise.

Autumn's arrival is very clearly spelled out in photo taken in Wakefield, West Yorkshire

The autumn equinox may mark the start of astronomical autumn, but it does not necessarily mean there will be a sudden change in the weather.

The first signs of autumn are already around us with falling leaves and conkers on the ground, and as the Sun gets lower in the sky and the days shorten, temperatures generally fall as we head further into autumn.

So far this September, UK mean temperatures have been above average overall, according to the Met Office.

BBC Weather Watchers captured some beautiful equinox photos and here are a few favourites of those sent in so far.

A spider's web is beautifully crafted in amongst the autumn leaves

The sunrise over Malborough in Devon on Wednesday filled the sky with tutti-frutti pink and orange colours

Fairytale-style toadstools popping up and changing autumn leaves are some of beautiful signals that autumn is here.

Although the equinox happens at the same moment everywhere, the change in hours of daylight is not the same across the UK.

The further north you go, the bigger the difference between the long days of summer and the short days of winter.

That means places in northern Scotland are losing daylight more quickly at this time of year than parts of southern England.

Leaves are already turning red and oranges setting off the mist still shrouding the fields behind

Sunrises like this one in Ventnor on the Isle of Wight, will will get progressively later as autumn continues

Around the autumn equinox the changes are particularly noticeable as sunrise gets later and sunset earlier.

The word "equinox" comes from Latin and means equal night.

At the equinox, the daylight measurement is taken from the point when the centre of the Sun is at the horizon, and is 12 hours sunrise to sunset and 12 hours sunset to sunrise.

However, it is the top edge of the Sun which is visible first at sunrise and last at sunset.

Because of light refraction - light being bent by the atmosphere - there is still light for a time when the Sun is not directly visible. This adds extra time to daylight hours.

In autumn, this means that the time when day and night are actually equal happens after the equinox.

This is known as the "equilux", which means equal light.

This year, that happens in the UK on Friday 25 or Saturday 26 September, depending on your latitude.

Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 05:24:56 GMT

Dario Osorio, 22, has won 25 caps for Chile and has featured twice for Crystal Palace since joining on loan this summer

The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.

"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.

Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.

It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.

Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.

"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.

"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."

From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.

"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any more in football," says Kjaer. "Sometimes it does, but it's rare."

Malick Yalcouye began his career at ASEC Mimosas, joining Brighton from IFK Goteburg two years ago and breaking into the first team this season following loan spells at Sturm Graz and Swansea

"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.

Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.

It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.

Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.

The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.

"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."

Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.

The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.

"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."

Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.

"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.

"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."

Both Kjaer and Turner see Uzbekistan as one of the emerging talent markets, with 22-year-old Manchester City defender Abdukodir Khusanov among those to feature at the World Cup for the debutants this summer

"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.

"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.

"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."

One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".

Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.

For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.

Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.

As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.

Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.

"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."

Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.

"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.

"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."

One of those markets continues to be Africa.

Winger Zadok Yohanna, 19, recently made his debut for Brighton after a year in Sweden at AIK

"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.

Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.

"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.

With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.

But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.

"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.

"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."

Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.

Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.

"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.

"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."

Striker Romaine Gandonou, 15, has already scored for the Benin senior side

Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.

Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.

"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."

Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.

The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.

It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.

Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.

Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.

Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.

"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.

"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.

"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."

Riyad Mahrez was 19 when he joined a professional club for the first time with Le Harve

There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.

A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.

"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.

"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."

Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.

Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.

Other Eyeball, external partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.

"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.

"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.

"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery

BBC News Wed, 23 Sep 2026 05:00:25 GMT

Warning: Graphic images and descriptions of surgery

"Everyone made it out to be so easy, but my face felt like it was on fire and there was a horrible smell of burning skin," says Nikita Morgan, as she describes her eyelid surgery.

She decided to get a blepharoplasty, or a "bleph", removing skin from just above the eyes - after seeing videos about it on social media. Even though she was given a local anaesthetic, Nikita felt extreme pain.

Oculoplastic surgeons - doctors specialising in surgery around the eyes - say a concerning number of patients are reporting problems from cheap bleph surgery, typically carried out abroad.

Contains some upsetting scenes.

They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.

Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.

As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight.

UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad.

Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than €4,000 (£3,400).

Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for €750 (£650).

She described its clinic in Düsseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".

The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.

It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.

The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.

Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.

She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before.

"I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."

Faceland says all patients have consultations and sign consent forms before procedures, to ensure they are "well informed and well prepared".

It added that Nikita's doctor had said Nikita was "very anxious and uncertain" during her procedure "which can influence the perception of pain".

Within hours, a "traumatised" Nikita was boarding a plane home. Flying on the same day of surgery is not advised by medical experts as well as Faceland, but she saw lots of people doing it on social media.

"I was struggling to see," says Nikita, "if I looked up, my stitches would bleed so it was like I was crying blood."

She really regrets flying on the same day as her surgery and advises others not to.

In the past three years, videos about blephs posted by UK social media accounts on four leading platforms were viewed nearly 150 million times, BBC analysis has found. This figure is five times greater than the previous three years.

Many people report positive results in their posts, and a lot have been treated at Faceland.

One woman told us her droopy eyelids had been restricting her vision and causing her headaches. She was not eligible for NHS treatment and could not afford to go private in the UK, but now she says, after going to Faceland, her issues have been resolved.

The company's website claims it is changing the market by focusing on "affordable, accessible and high quality care". Treatments are carried out by accredited medical doctors who receive internal training by Faceland in surgical procedures, it says.

Surgeons in the UK told us upper eyelid surgery typically takes about three hours, including preparation, surgery and post-operation care. But Faceland patients we have spoken to say they spent less than an hour at the clinics.

Faceland says allowing practitioners to perform a higher volume of treatments helps significantly lower costs.

Eight days after her Faceland bleph surgery, Laura, not her real name, made her first of four visits to A&E because her eyelid wounds had reopened.

Her procedure at the company's Amsterdam clinic in June had seemingly gone smoothly, but problems began when she took her stitches out back home in the UK, something many patients do when they have treatment abroad.

The crescent shaped cuts above her eyes which had been held together by the stitches came apart, exposing raw, red wounds which became infected. This should hardly ever happen if a practitioner has been properly trained, UK surgeons told us.

The first time this happened, Laura, who is in her early 40s, says she called Faceland's emergency helpline several times, but could not get through. Desperate, she rushed to A&E.

"When I closed my eyes for too long the tension would cause my wounds to open up again," she says. "I was scared to go to sleep and was in constant agony."

In the days after, Laura was communicating with her doctor from Faceland and, on several occasions, she offered to fly back for assessment.

"I was crying, literally begging: 'You can't leave me like this'," she says.

But Faceland told her the best course of action was seeking treatment local to her.

Laura was referred to an NHS eye specialist who said "excessive skin" had been removed.

How did Laura feel about the NHS picking up the cost of fixing her cheap surgery?

"I feel guilty... People will think 'it's your own fault', but I would never have gone had I known what could happen."

Faceland says it cannot comment in detail about Laura's case because she is pursuing legal action against the company.

As a goodwill gesture an independent complaints committee that works with Faceland offered Laura €175 (£150), which she has rejected.

UK surgeons tell us that, when they have seen patients with blepharoplasty complications over the past 12 months, those people have, in most cases, been treated abroad.

The most common issue following overseas procedures has been people not being able to close their eyes properly, according to a survey for the BBC, to which 63 members of the British Oculoplastic Surgery Society (Bopss) in the UK and Ireland responded.

"Removing too much skin from the eyelid is dangerous because it leaves the eye exposed to the elements," explains consultant ocuplastic surgeon, Colin Vize, who is on the Bopss executive committee. "Correction can be difficult and expensive."

He likens eyelids to "a pair of curtains". When you open them there needs to be a pleat, so when you close them there is enough skin to cover the eyeball.

Other issues from overseas procedures reported by the Bopss members include scarring, uneven eyes and wounds opening up.

Surgeons say they also saw patients with complications after having been treated by unregistered UK practitioners, including blepharoplasties that had been carried out in living rooms.

On Christmas Day 2024, Caryn Harte woke up struggling to see.

It was days after her bleph surgery at Faceland's Amsterdam clinic, her swollen left eye was weeping blood, and the wounds above both eyes had started to open.

"I was terrified I was going to lose my sight over a bit of excess skin," she says.

Caryn went straight to A&E, seeing no point in calling Faceland because it was too far away.

Doctors later reassured her she would keep her vision, but her face was badly infected. She was prescribed antibiotics and required hospital check-ups.

The BBC has seen emails that show Caryn contacted Faceland twice, to report what had happened, and that she received a short reply 12 days later. A few further emails followed, but Caryn says she has not heard from the company since.

Faceland maintains it "did not leave her without support or follow-up during the aftercare process".

It says it is sorry if patients felt insufficiently supported by its teams or experienced complications.

Like Caryn, Laura and Nikita, patients we have spoken to who have had cheap eyelid surgery abroad say limited aftercare is their biggest complaint.

"Aftercare for the typical bleph should be available to a patient 24/7," says Vize. "If your surgeon is hundreds of miles away, the ability to provide care with a sense of immediacy is impossible."

He also warns that patients should be aware that in some cases lower costs may mean lower standards.

A week after her surgery, Nikita removed her own stitches. She worked out what to do by watching TikTok videos.

"It makes you feel weak, like you're pulling something out of your skin," she says.

Faceland says patients are advised to consult its doctors about when to remove their stitches and are given information on how to do so. Nikita says she did not receive an aftercare pack or instructions.

The company also says patients can come back to a Faceland clinic to have stitches removed, but no-one we spoke to had done that.

Patients removing their own stitches is "a recipe for disaster", according to Vize, who says stitches should be taken out by a surgeon or a nurse to reduce the infection risk and the chance of wounds splitting open.

Nikita is mostly happy with her results, aside from a small scar, but she wants other people to learn from her experiences and fully understand the risks.

"If I'd had the money or if I hadn't listened to the spin on TikTok, I probably would have gone somewhere closer to home and not rushed into it," she says.

Nearly two years on, Caryn still has issues with her left eye, including some blurry vision and scarring.

Meanwhile, Laura fears she may have scars above both of her eyes for life.

"I tried to fix a problem that didn't really need fixing, and I've come back with a bigger problem that I need surgery for, and I can't afford that," she says. "It's pretty devastating."

Future of Amazon rainforest may hinge on Brazil presidential election

New Scientist September 23, 2026

On 4 October, Brazilians will go to the polls to elect a president and government. Former president Jair Bolsonaro, under house arrest, cannot run. But his son Flávio is on the ballot. If elected, the 45-year-old senator is widely expected to govern as his father did, which is sparking fears for the future of the Amazon rainforest.

During Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency between 2019 and 2023, deforestation in the Amazon soared, reaching a 15-year-high in 2021.

“We have nothing to believe Flávio will do anything differently from his father. If anything, the signs are that it’s going to be far worse,” says Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Brazil’s Climate Observatory. “This is a do-or-die moment for the Amazon, really.”

Advertisement

Super El Niño set to cause ‘terribly dangerous’ drought in the Amazon

Flávio Bolsonaro is looking to unseat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula. With the younger Bolsanaro currently embroiled in a corruption scandal, the environment has received relatively little attention during campaigning

“But for the rest of the world, the major question here is the Amazon,” says Philip Fearnside, an ecologist at Brazil’s National Institute for Amazonian Research (INPA).

The Brazilian Amazon’s 4.2 million square kilometres of rainforest regulate global climate patterns and hold huge stocks of carbon – roles that are increasingly important as climate change accelerates.

“The Amazon is a key element in whether climate change escapes human control, which is very close to happening,” says Fearnside. If the forest collapses, he says, the associated increase in emissions “would be the straw that breaks the camel’s back”.

Free newsletter

Annual Amazon deforestation surged from 7536 square kilometres in 2018, before Bolsonaro took office, to 11,594 square kilometres in 2022, shortly before he departed.

Experts say the former president encouraged a wave of land-grabbing and illegal mining with his pro-development rhetoric and gutted environmental agencies so they were powerless to stop invaders.

“It’s still hard to believe what happened,” says Izabella Teixeira, Brazil’s environment minister between 2010 and 2016, initially under the presidency of Lula and later under the presidency of Dilma Rousseff.

Since returning to office in 2023, Lula has restored the power of environmental agencies, halving Amazon deforestation to 5731 square kilometres between August 2024 and July 2025.

Deforestation could trigger Amazon tipping point in the 2030s

In a recent TV interview, Flávio Bolsonaro refused to say that climate change existed, instead referring to “extreme climate events” and “cyclical periods”. And during his time as a senator, he proposed legislation that critics said threatened Brazil’s native vegetation. Given this record, and his close ties to his father – and to Donald Trump – experts are concerned that his election would be followed by an increase in deforestation rates.

“We don’t know exactly what Flávio Bolsonaro’s policy will be,” says Teixeira. “But we do know he is a climate change denialist and believes environmental protections are irrelevant.”

Brazil’s largest Indigenous organisation, APIB, had said it fears Flávio Bolsonaro will open Indigenous lands to critical-mineral extraction, and that a Bolsonaro victory would mark “the return of a death project”.

Stark photos show quest for profit cutting swathes through the Amazon

Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign also pledges zero illegal deforestation by 2029. “There are two ways to achieve that. One is to actually stop deforestation. The other, more likely way, is to just legalise the deforestation that’s going on,” says Fearnside.

A spokesperson for Lula’s campaign told New Scientist that the president’s current term was about rebuilding environmental institutions after Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency of “total neglect and denialism”. The next term would be about “implementing and gaining scale”, with a focus on tougher enforcement, climate adaptation and Brazil’s 2035 climate targets.

The Flávio Bolsonaro campaign did not respond to questions about its environmental policy.

Testing the Amazon’s ability to soak up increasing carbon emissions

Angelo says Brazil’s environmental organisations fear a Flávio Bolsonaro government would resemble Trump’s second term. He says the political know-how gained from the Jair Bolsonaro presidency could allow them to enact laws more quickly.

Flávio is also likely to face fewer political constraints than his father, not least because he has said he would appoint five new supreme court judges.

“Wildcat mining would explode, deforestation would go up and everything we already had during the first Bolsonaro administration would come back even stronger,” says Angelo.

Lula’s environmental policy has also been criticised.

His government has promoted major infrastructure projects such as improving the BR-319 Amazon highway and backed new oil exploration near the mouth of the river basin – projects that would drive deforestation and lock in fossil fuel production.

We used to think that deforestation in the Amazon would dry out the local climate, but the effects may be even more extreme and varied

Still, the choice remains stark, says Angelo. The election will shape not only the future of the rainforest but also global climate diplomacy.

In an era of failing climate leadership, Lula oversaw new initiatives including a self-sustaining fund to pay tropical countries for keeping forests standing and a global road map to transition away from fossil fuels.

Under Flávio Bolsonaro, Angelo predicts that Brazil would probably withdraw from climate diplomacy and ignore its own international climate commitments.

“I don’t think a fourth Lula term would be great for the environment – but it’s really our only hope of keeping the forest standing and keeping any climate policies in place,” says Angelo.

Researcher finds that cats lie around for a ridiculous amount of time

New Scientist September 23, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Feedback’s felines are often nowhere to be seen. For hours at a time – in the case of the more free-range cat, sometimes several days – they vanish from sight. What might they be doing? Torturing the local small-animal population perhaps, or chasing fallen leaves around the yard, or visiting the local school to cause as much disruption to learning as possible, or perhaps just lazing in a warm spot to sleep. But who knows?

One person who does know is Michelle Smit at Massey University in New Zealand, because she and her colleagues put collar-mounted accelerometers on cats to follow their movements. Feedback learned of this from the UK’s Telegraph newspaper, which reported the study from the journal Pets on 12 September under the heading “Paws for thought: Science proves your cat really is that lazy”.

Advertisement

Smit’s team tracked 10 indoor pet cats and 18 free-roaming pets, as well as eight cats living semi-outdoors in research facilities. Their behaviours were grouped into eight categories: “active (walking and trotting), eating, grooming, littering, lying, scratching, sitting, and standing”. Presumably the data was insufficiently granular to capture other cat behaviours such as “pushing breakable objects off furniture onto hard floors” and “inexplicably hissing at one’s human after having previously been pleased with a cuddle”.

The most mobile cats were free-roaming pets: in summer, they were active a full 3.9 per cent of the time, though this fell to 2.7 per cent in winter. The indoor and research cats spent even less active time. Littering and scratching took up very little time, less than 1 per cent each. Instead, overall, the cats devoted between 2.4 and 7.8 per cent of their time to eating, 4.6 to 7.9 per cent to grooming, and 9.3 to 15.6 per cent to standing.

If you’ve been keeping track, you already know there’s a whole lot of day left. This the cats reserved for their two primary activities. Sitting occupied them for 20.1 to 41.4 per cent of their time, while a whopping 34.8 to 52.9 per cent went to the really important one: lying.

Feedback would say something about this, but first we’re going to lie down for 4 to 6 hours.

Feedback is on a quest to compile a definitive database of unfortunate abbreviations triggered by technological systems, such as the “suggested follow” box on social media that shortened the name of the Stroke Association charity by eight letters. Two more have come our way.

Some years ago, writer Dave Appleby was delighted to have been promoted to assistant headteacher. Soon after, “I applied to attend a conference and proudly filled in my new title on the form where it asked for ‘job role’. ” But Dave was in for a rough experience. “Arriving at the venue, I spent the day meeting other attendees with the name badge pinned to my chest: Dave Appleby, Ass Head.” Fortunately, no pupils were present.

Meanwhile, Mike Petty sent us a one-sentence email we will simply reproduce in full because we have nothing to add (and anyway, adding material seems contrary to the spirit of the exercise). “When I and colleagues set up in business in 1997 as Loughborough Surface Analysis Ltd, little did we realise that for many years to come the default length for the organisation-name field on conference name-badges would be 25 characters [including spaces].”

It has been over a year since Feedback last checked in on MrBeast, the most popular YouTuber on account of having worked very hard to become popular. Wondering what he might be up to these days, we discovered he has started a paid partnership with Google.

The tech giant announced on 2 September that MrBeast (real name Jimmy Donaldson) is “tapping into Gemini to help him execute wilder concepts, showing his fans how they can use AI to help turn impossibly big ideas into reality”.

Gemini, of course, is Google’s own-brand AI tool. In MrBeast’s first video using Gemini, he and his wife, friends and colleagues split into three teams and race across the Amazon (not all of it), the Arctic (likewise) and a desert to reach rescue helicopters. They use Gemini to help them identify hazards and come up with ways to survive.

By the way, while the official announcement mentions the Arctic, the video repeatedly says that the people in the chilly place were in the Antarctic, so Feedback isn’t entirely clear which end of the planet they went to. Details, amirite?

Anyway, we got a little over 5 minutes into the 23-minute video and didn’t find any instances of them using Gemini. At this point we had got so bored of the constant updates on how far each team had got that we stopped watching.

Our main interest in the video came about due to the recent post on X by Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, claiming the odds were higher than 10 per cent that AI would “kill all humans” in the next decade.

Extrapolating, we wondered whether MrBeast’s Gemini video might be his last. However, it was titled “I Survived The Most Extreme Places On Earth”, so we assume he made it. However, if his Google deal requires him to make 10 or more videos, the odds are against him.

What is an itch, and why can a simple touch calm it?

New Scientist September 23, 2026

What is an itch, and why are most so easily calmed with a simple touch?

Mark DirnhuberBristol, UK

Your questioner clearly hasn’t lost many nights’ sleep being driven crazy by, say, a mosquito bite on the back of a toe, seemingly refractory to all treatments other than scratching it until it hurts, which feels better than the itch. Maybe itching has evolved to alert us to attack by blood-sucking arthropods, and if the persistence of the itch leads to a visceral loathing thereof, then surely that too, given dangers like the plague or malaria, will confer an evolutionary survival advantage.

What is the fastest way to empty a full jug of water?

New Scientist September 23, 2026

What is the fastest way to empty a full jug of water: tipped upside down or poured at a particular angle?

Richard WaspeVia email

The quickest way to empty any cylindrical vessel without an aid is to tip it upside down and swirl it around rapidly. The induced vortex will create an air channel right up the middle to the bottom of the vessel. This lets air behind the water and so the whole mass of water is now free to fall under gravity. Without swirling to let air pressure in behind the water, it is held back because it begins to produce a vacuum as it falls, which pulls in the opposite direction to gravity. This wouldn’t work in microgravity and is highly discouraged in the space station!

When will the AMOC collapse? We don’t know, but should still prepare

New Scientist September 23, 2026

Most climate impacts are like repeatedly shooting ourselves in the foot: we keep emitting greenhouse gases, the planet warms and more heatwaves happen, and wildfires, and flooding, and drought. Science tells us that this is mechanistic: pull the trigger and you will get hurt.

But in some cases, large uncertainty remains. One particular concern is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), the system of currents that transport a tremendous amount of heat from the Gulf of Mexico to Europe. As ever more icebergs and meltwater from Greenland rush into the north Atlantic, the AMOC is thought to be slowing down. Eventually it could even collapse, bringing “ice age” winters to Europe, raising sea levels in North America and disrupting vital monsoons in Africa and Asia.

Will that happen? We don’t know. Some research says the AMOC could cross a tipping point in centuries, some says decades and some says it has crossed it already. If we start reducing emissions, it may not happen at all. Scientists have long described it as low probability but high impact. You might think of it as climate Russian roulette.

Advertisement

Scientists have long described the AMOC’s collapse as low probability but high impact

To tackle this uncertainty, scientists are trying to build an early warning system to alert us that the AMOC is going to cross a tipping point. It is unclear whether that warning would give us enough time to avoid this, or merely to prepare for the impacts, but both are better than doing nothing, which is what we are doing now. We may not know the probability of the AMOC collapsing, but we know it is increasing.

So far, the uncertainty around it has been an excuse to ignore it, or treat it as a distant problem. In fact, the uncertainty makes it even more important for policy-makers to take action now, in the same way we fund militaries for wars we hope will never come. Whether we decide to invest in mitigation or adaptation, we won’t regret it, since all of it will help with our bigger climate problem. Stop emissions, take the gun away and no one needs to get hurt.

Why can’t we cool water as quickly as we can heat it? part 2

New Scientist September 23, 2026

Why can’t we cool water as quickly as we can heat it? (continued)

Guy CoxSydney, Australia

Looking at the wider world, absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, is 0 kelvin (-273°C), while we can create temperatures of millions of degrees. So, heating is more readily available than cooling. Liquid helium (at -269°C) gives us the closest commercial approach to absolute zero, but it is a pretty expensive way to cool your cocktails!

Advertisement

Humans have been able to heat water for millennia, but prior to the invention of refrigeration, cooling it was more difficult. In a suitable climate, we could attempt to store ice through the summer, which would give us 0°C (32°F) as long as it lasted. More generally, we used cellars and caves, which are typically at ground temperature; the annual average is around 10°C (50°F) in temperate climates. Another approach was evaporative cooling. Keeping water in a porous earthenware container allows some to evaporate, so cooling the remainder. Welcome in summer, but not substantial.

Alex McDowellLondon, UK

We can cool water as quickly as we heat it: if, after heating the water we pour liquid nitrogen into it, or add ice cubes, it will cool very quickly.

When we heat water in a kettle, we put in heat (usually 2.2 kilowatts). When water is left to cool, heat leaks away to its surroundings; the higher its temperature is compared with its surroundings, the faster it cools. To boil a kettle, we must, at all times, put in heat faster than it escapes. If the element wasn’t powerful enough, the water’s temperature would rise until it reached equilibrium, whereby the heat from the element equalled the heat escaping and the temperature would rise no further.

If a cup of water at 100°C (212°F) is left standing in a room at 20°C (68°F), and we assume Isaac Newton’s law of cooling (that the rate of cooling is proportional to the excess temperature), initially the excess temperature is 80°C (144°F). However, it would be 120°C (216°F) if the water were put in a typical domestic freezer at a temperature of -20°C (-4°F) – i. e. the initial excess temperature would be 1.5 times higher and it would initially only cool at 1.5 times the rate it would if the ambient temperature was 20°C. Hence, reducing ambient temperature has limited effect on the cooling rate.

We can speed up the cooling rate by placing the cup of water in a breeze. Air isn’t very dense and doesn’t carry heat away very well. Hence, we can cool the cup of water faster by standing it in a cold liquid.

It takes a long time to make ice in the freezer because of water’s latent heat of fusion. It will cool down to 0°C fairly quickly, but latent heat is freed as ice forms, so it will stay at 0°C, with ice and water together, until all the water has frozen.

Why do we feel emotional about fictional characters? part 2

New Scientist September 23, 2026

Why do humans so readily adopt fiction into our lives, and feel emotion about characters as though they were someone close to us in real life? (continued)

John AstellHolden, Massachusetts, US

Advertisement

The question presumes humans can easily tell the difference between fact and fiction. Human evolution and archaeology indicate that for most of humanity’s existence, information was passed down by the spoken word, probably often to children. Even factual events and people would be subject to distortion and simplification, while completely made-up stories could have details that seemed factual and believable.

For most of humanity’s existence, information was passed down by the spoken word, probably often to children

Take the people and events mentioned in the Iliad. Sufficient details in the poem suggest it was partly based on some Bronze Age event. The poem’s “Catalogue of Ships” indicates a retained knowledge of the Bronze Age geography of Greece that differed from classical Greek geography at the time the poem was written down (circa 7th century BC). There is no written evidence that any notable people in the Iliad actually existed, but the name Achilles is a Bronze Age Greek name recorded in two different Mycenaean Linear B tablets, although not that of the hero Achilles.

So, if you are told stories of the Greek gods, the Trojan war, the Peloponnesian war (a recorded historical fact) or the sayings of Socrates, how could you tell fact from fiction? You simply have to believe some things on faith. If you care about what happened to Socrates, you will undoubtedly care about what happened to Achilles, who may or may not have existed, and Prometheus, who is a mythological character.

The rugby league community is mourning the passing of legendary coach Cameron Bell, who has died aged 87.

Bell died on Sunday at Thames Hospital and is remembered as a successful coach with Auckland and the New Zealand Māori, while he also had stints in England with the Carlisle Border Raiders and Barrow.

His most memorable achievements came at Carlaw Park when he led Auckland to a 30-14 win over Great Britain in 1988 and then Australia the following year, 26-24.

Among the players who played for Auckland during that time were Tea Ropati, Mark Horo, Kevin Iro, Tony Tuimavave and Duane Mann, all of whom went on to play for the Warriors.

Bell went on to coach the NZ Māori team, including an appearance at the 2000 Rugby League World Cup.

He was one of 13 siblings in his family. His son, Dean, was the Warriors’ foundation captain.

Mann, who is now the chief growth officer at Auckland Rugby League, said Bell was a magnificent coach.

“Cameron was one of the great rugby league influences of my playing career.

“I had the privilege of playing under Cam in his all-conquering Auckland representative teams of 1988 and 1989, before captaining the Counties Manukau Stingrays in 1996 when Cam coached us to the Lion Red Cup national title.

“Cam was a genuine players’ coach. He had an exceptional rugby league mind. He was a clever tactician who could see the game differently and communicate his ideas in a way players understood.

“His teams played tough, but Cam demanded skill, courage, discipline and commitment to the team. His philosophy was simple and memorable: the ball will always beat the man.”

After playing for Manukau, he began coaching them and led them to success by winning the Auckland competition.

During his time there, he won Auckland coach of the year, as well as beating top British side St Helens 26-10.

He then led the Auckland provincial side for two successful seasons, including wins over Australia, Great Britain and the Eastern Suburbs Roosters, 26-12.

Bell then moved to Carlisle in northwest England before returning home to coach the Counties Manukau Heroes to victory in the Lion Red Cup in 1996.

During that time, he was appointed coach of the NZ Māori team and led them to the World Cup in England, where they beat Scotland, but finished third in their group.

He then returned to England to coach the Barrow Raiders, who had merged with Carlisle in the late 1990s.

A Facebook fan page set up in memory of the former Border Raiders paid the team’s respects.

“Sad news of the passing of Cameron Bell, a top coach and great guy who brought in so many great players in his four seasons at Carlisle and gave us some excellent and entertaining rugby. Condolences to his family.”

A private memorial service will be held.

Ben Francis is an Auckland-based reporter for the New Zealand Herald who covers breaking sports news.
