Are fewer Kiwi kids starting school toilet trained?

New Zealand Herald September 23, 2026

Primary schools report more children starting school without toilet skills. Photo / 123rf

Esther Zweifel of RNZ

At a primary school in Henderson, about a quarter of new entrants are unable to use the toilet independently when they start.

“Things have steadily become more challenging,” Western Heights School principal Ash Maindonald said.

“We have a great many children who cannot, or will not, wipe themselves after a visit to the toilet and this is becoming a really prevalent problem for us. We also have some children who soil themselves during the day.”

This week, the National Party announced a new “school start check” for children at early childhood education (ECE) before they go to a primary school and would set expectations about the skills needed for school, including toileting.

“I hate being a doomsayer, but the problem is becoming much worse,” Maindonald said.

While there is no official data on how many children are not able to use the toilet independently when starting school, anecdotal reports from educators, nurses and specialists suggest it is becoming more common.

Lisa Smith is a paediatric nurse and runs the Children’s Continence Service. “I recently did a presentation for new entrant teachers and definitely the feeling is that many more children are not fully toilet-trained when they start school and a significant number are still in pull-ups.”

Research from the United Kingdom has also found a similar trend, with one in four children in England and Wales starting school not toilet trained, accounting for 2.4 hours of teacher time lost each day supporting children who are not school-ready.

That research also found the age of potty training has crept up from just over 2 years in the 1950s, to just over 3 in the 2000s, with more recent research suggesting about a quarter of parents are starting after 2-and-a-half.

Maindonald says the situation is putting teachers under real pressure.

“If I’ve got a child who needs toileting support, the teacher can’t walk out of the room and do that when she’s got 20 other new entrants in there who haven’t got social skills and are perhaps going to get into an argument or throw something.”

However, the early childhood education sector says they aren’t seeing more children leaving ECE unable to toilet independently.

Simon Laube, chief executive of the Early Childhood Council, says data is needed to understand who these children are that are struggling to use the toilet independently at school.

“What do we know about those children? There’s still quite an absence of data to show whether or not those children actually went to ECE at all.”

Laube says generally, children would be expected to be toilet trained by the time they leave ECE, although he acknowledges this is not always possible depending on the child.

“There does appear to be an epidemic of toileting troubles in the Western world,” Smith says.

She says constipation is actually one of the biggest issues impeding toilet training, affecting about one in three children at some point.

Smith says this can lead to toilet avoidance or stool withholding.

“I’ve seen kids hold on for weeks on end, and the longer they hold on, the more constipated they’re going to become. So then it just becomes a cycle of hard, painful poo.”

But there are many other reasons for a child struggling with toilet training, such as developmental or sensory issues.

“About one in five kids have a disability that could impact on their ability to be fully toilet trained and independent when they start school,” Smith explains.

Being too absorbed in playing is another common issue.

“The toilet is the most boring place in the world. It can be quite smelly. It can be quite cold. So why would they want to go?”

Moving from nappies to the toilet can also be frightening for some children, Smith says, especially if there hasn’t been enough communication about the toilet process.

Smith says children can often be “a regular, happy pooper” in their nappy, but become fearful of the toilet.

“Some kids have an amazing imagination. I’ve heard some kids say that they thought that this was part of their body that they were letting go … that their insides were coming out.”

Plunket is one of the providers for an existing B4 School Check run by the Ministry of Health, which looks at a child’s health, behaviour, social skills and development at age 4.

Clinical leader at Plunket, Kym Ward, says it’s an opportunity to speak to families, offer support, and refer children to a GP or specialists if necessary.

However, anecdotally, Plunket is also seeing increasing numbers of children aged between 4 and 5 who are not yet toilet trained.

One hypothesis, Ward suggests, is that fewer children attended ECE during the pandemic and in subsequent years.

“And in these financially strapped times, many parents also can’t afford to send their kids to ECE.”

She sees real value in the role ECEs can play in supporting families through this transition.

“If your child does attend ECE, quite often those ECEs want to work in collaboration with the parent to help with that toilet training.”

While there isn’t a specific age parents should start potty training, Smith definitely recommends beginning before 4.

“Because the longer they hold on to that nappy, the harder it is to get them out of it.”

When deciding when to start, parents should look for signs that the child is developmentally ready.

That could include staying dry for about one-and-a-half to two hours, being able to pull their pants up and down, recognising when they need to go to the toilet and communicating that, or recognising when they are wet or soiled.

However, not all children will show obvious signs that they’re ready, and parents can still start teaching them.

Night-time wetting should be treated differently from daytime toileting, Ward said.

“We’re not worried about the night nappies. It can be until they’re 7 or 8 years old before they can master not having a nappy on at night-time.”

Developmentally, it’s a reasonable expectation for a child to be toilet trained by the age of 5, Smith says.

“Most children should have the neural pathways, everything should have matured by the age of 5.”

Learning to use the toilet independently is a complex skill for children, and a major developmental milestone, Smith says.

“There’s actually 17 physical steps involved in the whole process of becoming fully independent with toilet training.”

She says it’s one of the most complex things a parent will guide their child through, followed by teaching them to drive a car.

Smith says toilet learning starts well before formal toilet training.

“Start right from the get-go and take a positive approach to changing their nappy.”

Then as toddlers, take your child into the toilet with you.

“Communicate and talk to them about you doing a nice, happy poo or a nice, happy wee. Normalise the whole thing.”

She recommends having one or two main caregivers establish the foundations, and that consistency and repetition are vital – and not to give up when it gets tough.

And when you do start training your child, make it a priority.

Some people even take time off work to focus on it, Smith says.

Ward says if you need additional support, PlunketLine provides free advice on 0800 611 116.

- RNZ

Pupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in England

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 21:30:01 GMT

Courses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’

Teenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system in England designed to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training.

From 2029, pupils will be able to supplement compulsory GCSE subjects such as English, maths and sciences with courses such as construction, creative media production and child development, marking the biggest changes to the qualification for more than a decade.

The Department for Education (DfE) said the new GCSEs would be two-year courses taken in year 10 and 11, “with nationally set content, grading and assessment” and regulated by Ofqual, England’s qualifications watchdog, to the same standards as academic GCSEs.

The courses are part of an effort by Andy Burnham to fulfil his pledge of “an education system that offers a path for everybody, academic and technical, in equal balance”, made the day after his election as MP for Makerfield.

Announcing the new courses, the prime minister said: “We’ve all heard someone say ‘school wasn’t really for me’ because they were not given the chance to study vocational courses as well as traditional subjects.

“That one-size-fits-all approach isn’t working, so we’re building an education system that values both academic and technical paths. I want to give all young people across Britain the hope that their future will be brighter, whether it starts at university or not.”

Whitehall sources said the courses were expected to be offered from September 2029 but that the education secretary, Lucy Powell, wanted to move more quickly if possible, with schools given the option to add vocational GCSEs to their existing subjects.

Powell said: “Time and again young people, parents and employers tell me they want schools to do more to help them understand and prepare for the jobs of the future. Our new vocational GCSEs will give young people a stronger connection to the careers and industries shaping our economy, helping them discover and develop their talents while maintaining high standards across our education system.

“This is not about creating different routes for different children. It is about ensuring every child has access to a rich and ambitious education that opens doors, creates opportunity and prepares them for life beyond the classroom.”

The change is part of a range of measures that Burnham has announced since coming to power to tackle the Neets crisis, with a call to “value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap”. It follows plans to give local businesses a role in setting curriculums in their areas.

In a review published in May, Alan Milburn said that without significant change the number of young people not in work or education could grow by 25% by the early 2030s, opening up a “generational fault line” between the young and old.

Critics, however, say the focus on technical education risks widening the gap between richer and poorer children. Sam Freedman, a policy adviser to Michael Gove when he was education secretary, wrote last month: “The more we ration a full set of academic GCSEs to children from better-off families, the more we will bake in existing inequalities.”

The shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said the courses would mean lowered expectations for disadvantaged children who had benefited most from high standards.

“Labour are sabotaging young people’s futures,” she said. “Just weeks after the latest Pisa results showed England’s pupils climbing into the world’s top 10 for reading, maths and science, they want to rip up the system and review existing GCSEs.

“Soaring up international league tables didn’t happen by accident. It followed years of evidence-led reform built around knowledge, rigour and high expectations. Labour risks throwing that progress away and if English, maths and science become merely a ‘common entitlement’, not a requirement for new qualifications, we risk repeating the mistakes of the past.”

The DfE said the subjects offered could include management and finance, creative media production, digital technology and building and construction, and would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels.

The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England, with travel and tourism and health and care courses among the most popular. About 350,000 technical awards and certificates were issued this year, compared with more than 5m GCSEs.

School leaders said the success of the new courses would depend on having the resources and staffing to teach specialist subjects.

The general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Pepe Di’Iasio, said: “Reshaping and rebadging vocational and technical qualifications is well intentioned but will not in itself address the barriers to more young people taking these subjects. Reform needs to be accompanied by a strategy to ensure that schools have the staffing and resources to deliver them, and a campaign to raise public awareness of vocational and technical routes.”

The general secretary of the National Education Union, Daniel Kebede, agreed. “These proposed changes will fall at the first hurdle unless there is sufficient investment in schools and the workforce,” he said.

The general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, Paul Whiteman, said: “In recent years, the content behind too many GCSEs became unwieldy and the over-reliance on final exams did not play to the strengths of all students.

“It will be crucial these pitfalls are avoided in developing these qualifications and that the government works closely with educators, local leaders and employers to ensure they offer high-quality learning which sets young people up for future training, education or employment.”

The government has also said it will launch a “national mission” by calling on employers to provide an additional 200,000 work experience placements to give young people exposure to the workplace by age 16. No 10 North will offer work experience for students aged 14 to 16 this academic year.

People claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”.

Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrapped after trials found limited evidence it changed behaviour.

While the proposals are billed by the Conservatives as a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job.

Under the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount to which they are entitled for six months, but after this point the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments.

This would have to happen for at least twice as long as the claimant period, meaning someone who has amassed two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC, before falling to the lower rate.

Set at 70% of the standard amount, this would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. For a couple aged 25 or over, under the plan they would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total.

Anyone placed on the reduced level would have their UC payments put on to a “back to work card”, which would block purchases of alcohol, tobacco and gambling, or cash withdrawals.

The plan would exclude those already in work – about a third of UC claimants have jobs – and those who are assessed as having what is called limited capability for work and work-related activity, because of a health condition or disability. Separate payments connected to housing or dependant children would be unaffected.

The Conservatives said the plan would affect about 350,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and save £538m a year.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the aim was to be “tough on those who exploit the system”, adding: “Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered.”

The party argues that in some countries such as Germany and the Netherlands, unemployment payments are contingent on sufficient contributions having been made and can be time-limited.

Those payments, however, are notably more generous and can be between 60% and 70% of someone’s previous monthly wage. There is also separate support for those who have not paid in sufficiently, with single people in Germany receiving about £480 a month.

Sara Ogilvie, the director of policy at Child Poverty Action Group, said: “The reality is that families are still paying the price of austerity cuts to our social security safety net. With living costs continuing to rise, these proposals are a fast track to increased poverty and are the last thing people need as they try to get back on their feet.”

Helen Barnard, the head of policy at Trussell, called the idea “deeply misguided”, saying UC already had strong conditions to ensure people seek work.

She said: “If you’re struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview, then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse.”

Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.

The prime minister, a committed Everton fan who still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.

The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, but police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.

Burnham has long opposed the ban, saying it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.

Asked by reporters on the plane to New York about lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.

“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.

The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.

A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.

“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”

A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”

Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.

Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.

How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 19:24:39 GMT

Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are pushing multiple false narratives

Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.

The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation.

Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago.

The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.

It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.

“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.

Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.

Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.

“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.

Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.

Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning.

It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.

The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.

It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals.

One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic.

The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.

Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.

Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.

Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.

The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.

One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News.

Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts

One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.

Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them.

He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.

“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.

AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.

The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.

The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 18:55:10 GMT

Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023

The international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at its Yemen office at serious risk.

The warning concluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham Al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.

The commission said weak governance meant staff at the Yemen office were not properly safeguarded in response to what it called a “live security concern”, and incidents of poor conduct by staff were not addressed.

The warning letter refers to “substantial policy breaches and a lack of accountability” at the office, and said local charity bosses failed to adequately assess and escalate complaints and reports made by whistleblowers.

An internal Save the Children investigation in 2024 after the death of Al-Hakimi found a “negative working culture” in the Yemen office had left staff “disillusioned and marginalised”.

It apologised to staff after admitting it had let them down by failing to properly appreciate the risks facing them amid the deteriorating security situation in the country.

In a statement to the Guardian, Save the Children International said that since 2024 it had made significant changes under new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve support for staff and rebuild trust. The charity has closed its north Yemen office because of security concerns.

It said despite its best efforts to understand the circumstances around Al-Hakimi’s detention and his death the challenges in Yemen meant it may never know what happened and why. Another Save the Children member of staff is understood to currently be in detention.

The commission’s warning comes amid a growing humanitarian crisis in Yemen, where the charity has been providing emergency medical help, shelter and drinking water to displaced families.

Official warnings are relatively rare, and are issued when the commission decides breaches of trust or mismanagement in a charity put its staff or beneficiaries at risk. They can be issued where charity trustees are deemed to have acted recklessly or without proper care.

The commission ordered Save the Children International to ensure sufficient resources are in place to safeguard and protect staff and other individuals working with the charity.

Stephen Roake, assistant director for high-risk compliance at the commission, said: “It can be incredibly difficult for charities operating in high-risk, volatile environments and we know that circumstances can change rapidly. However, it is for this very reason that trustees must ensure they have sufficient oversight of their overseas operations.”

In a statement, Save the Children International said it had accepted the commission’s findings of serious shortcomings in governance, management, oversight and compliance with policies and procedures in the Yemen office at the time.

Since 2024, it had installed new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve staff support and rebuild trust. It had also introduced detention risk assessments, taken steps to improve incident management procedures and strengthened crisis management.

It said: “We remain committed to learning from this tragedy and ensuring a safe, supportive environment for our colleagues.

“We will continue to work closely with the Charity Commission to address any outstanding matters, while continuing to support our colleagues in Yemen and deliver for children in extremely challenging contexts.”

Save the Children’s Yemen office warned last week that the country faced a “catastrophic humanitarian situation” as a result of escalating conflict, collapsing health services and outbreaks of disease.

More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced by fighting in recent weeks between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.

An RAF jet crashed and exploded moments after two pilots ejected during a training flight over Anglesey (Ynys Môn) in north Wales on Wednesday.

The aircraft, a Hawk T2, had just taken off from RAF Valley on the west of the island when the incident occurred, witnesses said.

Both pilots parachuted to the ground and were reportedly treated for minor injuries.

An RAF spokesperson said: “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time.”

The site of the crash, at Pencarnisiog, is less than two miles from the airbase. RAF Valley is home to the air force’s No 4 Flying Training School, which trains fighter pilots using Hawk T2 and Texan T1 aircraft.

A spokesperson for North Wales fire and rescue service said: “Crews and officers attended an incident involving an aircraft in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey, working alongside colleagues from Royal Air Force, North Wales police, Welsh ambulance service and Wales air ambulance. The fire is now under control.”

They added: “Members of the public are asked to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work safely.”

Due to the crash, local train lines were closed and replacement buses were running between Bangor and Holyhead.

Pete Bennett, a local resident, told Wales Live it appeared the plane was in trouble as soon as it left the runway. He said: “I knew straight away that it was in trouble. Right on takeoff there was an orange flame, and as it accelerated it was basically on fire.

“As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble. It climbed at an aggressive pitch – like the pilot was trying to gain altitude. It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear, loud bangs. It was probably at around 800ft at this point. The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened.”

He said the explosion caused a “huge wall of fire and black smoke”. He added: “The aircrew came down around halfway between the runway and where the plane crashed, which I’m guessing was around a mile inland from RAF Valley.”

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said in a post on X: “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.”

North Wales police said: “Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries.”

Alan Dale was in two minds as he gazed across at Portsmouth harbour in the late September sunshine and reflected on the latest show of force by far-right activists on the south coast against a supposed disembarkation of asylum seekers.

A stone’s throw away, masked followers of the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas had been cheered on Tuesday night by hundreds of people, many of them local, who had gathered after social media posts suggested authorities planned to land the migrants in the nearby town of Gosport.

The gathering had at least “sent a message”, said Dale, a retired Royal Navy veteran who echoed a common local sentiment that Gosport and Britain more widely had changed, and that migrants were being put “to the front of the queue” for public services.

“Is it going to be heard though? I don’t think so. It’s almost like the government is sticking its fingers in its ears and saying: ‘We are not listening to you.’”

As for the masked vigilantes who answered the call from Thomas – who calls himself “Danny Tommo” and was filmed earlier in the day using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard – Dale admitted to feeling uncomfortable about their face coverings, but insisted: “With any protest you are always going to get troublemakers.”

Many local people from a block of flats close to Gosport’s marina indeed appeared have swelled the numbers of those who turned up in what senior Reform UK figures, including the Hampshire MP and former home secretary Suella Braverman, had cheered on as a show of “people power”.

But a far-right presence – and hostility towards migrants – was discernible in the town in a part of England where organised activists from their ranks have been building links for a number of years with anti-migrant campaigns.

Most shockingly to outsiders unfamiliar with the depth of vitriol towards migrants among some here, children had been seen and heard chanting “let them drown” into a megaphone.

Red and white far-right posters emblazoned with the word “resistance” and slogans such as “protecting our children’s future” were plastered on lampposts around the bench where Dale sat in Gosport’s Falkland Gardens.

At least two outsiders were among the six people arrested on Tuesday night by police: a 19-year-old and a 36-year-old, both from Salisbury, who were detained on suspicion of aggravated trespass.

In the end, the small boat carrying 51 people docked in Dover, Kent, at about 12.30am on Wednesday after spending 33 hours at sea.

While there was no plan to land them in Gosport, Home Office sources have insisted, the events have once again placed Thomas in the spotlight – even as he faces the prospect of a police inquiry into his knife-wielding at sea – and saw a blurring of the lines between his activities and local protesters who were praised by Reform.

“It’s a depressing situation that so many people turned up but there is another side here as well and you have people in Portsmouth who are organising gigs to raise funds for the RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution],” said a local man who had worked with young people in the area where the protest took place but declined to give his name.

He also cited the fact that Gosport’s nearby Rowner area had been allocated money – as much as £20m – from the government’s Pride in Place initiative, a long-term strategic effort launched under Keir Starmer’s premiership to counter the electoral threat posed by rising nationalism and the far right in areas where such sentiment finds some sympathy.

A diversity of views could be found again on Wednesday morning among those gathered for a Bible study group inside Gosport’s Holy Trinity church, a short stroll from the seafront.

They included the retired priest Margaret Hay, who said the first thought that came to her mind was that Jesus was an immigrant too, while at least one other participant voiced discomfort that many of those crossing the Channel appeared to be men.

The group also included Tyler Palmer, a young churchgoer who watched the protests on Tuesday night from the edge of the crowd.

“We’ve always been diverse here in Gosport and it’s forgotten. Turkish sailors who fought alongside us in the second world war were housed here,” he said.

“But we’re also a naval town and people are very proud. They’re reading things that scare them – whether that’s GB News or fearmongering on social media.

“These are everyday people, your plumbers, your plasterers, who you wouldn’t expect to be at protests.”

Bentley launches first fully electric car – with fake engine sounds to replace classic growl

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 18:15:55 GMT

Torcal SUV can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge and is part of a £350m investment in the VW-owned carmaker’s UK business

Bentley is launching its first fully electric car – complete with a drum soundtrack to replace the growl of a combustion engine – as part of a £350m investment in its UK business.

The vehicle, an SUV called the Torcal, is Bentley’s cheapest, starting at £173,000, and will be built at its factory in Crewe, securing the jobs of the 4,000 workers there.

Bentley hopes to win over both EV refuseniks and younger customers with a new synthetic engine noise built from drum recordings based on its old eight-cylinder engines. The feature is designed to give “emotion to the car” and “bridge the gap” to new buyers, said Bentley’s chief executive, Frank-Steffen Walliser.

“We expect a younger clientele,” he added, pointing to a more muscular vehicle body shape than previous models and the comparatively low price, which gives “easier access” to the brand, whose cars can cost up to £1.7m for one-off vehicles built to be showstoppers for billionaires.

The Torcal launches into a thin market for fully electric luxury SUVs. Arch-rival Rolls-Royce’s only EV is a two-door coupe called the Spectre, which starts at about £330,000. The recently announced Range Rover Electric – considered part of the premium segment rather than luxury – begins retailing at £154,070.

It also marks a more tentative entry into the EV market than Bentley once predicted. In 2024, it was forced to abandon plans to launch new electric cars each year from 2025 to 2030, citing poor demand.

Walliser said that while early indications showed demand would be strong in the UK, Europe and the Middle East, he admitted: “We managers always say we know but to be honest we don’t know [how much demand there will be].”

There are “no plans at the moment” for a second EV launch, he added. “I revised so many long-term plans in the last 10 years that one has to be careful of it.”

It is the third big funding announcement in just over a week for Britain’s automotive sector. Nissan has said it will invest £170m to build a new model at its factory in Sunderland, while McLaren will spend £500m on a new factory, creating 1,000 jobs and its first SUV.

However, carmakers remain under significant pressure from US tariffs, competition from Chinese rivals and high industrial energy costs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it would cut 4,000 jobs, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”, while Bentley’s owner, Volkswagen, is cutting 100,000 jobs by 2030.

Asked if Bentley was immune from the cuts at VW, Walliser said: “Immune would be the wrong wording. But there’s a very simple rule in Volkswagen. If you’re successful you can run your business. And we consider we are a successful business … it doesn’t bother me too much at the moment.”

Bentley itself cut 245 jobs in Crewe earlier this year to reduce costs, and sales have fallen by a third since a 2022 peak of 15,200 cars. Walliser said a period of strong margins after the pandemic was a “post-Covid boom … now we are back to normal”.

Walliser said headcount in Crewe will not grow with the investment “for profitability reasons”, but he insisted that “the statement cannot be clearer” about investing in the UK and that the money will partly go towards a new assembly line.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said it was the “third win in just seven days for our world-class automotive industry, which truly shows the confidence that businesses have in Britain”.

But Walliser said the landscape remained “difficult” for Bentley suppliers. “We see a lot of impact on especially the smaller businesses,” he said, citing new EU rules of origin and high industrial energy prices both in the UK and Europe. “There’s a lot of pressure,” he said.

The Torcal can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge, and can power up from 10% full to 80% full in 20 minutes using an ultra-fast charger. The car marks the fourth model in Bentley’s lineup, alongside the Continental, Flying Spur and Bentayga.

It was put to Kane that it was a healing process. “It kind of is,” he replied. “But you have to heal while getting on with it. In football, you don’t have time. Before you know it’s the next one. “Our bowling has massive depth,” he says. “Ethan Bamber has had an outstanding year with 60 wickets, and then Chris Woakes has been around the majority of the season. Warwickshire, after starting the season as if they had a nail in their shoe with two wins from their first eight games, have stepped up when it mattered. With four wins from the last five matches – and the past two victories, against Essex and Glamorgan, notched up in two days – they have leapt over the 2025 champions, Nottinghamshire, and caused the usual heartbreak to Somerset.

After being ahead before the penultimate round, Somerset stumbled at Headingley last week, leaving Warwickshire 11 points clear. Win their last match, at home against the relegation-threatened Leicestershire, and they are champions. A draw with six bonus points would also get the job done.

Hannon-Dalby has more than played his part and, having spent the first four games of the summer on loan to Worcestershire, he now tops the Edgbaston averages with 27 wickets at 18.

“I’d never been on loan before. It wasn’t the way I would have designed my season but we have a really strong bowling attack and my opportunities were limited. To be able to get some overs in my legs in those early weeks of the season was brilliant and I’m really grateful to Worcestershire for taking me.

“I could have stayed at Edgbaston and played for [Warwickshire’s] second team but it is different to championship cricket. To know that I was playing, bowling well, contributing for Worcestershire, meant I was ready to hit the ground running.” And when Warwickshire recalled him, he did.

An unfancied Warwickshire last won the championship in Covid‑affected 2021, and went on to win the Bob Willis Trophy at Lord’s the same year, a match that dragged on until a properly autumnal 2 October. Hannon‑Dalby was injured for the second part of that season, supporting in the dressing room but desperate to get on the pitch.

“This time around is very exciting from a personal point of view, to be fully involved,” he says.

When this last batch of games started five weeks ago, we just wanted to give ourselves the chance to be in the hunt, and now we have destiny in our hands going into the last game.

“We’ve just got to bat and bowl and field well and if we can do all those things, well, hopefully … also, everyone is fit for the last game of the season, I’ve certainly been involved in campaigns when there are only one or two fit bowlers still standing.”

Hannon-Dalby is able to empathise with Leicestershire – he has experience of last-round blues. On the final day of the 2022 season he was bowling at the other end (one for 40) when Liam Norwell’s nine for 63 blew away Hampshire and saved Warwickshire from relegation.

And the coach knows the players from television. I actually know more of the Dutch players personally than Xavi does. Whether that’s an advantage, I don’t know, but it’s still a fact.”

In his public appearances Klopp has been on irrepressible form since taking the role in July. The task of whipping Germany back into shape has visibly and audibly topped up the energy levels that had drained by the time he departed Liverpool. Klopp, his wit sharp and appetite piqued, looks a far cry from the character who, to most trained eyes, was going through the motions upon his unveiling as Red Bull’s head of global soccer early last year.

Securing Klopp was a coup for the German football federation even if it came with a caveat, issued within seconds of his introduction to the media, that he would not be seen for dust if his family were hounded by the media. Xavi’s arrival in Amsterdam is no less fascinating even if, in the Dutch way, no bones were made by his employers about the fact Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot had been higher in their sights after Ronald Koeman’s departure. He is the Netherlands’ first foreign manager since Ernst Happel’s 10-month stint ended in 1978 but the fit is instinctively pleasing. Even if Guardiola was out of reach, they could land upon another product of the Johan Cruyff school that created modern-day Barcelona.

If Xavi is to take the Netherlands, occasionally exciting but frequently unstable during a World Cup run that shuddered to a halt in the last 32, back to their roots it will require a measure of patience. The pool of players does not allow much else; the recall of Borussia Dortmund’s Joey Veerman, who has not played international football for more than two years, speaks of the need for a technically adept midfield fulcrum but otherwise Xavi has scant scope for surprises. Virgil van Dijk will continue as captain despite considering international retirement during the summer; the head coach’s options may feel more complete when Frenkie de Jong and Donyell Malen have returned from injury.

Xavi has resisted any temptation to engage in analysis of the Netherlands’ performance in the United States. “I don’t talk about the past,” is the standard line, ironically an easier one to roll out if the Nations League opener in Amsterdam brings a performance redolent of headier times. The revolution may have to be conducted with minimal effusive pronouncements from the coach. It is certainly a less dramatic shake-up than the one Klopp, acting like a man licensed to break a few moulds, has enacted before the next fortnight’s four-game baptism.

It raised eyebrows when Klopp named a squad of 44 players for the matches against the Netherlands, Serbia and, home and away, Greece. The expanded unit will be split into two: half will play on Thursday and in Germany’s next game, at home against the Greeks, and the remainder will be involved in the second two games. Only Finn Dahmen, the Augsburg goalkeeper, will be required across the set.

“I want to get to know as many players as possible,” Klopp said. “There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.”

Club managers feeling squeamish at their players’ workloads during this expanded break will immediately have warmed to Klopp’s split selection. But the priority is to discover who best fits his vision for an intensely committed, front-footed, enthusiastic Nationalmannschaft that places round pegs, even unexpected ones, in round holes. Four players from Freiburg have made his sprawling selection; so has Felix Keidel from promoted Elversberg. Mika Baur of Celtic and the Hoffenheim winger Bambasé Conté were both stunned to receive first call-ups. The Brentford midfielder Vitaly Janelt joins his teammate Kevin Schade in the fray. Sixteen are uncapped.

The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 17:30:08 GMT

Andy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problem

In November 2020, Barack Obama warned of an “epistemological crisis” facing western democracies. Polarisation and radicalisation were corroding trust in established information sources. “If we do not have the capacity to distinguish what’s true from what’s false, then by definition the marketplace of ideas doesn’t work,” the former US president said.

That vulnerability has grown since then. Democracy’s enemies have become more determined to exploit it. This is the threat that Andy Burnham highlighted in a speech at the United Nations this week. The prime minister accused Russia of waging an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK’s information environment using bot armies and fake websites to spread falsehoods, interfere in elections, foment discord and poison inter-community relations.

The prime minister announced the creation of a National Centre for Information Defence to thwart campaigns of epistemological sabotage by hostile actors. It is an overdue enhancement of Britain’s civil defence capabilities.

Mr Burnham is right to highlight the threat, but he told only part of the story. The Kremlin would be wasting its money pumping out disinformation if large US tech platforms didn’t provide convenient channels for the toxin to spread, if there weren’t a complicit audience in Britain sharing the offending material and if the market for spreading pernicious propaganda weren’t so lucrative. Information warfare is only effective when it exploits structural vulnerabilities in the target society. Far-right material sowing hatred against migrants is most fruitful where the terrain has been fertilised by domestic politics.

Earlier this year, analysis by the Guardian found that more than half of accounts on X that were posting about racially aggravated riots in Belfast and civil disorder in Southampton were based outside the UK. Seven of the most-read tweets originated in the US, including one posted by X’s proprietor, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man.

Mr Musk has been assiduous in promoting a warped, dystopian idea of Britain as a failed state whose culture is being corroded by mass migration. His platform has been invaluable to far-right activists who have mustered gangs of masked men into mobs that obstruct roads, intimidate people and threaten asylum claimants at British ports. Last year, Mr Musk addressed a rally organised by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, where he called for the Labour government to be removed. Earlier this year, Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, travelled to Moscow on a trip funded by the Musk Foundation. He said the purpose of the trip was to “see the beauty of a civilised society”.

Mr Burnham did not address that side of the anti‑democracy equation in his speech, perhaps because he felt that it would be impolitic to impugn US big tech under the president’s nose. Mr Trump is also an originator and disseminator of falsehoods online, but the nature of transatlantic diplomacy prevents a UK prime minister confronting him with that record.

Under the circumstances, it made sense for Mr Burnham to concentrate his remarks on the threat from the Kremlin, but that must not signal the limit of his policy focus. British democracy is indeed under attack from Russia, but an effective campaign to build resilience has to recognise also the complicity of domestic extremists and the digital privileges they enjoy thanks to US technology companies.

The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 17:28:51 GMT

As the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challenges

The United Nations was created, its charter states, to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran, another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles.

The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking as he is in Washington to meet the US president. India’s Narendra Modi is not present; nor are Cyril Ramaphosa, Bola Tinubu or Abdel Fatah al-Sisi – the leaders of Africa’s three giants, South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt. While their reasons are various, the gaps speak collectively to Mr Trump’s wrecking capability and the broader challenges faced by the UN.

In a world where “cracks have become canyons”, to quote António Guterres, the body is more necessary than ever, and under greater strain. The outgoing secretary general has struggled with a “might is right” world: an authoritarian resurgence, the rising tide of conflict and a deadlocked security council. Mr Trump sought to supplant the UN with his “Board of Peace” for Gaza before largely losing interest. Even the biggest champions of multilateralism, such as Canada’s Mark Carney, are looking primarily to other mechanisms rather than UN reform.

With extremely limited powers, secretary generals usually fall into mediator or activist roles. Critics argue that Mr Guterres should have been more hands-on in diplomacy, in conflicts such as Sudan, as he was in brokering a Black Sea grain deal in 2022. But he has been a powerful voice of conscience: early to raise the threats posed by AI, passionate in calling for climate action and heartfelt on the suffering in Gaza, Ukraine and beyond. He has also kept the organisation on its feet – no mean feat given the disappearance of essential US funding (though Washington is now paying some of its debt).

The first female secretary general is long overdue and the informal regional rotation would suggest that a Latin American or Caribbean figure may succeed him; Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana have been frontrunners. But major powers may be biding their time, with serious contenders still to emerge. Observers think that there is a real possibility that a successor may not be agreed before Mr Guterres’s departure date of 31 December, underlining the UN’s challenges.

Yet it remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign – resulting in important action on issues from landmines to global heating and its consequences. And major powers will eventually have to recognise that the case for security council reform, stressed again by Mr Guterres, cannot be ignored for ever. The charter reminds us that the UN was born from the desperation engendered by two world wars rather than a utopian dream. It endures not because of glorious successes, nor because it has avoided glaring failures, but because a world without it would be far worse. The troubles it faces are all the more reason to defend it.

No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 17:26:00 GMT

Agreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believe

The Chagos Islands deal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president.

After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during a meeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea.

But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.”

The UK signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year.

Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the deal could not go ahead without US support.

“This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme. “So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.”

The US had supported the plan, but Trump changed his mind amid a wider deterioration of relations with Keir Starmer over the lack of UK support for the US attacks on Iran.

Speaking after their first in-person meeting at the UN in New York on Tuesday, Trump praised Burnham but gave no ground on his scepticism about the Chagos deal.

“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible,” Trump told reporters. “It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before, after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.”

Burnham later said he had “inherited the situation” and had told Trump “that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides”. He added: “It was clear that we need to come to that agreement, but I’m confident we can find it working with our US partners.”

Given Trump’s objections appear based on the core element of the deal – the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius – there appears to be no immediate way forward. The UK government has previously made clear that Washington’s approval is a prerequisite for the plan.

UK officials stress, however, that while Burnham inherited the impasse from Starmer, there is no intention to deprioritise a plan, begun under Rishi Sunak, that the government says is vital to ensure the future of the strategically vital Diego Garcia base, given Mauritian claims to sovereignty of the archipelago.

“It’s not back to the drawing board, as we do need to find a diplomatic solution to this,” another UK official said. “Everyone agrees something has to be done, which is why several prime ministers and even more foreign secretaries have tried to get it over the line.”

Streeting stressed the same point to the BBC, saying: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”

‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle East

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:40:44 GMT

‘I love going to the Middle East,’ says Ferrari driver

Qatar and Abu Dhabi races could still be cancelled

Lewis Hamilton said he hopes the Formula One season can still end at the two scheduled rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with the finale still in doubt because of the war in the Middle East.

Formula One is pressing ahead with its original plan, although a contingency is understood to be in place to host a final round in Imola if the volatile situation means both meetings have to be cancelled.

Speaking before this weekend’s grand prix in Azerbaijan, which borders Iran, Hamilton said he trusted the sport to make the right decision, given the unease among many in the paddock of racing in the region while the conflict continues.

“I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East,” he said. “From what I have read, things seem OK out there, but I don’t have all the information and I don’t know what the risk levels are. I trust in Stefano [Domenicali, F1’s chief executive] to make the right decision for the sport. And I do hope we get to go there.”

Whether the races take place or not could affect the world championship. Kimi Antonelli leads his Mercedes teammate George Russell by 81 points with nine meetings remaining. If that number was reduced to eight the Italian could close it out even sooner than might be expected. As things stand a lead of 100 points after Mexico, in five races time, or 75 after Brazill would suffice.

A decision is unlikely to be forthcoming until after Antonelli has the championship won, however, at the very least to keep the title fight alive as long as possible.

In March the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix were called off because of the ongoing US-Iran conflict. The Bahrain race has been moved to next weekend at Sepang in Malaysia and it is believed F1 must deliver at least 23 races to meet its commitments to broadcasters, meaning the cancellation of Qatar and Abu Dhabi would make a finale at Imola imperative.

The promoters of the races are bullish that they will go ahead but are always reluctant to cancel as they would still be liable for the race fee payable to F1. If the sport cancels, the fees do not have to be paid.

Abu Dhabi organisers have gone as far as confirming musical acts set to perform including Zara Larsson, the Script, Imagine Dragons and Lewis Capaldi. However, that the situation was far from settled was illustrated this week when Larsson said she would not be performing.

Responding to a post on social media asking her: “Please read about what UAE is doing to Sudan then cancel your Abu Dhabi show,” the Swedish singer posted: “I will not be going to Abu Dhabi.”

This was later deleted but Larsson did go on to confirm she would not perform at the meeting. “Maybe it came off as a impulsive response to a comment,” she said. “But I have spent some time thinking about everything and decided that to not do the show aligns with me the most right now, for many different personal reasons beyond politics.”

Stop the Ofsted inspections that are harming teachers

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:40:36 GMT

Readers on the new grading regime that is causing more stress and health issues for school staff than ever before

Your report (New Ofsted inspection regime is damaging our health, headteachers say, 21 September) reflects what those of us supporting school leaders are hearing. As a volunteer with Headrest, a school leader wellbeing helpline, I cannot discuss individual cases. I can, however, describe the disturbing patterns we encounter.

We have spoken to headteachers whom mental health professionals considered suicide risks following their experience of the Ofsted process. We have spoken to leaders whose physical or mental health has been seriously damaged by inspections. We have heard from headteachers who successfully navigated inspections but then chose early retirement rather than face that level of stress again.

We have also heard from school leaders facing serious personal circumstances who have sought inspection deferrals and had their requests refused. Whatever the administrative requirements of an inspection system, there must surely be circumstances in which compassion and humanity take precedence over process.

These are not arguments against inspection. Schools must be accountable and children must be safeguarded. However, accountability without humanity serves neither school leaders nor the children whose education depends on them.

The death of Ruth Perry should have represented a watershed. The coroner concluded that an Ofsted inspection contributed to her suicide. Yet we continue to hear accounts that should be unacceptable to every politician and education policymaker.

Nobody should wait for another tragedy before asking whether the system has genuinely changed enough. Accountability is necessary. An inspection system that places those leading our schools at avoidable risk is not. Pete CrockettRoyal Wootton Bassett, Wiltshire

School leaders are sounding the alarm about the mental health impact of the new Ofsted regime. As a researcher on accountability in the education sector, I have contributed to the parliamentary consultation on the work of Ofsted, and the evidence on the impact of poor Ofsted outcomes on teachers’ careers is overwhelming.

Although the new framework was designed to create greater nuance, it has not dealt with the underlying issues of validity: do inspection outcomes accurately reflect the quality of education? England has arguably the most stringent school-inspection regime in the world, yet little attention has been given to how well the system works. The lack of serious empirical scrutiny that Ofsted has come under is at odds with the power it wields. To make Ofsted truly fit for purpose, we need hard evidence on basic questions such as whether children gain more from enrolling at a school that is highly rated by inspectors. Dr Iftikhar HussainUniversity of Sussex

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is proposing major changes to the education system. To achieve these, she needs the support of school leaders. There would be no better way to help secure that support than by agreeing to re-examine the Ofsted regime. It has lost the confidence of leaders in its overall direction and management, in its detailed operating procedures and, in particular, its ability to inspect schools without causing undue harm to the health and wellbeing of headteachers and staff.

The education secretary should welcome the National Association of Head Teachers’ proposals as a first step to reforming a deeply flawed inspection regime, but needs to go much further. Colin Richards and Frank NorrisFormer HM inspectors of schools

It’s a sad and shocking indictment of our school-inspection system when an article about Ofsted ends with the Samaritans’ phone number. Toby WoodPeterborough

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline. org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org

The failure of many to speak out against the rise of nazism in Germany and against fascists in Italy during the 1930s certainly allowed a fatal normalisation of dictatorial fascism. Let us not allow the same thing to happen again. We artists have a positive duty to speak out. David ParryAntingham, Norfolk

Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:25:57 GMT

The biggest flotation in five years was a bit of a shoo-in. Let’s see what happens when overseas competition is tougher

Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years

A win is a win, but we should probably contain our excitement about the biggest flotation in London for five years. Airtel Money, a payments processor that operates in 13 African countries and should be worth between £6bn and £7bn, is a welcome addition to the stock market but it would be a stretch to say the event marks a definitive change in the weather to end the listings drought.

Why? Because, in a sense, Airtel Money is already here. It is a 78%-owned subsidiary of Airtel Africa, an established FTSE 100 firm with a market value of £11.3bn ultimately controlled by Bharti Enterprises under the Indian billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal, also known for his 25% stake in BT.

That means this was a home fixture for London in the competition with other venues. The Airtel/Bharti collective still had a look at the Middle East, the US and the rest of Europe, we’re told, but London will have started as a heavy favourite. It is simply easier to spin off a subsidiary on a market where the parent is already known – and, indeed, a market where Airtel Africa was a top-performing Footsie stock last year.

Ian Ferrao, the chief executive of Airtel Money, still made all the right noises to please exchange officials. London got the nod on account of its deep capital pools plus investors’ enthusiasm for fintech firms and their general understanding of African companies, he said. All true, but it’s also the case that it would have been simply odd to list Airtel Money on a different market to Airtel Africa.

The latter is likely to remain the largest shareholder for years yet, and the two businesses are closely linked operationally. Airtel Money has grown out of Airtel Africa’s telecoms business, and one of its key growth opportunities is to persuade even more of the telephony customers to join the payments service. There are 75 million potential recruits to go at, on top of the established 53 million monthly active users, so there is a decent story to tell.

It is one reason why the listing should go well, assuming the wider stock market environment remains calm. Airtel Money is capital-lite, converts a chunky proportion of its earnings into cash, carries the buzzy fintech vibe and is growing at about 20% a year. The cash-generative qualities mean no new equity is being raised, so it is really an opportunity for existing shareholders – including minority owners including TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding – to cash in a few chips. As long as they don’t get greedy on price, it looks a relatively easy pitch for the promoters.

For London, the listings game is really about winning a few high-profile names where the competition from overseas markets is tougher. The biggie remains Norway’s Visma, one of Europe’s biggest software companies. A listing was delayed earlier this year because of the so-called “Claude crash” – the sell-off in data-related sectors deemed to be under threat from AI tools – but private equity-backed Visma remains a top target given its valuation a year ago was put at almost €20bn (£17.2bn).
