‘And you will be the People’s Earl’ – Charles Spencer’s Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, digested by John Crace

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:18:22 GMT

The earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbs

Cheers were heard up and down the land. Halley’s comet made an unscheduled appearance in the ethereal night sky. In very heaven, angelic choirs rang out. A saviour had been born. A light to lighten the world. But enough about me. For this paragraph at least.

In my universally acclaimed funeral address, I aimed to speak for my sister. The real Diana. For only I truly knew her. She had the heart of a lion. And I had a glut of cliches. Yet when Diana had swept so triumphantly into the arena of royal life, I was but a callow youth awash with hormones and gripped by the self-centredness of adolescence. Nothing much has changed. Yet I know, with all my heart, that Diana would have wanted me to tell our story.

Why now, you may ask? The answer is simple. I could do with the money. And with the 30th anniversary of the most tragic death in human history approaching, I wanted to get in before someone like Amol Rajan did.

Quite simply, the Diana I knew is not the Diana that has been portrayed up till now. We have been told she had an unhappy childhood. But let me say, we were both the secure recipients of parental love.

Never were we more content than when our parents separated. Or when we were carted off to boarding schools that thrived on neglect. And we adored the way our father was miserable for so much of our lives, his latter years made still more miserable by marrying the venomous Raine.

Back to me. I was in Cape Town when I heard Diana had died. At first I could not comprehend what had happened. I was stunned, watching the TV as the story unfurled.

The initial reports had been more hopeful. She was merely slightly injured. My lips curled as the commentators implied that she had got what she deserved for betraying the royal family.

Then, when her death was announced, they had to change their tone. That will teach the media to be mean about my sister, I thought. My lips grimly broke into a grim smile.

Quick pause as I go into yet more unimaginably dull guff about our privileged childhood and how we were always happy except when we weren’t. Then to remember how Prince Charles had sounded so giddily elated when he had phoned me to offer his congratulations. “Get in there,” he had said. “Finally I can be left in peace with my top bit on the side.”

With that, the cold finality of death struck home. Never again would my heart soar at seeing my beloved Diana alive again. On the plane back to London, my thoughts turned to her eulogy. We would need someone utterly brilliant. Someone who could capture the vibrant essence of Diana and represent her true blood family. One of far more noble lineage than the House of Windsor.

With that, I realised it could only be me who could be entrusted with such a solemn duty. And I would do a lot better than Norman St John-Stevas, who had ruined my father’s service with his crass middle-class antics.

Time now for a digression into some pointless filler about the Spencer family history. How for many centuries we had fulfilled our duty of opening fetes and losing money because working for a living was beneath us. How Diana and I had once gone swimming with Prince Andrew. Even then he had been even more stupid than the average member of the royal family, and I remember thinking that one day he would get into trouble for hanging around with a paedophile.

Such carefree lives we all led back then. Apart from the eating disorders and the other undiagnosed mental health conditions. Little did I know that Diana’s life would be ended by a tabloid press. The paparazzi who chased her down the Alma tunnel were all wearing Piers Morgan masks. How ironic that Diana, the goddess of hunting, should be the most hunted woman on the planet. By the way, that’s a line you might recall I wrote in my superb oration. Genius, isn’t it?

I’m not sure who nominated me point man for liaising with the royal family – I’m guessing it might have been me. I recall other disturbing conversations with the prince. “You’re so lucky your dad has died,” he confided. “I wish my mum would. They just treat me like a child. I even have a footman to lay out my electric train set each morning. I’d love to do it for myself.” I cut short the conversation, my mind once more returning to the magnificence of the eulogy I was shortly to deliver to a stunned world.

But the pressure from the palace was relentless. Time and again we were told that the Spencers had always been too common for the Windsors. The funeral arrangements soon took on a darker, more sombre tone.

“William and Harry must walk behind Diana’s coffin,” Colonel Ross insisted. That wasn’t going to happen, I firmly replied, firmly. “I think you will find it will,” Ross snapped menacingly with menace. The Prince of Wales needs a human shield in case people heckle him. One of my happiest memories of the funeral procession was a lone piper in the crowd playing the ancient lament, “Who’s that wanker in the crown?”

“Don’t worry too much,” said Prince Charles. “Everyone will have forgotten about her soon enough.” I couldn’t believe my ears.

“No one will ever forget Diana,” I tartly snapped, tartly.

“Diana who?”

All such a long way from the fairytale that had begun in 1980. Then the country had been in thrall to the fact that the future Earl Spencer was about to become brother-in-law to the next king of England. Diana, though, was already a broken butterfly, crushed by a man who had told her he would never love her but would marry her because he couldn’t really get out of it. “Thing is,” he said. “Not only do I adore Camilla with all my heart but you’re actually a bit podgy.” How I wish I had been there to say: “You’re no oil painting yourself, sausage fingers.”

Diana later told me she had sobbed, sobbingly to my father that she could never marry a man who didn’t love her. But my father wouldn’t countenance such a thing. The Spencers always do their duty dutifully. Till death us do part.

And so the inevitable train of events that would lead to her death were put in train. She was to be the royal family’s sacrifice to an insatiably, ravenous tabloid press who would not relent until she lay dying in the back of a car in Paris.

“Oh Carlos,” Diana said to me.

“Oh Duch,” I replied, replyingly

“Oh Carlos.”

“Oh Duch.”

I find it almost too unbearably unbearable to recall some of the all too fleeting moments we had together. Though I sincerely believe that Diana was always at her happiest when she was with me. And we were so in tune with each other that silently we often didn’t need to talk.

Only once did I try to dissuade her from getting a divorce, but she quickly shut me up. I like to think that Diana, like me, would be on to her fourth marriage by now, had she lived. Then we could have had a good old moan about our exes. And how expensive they are.

Now we get to the most solemn moment of the entire book. I find it incredible that no one in all these years has stopped to enquire how I felt when making the most celebrated eulogy in the history of mankind. Do I not count for something?

Only Tony Blair fleetingly acknowledged the nation’s debt of gratitude to me. “Diana will always be the People’s Princess.” He paused, for effect. Clearly he had learned from my oratorical oratory. “And you will be the People’s Earl.”

My years as a journalist for NBC filing meaningless stories that no one had ever watched was the perfect training for someone about to write a eulogy to end all eulogies. Have I mentioned that I was writing the eulogy?

Once I was satisfied that I had achieved perfection, a car drove me to the chapel where Diana’s coffin was resting. It was almost as if she was tired of life. There I read her my eulogy. And at that moment, the sun shone through the stained glass and crowds bowed down in the streets, and from the coffin came Diana’s disembodied voice: “You’re a leg, Carlos.”

The funeral passed almost in a daze. I remember Elton John singing Candle in the Wind and thinking: “Who is this idiot who has been brought in as my warm-up act?” After all, this was a day for me as much as for her. As for the eulogy? Let’s just say that the whole world bowed down to remember both me and Diana. Though let’s be clear, I was doing this for William and Harry. In the same way that this book is dedicated to them too.

And so we come to the end of this book. Who knows what lies ahead for me? More divorces probably. But I can face the world knowing I have done right by my sister. Her memory will live for ever. Who knows what she might have become? The first lady of the US? Nelson Mandela’s wife? But at least she can rest in peace knowing that in death, at least, she had my eulogy. The eulogy which is mine.

AAAGH. MAKE THIS STOP.

Itauma is a complex character and Hrgovic suggested that doubts remain about his mentality. “We’ll see. It was a big shock for him, a big humiliation, so maybe it’s the end of his career if he’s not mentally tough.

Something in your eye? Here’s how to get it out – without making it worse

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:00:53 GMT

It’s natural to want to soothe eye irritation, but mishandling could lead to more problems, experts warn. We asked them for advice on how to deal with it properly

It may feel like a gritty, annoying sensation, or a sharp pain. Either way, you may have the same problem: something is stuck in your eye and needs to come out.

Addressing the situation incorrectly can lead to bigger issues such as infection, scarring, an ulcer or corneal scratches, which are abrasions on the clear covering of your eye. Ignoring the dilemma can lead to similar consequences.

Experts explain how to handle this predicament, when it’s time to see a medical professional, and some of the most common mistakes.

As innocuous as they may seem, eyelashes are some of the most common foreign bodies to get stuck in eyes. If an eyelash ends up under an eyelid, it can be quite painful, explained Dr Douglas Lazzaro, an ophthalmologist and professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Other common examples Lazzaro encounters include dust and other small debris kicked up on a windy day and glue from attaching false eyelashes. Those working in construction may encounter flecks of industrial materials such as fiberglass, metal and wood.

Contact lenses are another frequent culprit, he said. These can roll up and hide under the upper eyelid, break in the eye, or may be forgotten and not removed before another is put in.

The feeling of having something in your eye can depend on the object, but general symptoms include burning and irritation, blurred vision, a scratchy feeling or sensitivity to bright lights.

For some small objects, like eyelashes, sand or mascara flecks, blinking and your own tears are often all you need to get them out.

But if that doesn’t work, you may need to do more. Wash your hands first and work in a well-lit area. Lazzaro recommends carefully examining your eye to locate whatever may be stuck. This may include gently pulling down your lower eyelid with clean fingers, or using a cotton-tipped swab to slowly lift your upper lid.

If the object is small and not penetrating your eye, blinking and irrigating the eye with artificial tears may flush the object out. If irrigation doesn’t work, then it’s likely best to seek professional attention, said Lazzaro.

If a foreign liquid gets in your eye – such as detergents and disinfectants – you’ll want to act quickly, said Dr Keith Baratz, an ophthalmologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. He recommends rinsing your eye with tap water as soon as possible.

A general rule of thumb is that liquids with a high pH (for example, bleach, ammonia and most drain cleaners) are more damaging than those with a low pH – but you should hasten to rinse your eyes with tap water regardless.

“Speed is the important thing,” said Baratz. “You want to do it right away, not wait a half hour while you drive to the emergency room.”

After you rinse the eye, you should then go to the emergency room, said Dr Avnish Deobhakta, an ophthalmologist at the New York Eye and Ear Infirmary of Mount Sinai.

“There can still be ongoing damage even if you flushed it,” he said.

Experts’ advice falls into two categories. On some occasions, you should go to the doctor to remove something from your eye. There are also times when you should go even if you have been able to remove the object.

A common mistake is assuming that something in the eye will come out on its own, said Lazzaro. According to the Mayo Clinic, avoid removing anything embedded in the eye or sticking out between the lids. Doctors have tools that make the process easier: numbing drops, magnifying devices (for instance, a slit lamp microscope) and sterile tools such as forceps or needles, which are used to dislodge particles. You should not use these tools at home, said Lazzaro.

But let’s say you removed the object and your eye still hurts. For the first 24 hours, you can continue to irrigate the eye with artificial tears, Lazzaro said. Cold compresses can also make the eye feel a little better, but don’t provide any healing benefits.

after newsletter promotion

If irrigating your eye doesn’t work, and you still have “something that’s bothering you, causing vision problems, or is hard to reach”, then you “really do need to seek professional care”, said Deobhakta.

Generally, the rule is that if you don’t feel better within 24 hours – there’s still inflammation, redness, tearing or vision changes – then you should seek medical attention, said Lazzaro.

It’s possible that, when removing the object, either you caused harm or injury had already been inflicted by the object, explained Deobhakta. Another likelihood is that the injury exposed the eye to infection. A doctor can examine the wound and provide the correct aftercare, he said.

Medical care can help you avoid more than just pain; even if the foreign matter is removed, there can still be downstream effects, Lazzaro said. For example, a removed piece of wood or vegetable matter could leave behind a fungal infection. Or if a piece of metal is on the eye, rust can accumulate and become stuck to the cornea. If left untreated, this can lead to infection and scarring that can affect vision. Doctors have special instruments that brush away rust, and can follow up with an antibiotic treatment, said Lazzaro.

Rubbing the eye is heavily discouraged, said Lazzaro. If the object is still in your eye, you can “actually rub it further into your cornea”, he said. Rubbing can introduce bacteria from your hands into the eye and can also increase inflammation.

People should not use metal tools at home, like tweezers, to remove something from the eye. This can cause further injury.

“One of the worst-case scenarios is that the individual goes to a mirror and tries to pick at the foreign object with a toothpick or tweezers,” said Deobhakta.

You also don’t want to try to use your fingers to pick something out of your eye, said Baratz, adding that “this is the number one mistake we see”.

Culprits often include people who wear contact lenses and, in turn, are used to touching their eyes, he explains. But using your fingers can increase the risk of infection and injury.

Patients who wear contact lenses also tend to leave their contacts in, even if something is irritating their eyes. Another tendency is to put contacts back in immediately after an eye injury, sid Deobhakta.

“Do not put a contact lens on an eye that is already sore,” he advises. “If it’s getting better and you feel OK, use lubricating drops and wear your glasses.”

Generally, people can underestimate the inherent danger some activities pose to their eyes, said Deobhakta. He has seen patients use their glasses instead of safety goggles during a debris-causing activity such as mowing the lawn. In this case, grass can still fly up under the glasses into the eye, or a rock could hit and break the glasses, causing injury.

“Be mindful of what you’re doing, react quickly, and don’t do something silly like trying to fix the problem yourself when something does go wrong,” he says.

Prem agrees to revamp refereeing in boost for England’s Rugby World Cup hopes

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 16:00:52 GMT

League agrees new interpretations to help Borthwick

Scrum and breakdown targeted as areas of inconsistency

Steve Borthwick has secured a boost to his preparations for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes in Australia.

The Guardian understands that in the formal absence of relegation from the Prem for the first time this season, agreement has been reached over a number of law interpretations that will better align officiating in club matches with the international game.

The areas that will be policed differently include the offside line as well as the scrum – specifically the brake-foot law – as England’s head coach seeks to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia next year. Borthwick has also previously lamented how differently the breakdown is refereed in the Prem – in which there tends to be less of a contest – than the international stage. Indeed, the breakdown was a frequent problem during England’s miserable Six Nations campaign, while the four-Test series between South Africa and New Zealand over the summer highlighted the ferocity with which elite nations are contesting that area of the game.

It is understood that Borthwick met the directors of rugby last month and a presentation was given by the Rugby Football Union’s refereeing team on the intended law interpretations. England’s scrum has markedly improved since the appointment of Borthwick, under the guidance of the assistant coach Tom Harrison.

Borthwick, however, will be mindful of how dominant South Africa, who have won the past two World Cup tournaments, are in that facet of the game and how influential it was in their series win against New Zealand.

Interestingly it was Karl Dickson, one of the RFU’s professional officials, who twice penalised the All Blacks hooker Codie Taylor for brake‑foot infringements in the fourth Test in Baltimore. The brake-foot law was introduced in 2022 as a safety measure and requires the hooker to position one foot forward before engagement at the scrum. The New Zealand assistant coach Neil Barnes said afterwards that it is a law “which no one really gives a shit about, but the referees are concentrating on”.

In February it was announced that the coming season, which begins on Friday with Northampton hosting Newcastle and Harlequins facing Bath, would be the first in which the Prem is formally a closed league. It is understood that the absence of the jeopardy of relegation has been a significant factor in allowing for the aligned law interpretations.

Sleep payments: could they lead to better rest – and better health?

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:59:22 GMT

We all need a good night’s rest, but regular, sufficient sleep is hard for many of us to come by. Students in Pittsburgh have been offered a novel incentive

Name: Sleep payments.

Age: A new strategy for an age-old problem.

Appearance: Nice work if you can get it.

Paying people to sleep? I’m in. The idea is not without precedent – there is such a job as a professional sleeper, for research purposes.

Sounds good. Where do I sign up? A new study has taken a slightly different approach: they rewarded students with money whenever they managed more than seven hours’ sleep.

What kind of students? University of Pittsburgh undergraduates, with an average age of 19.

How much money? Not a lot – about five bucks (£3.76) each time.

Why would they do that? To see what happens.

And what happened? The students who received the money got on average 19 more minutes of sleep per school night than the ones who didn’t.

I’m no research scientist, but 19 minutes doesn’t sound like five dollars worth of sleep to me. It’s enough that those students hit the seven-hour target – considered to be an optimal amount – on 26% more nights.

Does that really make a difference? The rewarded students also saw an improvement in their marks – their GPA rose by an average of 0.08 points.

I don’t even know what GPA stands for. It stands for grade point average – imagine a scale where an A equals 4, a B is 3, and …

No maths, please. What you’re saying is, academic improvement was modest but significant. It was even more marked among first-year students.

And all it took was money? The students were also given sleep trackers that issued bedtime reminders and morning feedback, but without the monetary incentive, these had little effect.

While I like the idea of cash as a form of therapy, I worry it could get expensive in the long run. Interestingly, some of the effects of the incentive persisted: students still slept an additional eight minutes on average in the weeks after the money stopped, and their grades remained higher through the following semester.

How has news of this intriguing study been received by the British public? “Great preparation for the UK benefits life,” read one comment under the MailOnline article on the subject.

Honestly, that sounds like a wilful misreading of the study’s aims and its … “Great training for the next generation,” read a comment under a similar Times article. “Get paid $ for doing nothing.”

Do say: “Modest incentives may improve sleep and improved sleep can improve performance.”

Don’t say: “I’m going to a nightclub, so I’ll be needing this week’s sleep money upfront.”

Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:56:14 GMT

Sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in case involving former TV production assistant Miriam Haley

Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment.

Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement.

In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image.

Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration.

New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes.

Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said.

Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions including blood cancer and heart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence.

Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry.

“You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.”

The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case.

Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann.

But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case.

Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley.

Jurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial.

Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate California rape case.

In June, a California appeals court upheld Weinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival.

He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently.

The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.

Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:30:52 GMT

It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump

Donald Trump’s speech on Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UN charter’s emphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address.

For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”

But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influence negotiations where he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice.

He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime.

In July, he already vowed to destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself a threat to commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russian military commanders for doing precisely that in Ukraine.

Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal.

He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated a deal to constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trump ripped it up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran far closer to a nuclear weapon than ever before.

Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls now predict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that he belittles.

Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, although hundreds remain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting his might-makes-right beliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.”

He noted the new agreement on Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member.

He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there is no real war, only a rhetorical one.

Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguably crimes against humanity.

Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may be why Trump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”.

It has been reported that Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’s statute.

Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated.

He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise the death toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues to kill Palestinians and block needed supplies, while Hamas has not disarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”.

Indeed, the Trump administration has rejected a leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny this reality.

He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues to occupy large swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’s mineral riches to the western market.

He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but to hand over additional chunks of its territory as well.

Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormous risks posed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.”

This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”.

Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

Eric Idle has had tons of celebrities staying at his house. God, it must be exhausting

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:08:50 GMT

Whether it’s an A-lister or an old schoolfriend emerging blearily from the spare room, those first moments of the day are tricky

First thing in the morning, that’s the hardest time. Eric Idle told me this. A wise man, is Eric. Actor, comedian, songwriter, musician, screenwriter and playwright and, when it comes to mornings, a man of wisdom.

I interviewed him about his new book, which is a love letter to his house in Provence. He bought it more than half a century ago, before he hit the big time. It didn’t cost him much, because it was tiny, tumbledown and without water or electricity. Slowly, as the money came in from this job or that, he made improvements. By hook or by crook, the water and electricity started to flow, and with them a steady stream of guests coming to stay. These weren’t just any old guests: they were superstars, among them David Bowie, Art Garfunkel, Penny Marshall, Lauren Hutton, Brian Cox (the professor and the actor too, I think, although possibly not at the same time), Paul Simon, Carrie Fisher, Robin Williams and George Harrison. Also Michael Palin and assorted Pythons; Ronnie Wood and assorted Stones. And so on. There are photos of Wood sitting on the floor strumming his guitar; Bowie mooning about clad only in short shorts. Quite something, but all I could think about was how tiring it must have been to have so many guests turning up all the time. Let’s be honest: guests are a bit of an effort. A-lister or Joe Bloggs, a guest’s a guest.

This isn’t an issue raised in the book, which I should say is a moving, elegiac affair, and not just a torrent of name-drops as I’ve rather implied. But the guest question nagged away at me until I plucked up the courage to interrogate Mr Idle on the matter. Who was the best guest? Who was the worst? And what did he do if they were getting on his wick? After all, since they’d gone all that way, he could hardly turf them out.

Sensibly, Eric wouldn’t be drawn on any of these questions, although much as he plainly loved them being there, he did tacitly admit that having guests in your space – even guests of this calibre – does have its challenges, and that it’s the mornings that are hardest.

He’s dead right. It doesn’t matter who it is emerging blearily from the spare room. Be it Bowie, Fisher or an old schoolfriend, those first moments of the day are tricky. When you’re a kid, a teenager, a student, sleepovers happen all the time, and they’re kind of normal, so you know the drill. But as you get older, they happen less and less. I have close friends who I’ve known since primary school, but I can’t remember the last time we had a sleepover – a word we obviously no longer use now we’re middle-aged. However well you know your guest – or, in Eric’s case, however well the world knows your guest – you’re unlikely to have spent much time with them straight after they’ve got out of bed. And in this phase of the day, we’re all different animals.

Morning. Oh, hi. Morning. What’s for breakfast? Awkwardness, that’s what’s for breakfast. Tea? Coffee? Toast? Can I get you an, erm, egg? Cereal? Oh, right, granola. I’ll have a look. Skimmed? No, sorry, no skimmed. Decaf? Sorry, no. Earl Grey? Hang on, I’ll check. Er, no, sorry. Silences of various lengths punctuate what passes for conversation. Sleep OK? Good. Silence. Clink of cutlery. Slurp of tea. Silence. An embarrassed request. What? No toilet paper in the loo? How embarrassing! So sorry. I’ve left some on the stairs. Then there’s another silence while whoever it was who lacked the toilet paper waits for a little time to pass before sloping off for a poo. Awkward, awkward, awkward.

All are welcome at mine, but don’t mind me if I slip out and take the dog for a walk first thing, leaving you enough time to sort yourselves out.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Bats originated in Europe, rewriting mammals’ family tree, study reveals

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 15:00:52 GMT

Biggest study of its kind provides insights into bats’ evolution – a potential gamechanger for research into treating viruses and cancer in humans

In the northern forests of the Congo-Brazzaville, as the sun slips away, a distinctive honking fills the dusky sky. Every evening, thousands of hammer-headed fruit bats depart their daytime roosts in search of mates, calling out through large, box-shaped snouts that give the flying mammals the appearance of a winged moose. Here, along the Congo River, scientists have been collecting DNA swabs and tissue samples from the bats for years, working deep into the night in spacesuit-like protective gear.

Those hard-won samples are now among the thousands of specimens gathered from bats across the world that have helped to reshape what we know about the bat family tree.

In a landmark study published today in the journal Nature, a team of more than 130 international researchers combed through ancient bat fossils and genomic data from living species to establish that bats likely originated in Europe about 65m years ago – not in Africa, Asia or North America, as had previously been thought.

Rather, it seems that the earliest ancestors of modern bats dispersed from Europe into Africa, then expanded onwards to Asia, the Americas and Australia. The findings also reveal that echolocation, like flight, also evolved near the dawn of bat evolution.

“Bats, on a scale of amazing to amazing, they’re super amazing,” said Sarah Olson, one of the study’s authors and director of health research at the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Society. “It’s fun to have part of that puzzle piece in the block, and then we can keep finding and adding other puzzle pieces to it now.”

The work is part of a larger global effort known as Bat1K, launched in 2017, which seeks to sequence the genomes of all the living 1,500 bat species – the second most diverse mammal species in the world, and accounting for one-fifth of all mammals. Genomes are an organism’s complete set of genetic constructions, containing all the DNA needed to build, grow and live.

The Nature study ultimately drew on 103 bat genomes from 21 bat families, alongside 44 fossil bats – mostly their teeth – unearthed across the globe.

Olson said their findings lay the groundwork for better understanding bat physiology and, critically, how the mammals have evolved to be so resistant to disease. Bats are often identified as reservoirs of fatal zoonotic viruses, including Ebola, Nipah and Marburg – but the bats don’t get sick themselves.

“How are they living with these viruses that, when they get into us, they cause so much damage?” Olson said. “What we have now is a kind-of code book of life.”

A 2025 study based on the Bat1K genomic work found that early bat ancestors seemed to have excessive immune gene adaptations. “We showed for the first time that these adaptations associated with viral tolerance and disease resistance probably evolved at the same time that all bats evolved,” said the evolutionary biologist Ariadna Morales, who worked on both studies.

Bats are also unique among mammals in that they live exceptionally long for their size, showing few signs of ageing or cancers. Now, scientists say they will be able to investigate the genes driving those traits. What they learn could be a gamechanger for research into human ageing, immunity and disease resistance.

“With the genetic information that we can find in bats, it could be used to develop therapeutics associated with zoonotic disease. And they could also be models to develop treatments for cancer,” Morales said.

Olson added that the research can also strengthen our understanding of “what makes a healthy bat a healthy bat, and what are bats going to be susceptible to?”

About half of the known bat species have unknown or decreasing populations, with 18% of species considered threatened by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature.

Bats are at risk from the climate crisis, habitat loss, and bat persecution and harvesting, said study co-author Liliana Dávalos, a conservation biologist at Stony Brook University in New York. At the same time, bats play an important role in ecosystems, helping to pollinate plants, spread seeds, and keeping insect numbers – particularly mosquitoes, another spreader of disease – in check.

“Unlike most small mammals, all but one bat species have very small litters of one or two pups, so when individuals drop dead from scorching temperatures, or get killed through persecution or harvesting, populations cannot quickly recover their numbers,” Dávalos said.

And while bats have shown resilience to Ebola and Marburg, in Canada and the United States bats have perished by the millions from a fungal pathogen called white nose syndrome, which grows on the skin of hibernating bats.

“This research can help us go back and look at what makes the myotis bat species more susceptible to these fungal diseases,” Olson said. “There may be some interesting findings that other researchers can take from this study … to go back and piece together what’s happening with white nose syndrome.”

‘Watermelons’: Zack Polanski and the rise of the ‘green outside, red inside’ eco-populists

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 13:52:20 GMT

Author Russell Warfield argues the Green leader’s brand of politics is not new but has evolved in the party over time

Watermelons: the term used to describe the members of the Green party of England and Wales who are green on the outside and red on the inside. People in this faction are environmentalists but bleed socialist ideologies.

Of the roughly 160,000 people who have flocked to the party since Zack Polanski became leader last year, most are thought to be in this camp, drawn to a political space on the left that they see as vacated by the Labour party.

But the author of a new book – The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future – says this flavour of Green is nothing new. “What you’ve got to understand is that the party has been watermelon for at least 10 years,” says Russell Warfield, a former party staffer who has worked on election campaigns, including Polanski’s.

“There’s often this dichotomy presented that there’s this ‘real core’ Green party who are these ecologists who really just care about conservation of the environment, then there’s this new cohort of hard leftists,” Warfield says. “Actually, this has been both an organic process but also one which reaches much more deeply into the past of the party, where a lot of the fundamental positions of the party can be traced back to the early 1970s.”

His book unpacks the history of the party to explain how Polanski fits into it, arguing that the leader and his “eco-populist” package is not a departure from Green tradition but the culmination of a 50-year evolution that has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left.

Not everyone agrees. During the leadership contest between Polanski and co-runners Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns in 2025, a senior Green source described Polanski’s rise as a “hostile takeover”. Even Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ first MP and a former party leader, has said, when pressed, that she would love him to talk about the environment more.

“It’s just obvious nonsense,” Warfield says of the hostile takeover comment. “Look at the mandate, it was 85%,” Polanski’s landslide leadership win. “He won across every wing of the party.”

But how green are the Greens? Since Polanski took over, he has been splashed across newspapers and TV screens discussing subjects ranging from Gaza to wealth taxes – progressive politics, but not necessarily or overtly green.

Warfield responds with a statistic: 34% of voters trust the Greens more than any other party on the environment, according to YouGov polling – the highest level of trust recorded for any party on any issue. “There is not a voter in this country, leftwing, rightwing, old, young, rural, urban, whatever, that does not strongly associate the Green party with taking action on the environment.”

Because of that starting point, he argues, the sensible move forward was to evolve into a broader message – one previous leaders paved the way for. “The reason the party exists is in recognition of the fact that just having a bunch of environmental conservation movements isn’t addressing the root political and economic causes of environmental degradation.

“We tried 50 years of that. And it got us so far, but the manifest moments of material advancement have been tied to moments where we’ve been able to be more responsive to the actual political context of the day.”

Warfield points out that many of Polanski’s positions are not his alone. Green party members vote on policy and the leaders are constitutionally duty bound to advocate for it. “Take the wealth tax,” Warfield writes. “He did not arrive at this policy personally. A ‘wealth tax’ is called for as ‘a means of limiting large accumulations of wealth’ in a Green party manifesto published long before Polanski’s leadership.”

The book finds links between the party’s past and present, even in unlikely places. It’s unavoidable, Warfield writes, that there were “some distinctly rightwing people present at the formation of the Green party”. The first key figure was Teddy Goldsmith, an environmentalist part of a famous Tory family. His writings formed key texts for People, the political party from which the modern Greens descend.

Sign up to First Edition

after newsletter promotion

But even Goldsmith – whose “deep ecology” philosophy leaned into Malthusian concerns about human population and misanthropic views that blamed humanity as a monolith for ecological degradation – shares threads with Polanski’s Greens, Warfield says. Both share the golden Green rule that infinite economic growth and endless extraction are impossible on a planet with finite resources. Both reject the idea that capitalism can simply carry on with business as usual, green or otherwise.

As the party has shifted towards social ecology over the years, Warfield says Polanski’s eco-socialism simply represents a modern evolution: arguing that capitalism and the 1% – not all of humanity – are the root cause of environmental destruction.

But Polanski’s tenure has also brought controversies. There was his criticism of the police response to the Golders Green attack, which the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley, called “inaccurate and misinformed”. There was the false claim he was a British Red Cross spokesperson and the sharing of a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, a reference to Nigel Farage. YouGov polling shows Polanski’s approval rating has slumped since he became leader, while Green voting intention has dropped from 21% of the electorate in March to 11% this month.

Should the party take Polanski’s social media away? “Golders Green was a misstep,” says Warfield. “But what you don’t want to do is to get to a situation where every post needs double-tick signoff from different members of staff and you can’t just let Zack engage with social media in the way that allows him to reap the political points of authenticity.”

Polanski was criticised for his refusal to apologise for sharing the Farage guillotine picture. “Reform were trying to goad him into apologising for incitement to murder,” Warfield says. “If you do that, you legitimise the claim that they’re making. I think there’s a lot of strength in not succumbing to the pressure of playing that game.”

On 8 October, Polanski will contest the Holborn and St Pancras byelection after Keir Starmer announced his decision to vacate the seat. Warfield thinks Polanski can win. “You could vote Labour again and you get another backbencher who is one among literally hundreds of Labour MPs and that doesn’t make much difference to anything,” he says. “Or you can put a really prominent, independently minded Green in there and continue to put pressure on the Burnham project from its left.”

Manchester United report seventh straight annual loss and sell fans £125 grass clumps

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 13:41:16 GMT

Net loss of £43m for year ended 30 June 2026

Revenue hits record £677.6m and forecast to grow

Manchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh ­successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019.

The financial results were released as it emerged United are raising revenue by selling small clumps of grass from the Old Trafford pitch to supporters. United relaid the playing surface for the first time in 14 years this summer, and an email to fans has offered them the chance to buy 7cm x 7cm clumps of turf for £125.

The £43m net loss for 2025-26 is a significant increase on the £33m for the previous 12 months, with compensation paid to the sacked manager Ruben Amorim a contributory factor along with the decision to increase the club’s borrowing facility by £93m to help fund the redevelopment of Old Trafford.

United’s continued losses come despite record revenue of £677.6m – up 1.7% on the previous 12 months – and the implementation of a major cost-cutting regime by Sir Jim Ratcliffe under which hundreds of staff have lost their jobs.

In discussing United’s results on an investor call, the chief executive, Omar Berrada, said the club’s summer transfer window, during which they spent £155m on three players, had been planned with “financial sustainability in mind” in an indication that the budget will continue to be tight for newthe manager, Michael Carrick.

That is underlined by the fact that United’s wage bill dropped to £301m, down 3.6% on the previous year, more than £100m lower than Manchester City’s.

While United reported operating profits of £22.6m for the 12 months to 30 June 2026 the increase in revenue was more than offset by the cost of financing the club. Net finance costs more than tripled to £69.2m from £21.2m in the previous year, partly owing to foreign-exchange ­movements, and the club refinanced several loans, increasing their net debt from £471.9m to £577.6m.

United sources have said the refinancing provided funding for the £63.5m purchase of a plot of land next to Old Trafford required to build their proposed new 100,000 capacity stadium, the first major investment in a complex project that could end up costing more than £2bn.

It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength. While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.”

United are confident their financial outlook will improve over the next 12 months owing to the club’s return to the Champions League and the start of increased sponsorship deals with the training-kit partner Betway and shirt-sleeve partner SumUp, which will bring in £20m and £22m a year respectively. The club is forecasting revenue of between £740m and £760m for 2026-27.

Sindhu Vee: ‘Makeup, music to feel reckless, two pieces of milk chocolate – and then I go on’

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 13:31:53 GMT

The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa Claus

How did you go from investment banker to standup comedian? I didn’t go on purpose from one to the other. I transitioned from banking to stay-at-home mother to standup comedian. There was absolutely no previous thought process. I got on stage almost by chance, and a lot of alcohol was involved. Standup found me, and I’ve never left it alone.

What inspired your latest show, Swanky?It’s just the continuing story of Sindhu Vee! The trials and tribulations, the victories and losses. My parents passed away in quick succession recently and, in their absence, I realised I had to champion myself. I took a long hard look at my life and I thought: actually it’s not going that badly. A word my father used for things that were good but kind of like mysterious and cool was swanky. I suppose one could say that my life is swanky. Why not? Then I got a very swanky hairstyle and a dress for the poster. In the absence of my parents, I had to do it. They were big champions of me.

Do you have any preshow rituals?I don’t typically wear a lot of makeup, but for shows I have a very small, neat makeup routine. I listen to a playlist which is made up of primarily old music that I’ve always loved, nothing new. It’s music that makes me feel reckless. I’ll always have two pieces of milk chocolate before going on. That’s it.

Did you decide to become an actor, or did it happen to you?I think a lot of standups will tell you, as you start becoming known, sooner or later your agent will get a call and say: “Would you like to read for this part?” That’s how I got everything from Sex Education to Matilda to Feel Good to Starstruck. I didn’t think I was an actor. I genuinely thought, “This is a diversity casting issue.” It turns out I can act, and a number of people who have absolutely no upside in lying to me about it have said, “No, no, you can act.” So that’s been fantastic.

Standup now is very familiar. I understand it. Acting is like being in some seductive foreign country where you want to try the food and wear the clothes. It’s all very cool, but you don’t really know what’s going on. So I’ve been lucky to have directors who have been very generous.

What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had?One happened a couple of weeks ago in an airport lounge. We were all getting in the lift to go to our flight and suddenly someone said, “Oh no. Really?”, then started sobbing. We all turned to this woman. She was staring at me, so everyone then turned to stare at me. Because it was in America, I thought, “Have I said something and she’s offended?” She was crying and she said, “It’s you and I have been trying to see your shows.” Then she asked, “Can I give you a hug?” And I could not, in front of 30 people, be like: maybe that’s a step too far. So she walked across the hallway and hugged me and sobbed. I told her it was fine, wished her well, and she calmed down. I would be nowhere without fans and without my audience, but I find this a little disconcerting.

What was one of your all-time favourite gigs?There was a gig in a big marquee in St Albans one Christmas many years ago. We got there and it was cosy but gross because everyone had been stuffed in. It didn’t have glass windows, but if it did, they’d have fogged up from everyone’s breath. I remember I was trying out a joke about Santa Claus. I was sort of commenting on poverty in India and how that made Indian Santa Claus very skinny, so it was difficult for children to believe in him. It was a little bit tricky because I think it’s not easy to make fun of poverty. But again, as a comic, I think: this could be funny. It went down really well, and that’s when I realised how you can bring people into seeing that something is funny without punching down.

Can you recall a gig so bad it’s now funny?I gigged in Delhi early on in my career. I had to do 20 minutes and for some reason the MC brought me on and said, “Here’s Sindhu, who left India to go to the UK and become a comic there.” It really alienated me and everyone was furious. I started some of my best material and someone said, “Why don’t you fuck off back where you come from?” I was like, “Bro, I’m from Delhi.” Everyone hated me. People jumped on stage, stood in front of me, and said, “Look, we can tell jokes better than her.” I went home and drank half a bottle of whiskey.

What have you learned from standup?If you can make people laugh, no matter how divided they are, they will feel all part of the same humanity while they’re laughing. Human beings have a capacity for that. I’ve always known it, but now I’ve experienced it. My audiences are from 20 to 80 years old. Politically, I think, they’re quite varied. But they can all laugh at the same thing. I think that means I’ll never be cynical about what human beings are capable of.

What’s next for you?There’s this skin treatment called XERF. It’s a kind of a radio frequency thing on your face. One day I may get a facelift because never say never. But before that, you can try this and see what it does to your face. I’m going to try it – I’m so excited. So if you see me in the papers with a super sharp jawline, it’s because I’ve done XERF. And I’m in The Split Up, coming out on the BBC.

Sindhu Vee: Swanky is on tour in the UK until 17 April

Britain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solution

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 13:00:50 GMT

Young men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspiration

There it was: a pool of blood spreading across the pavement. A section of the high street had been cordoned off and a uniformed police officer gestured for bystanders to move along. It was the long hot summer of 1976, and a racist murder had stunned Southall in west London.

“What has happened here, officers?” asked Suresh Grover, then a curious 22-year-old, later to be widely known as a leading racial justice activist. “Go away, it’s just Indian blood,” was the response. Grover was soon to learn that 18-year-old Gurdip Singh Chaggar, an engineering student, had been stabbed to death by racist thugs the night before.

The late 1970s was the era of “Paki-bashing”: homes, shops and places of worship were attacked, while south Asians – young and old – were murdered on the streets. That day, Grover acted instinctively, taking some paint and daubing the pavement near the blood with the words: “This racist murder will be avenged. We’ll get you racist scum.”

This is the story of working-class youth who refused to turn the other cheek. From Southall to Sheffield and from Brick Lane to Bradford, the Asian youth movements were set up to physically defend communities from racist attacks. It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us in diverse towns and cities have grown up in safer environments.

But more than 50 years on, that racist violence has returned with shocking ferocity, a deterioration traceable to the summer of 2024, which marked some of the worst racist rioting in living memory.

In Hartlepool, a young south Asian man was walking down a street when he was punched in the face. Onlookers cheered, laughed and yelled racial slurs. “A Paki got banged,” one shouted, as those around him began to smash the windows of small businesses and kick down the door of a nearby house. In Middlesbrough, a group of white men stopped motorists and questioned them about their ethnicity, asking whether they were “white” before letting them through. In Rotherham and Tamworth, racist mobs tried to burn down hotels housing refugees.

And now? A seemingly relentless rise. Every five days, a mosque in Britain is attacked. The rhetoric of the far right has been mainstreamed.

After years spent researching and writing a book on the rich and proud tradition of political activism in the south Asian community, it seems clear to me that we cannot fight racism in silos. We must build broad movements that transcend racial and religious divides.

The Asian youth movements had a belief in the concept of political blackness as a banner that people of colour could unite under. To Tariq Mehmood, an Asian youth movement member who was born in Pakistan but raised in Bradford, there was no real difference between south Asian, African and Caribbean people: they were all the same to those who wanted to harm them. “We were called ‘black bastards’ on the streets,” he recalled. “We were commonly united with our African and Afro-Caribbean friends. They didn’t know they were black until they came here — I didn’t know I was a ‘Paki’ until I came to Bradford. We were united on those common issues of our oppression.”

They saw themselves as part of a broader working class. The Sheffield Asian Youth Movement and the Indian Workers’ Association, for instance, sent minibuses of their members to picket lines during the 1984-85 miners’ strike. They stood with white working-class communities fighting to save their industries, providing much needed financial support while challenging prejudice in these communities. Grover tells me that more than a decade after that strike, Kent miners were still attending Punjabi Sikh weddings in Southall because of the links that were built during that dispute.

These were movements rooted in their communities and strategic in their organising. They monitored the far right and mapped out who was most vulnerable to racist attacks. The Sheffield Asian Youth Movement had a big thick folder called the “fascist file”, in which they would compile information on local racists.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But things changed. As the 20th century wore on, anti-racist activism was increasingly institutionalised as the struggle moved from the streets to council chambers and boardrooms. Where we once had grassroots anti-racist movements rooted in communities, we now have a race-relations industry in which a few people are paid to tackle discrimination. We also have the rise of self-proclaimed community leaders under the policy of state multiculturalism who often speak on behalf of entire communities. Too often, they become the prism through which authorities engage with ethnic-minority communities.

A revival of grassroots anti-racist movements is long overdue. But it must be of this time, attuned to the changing circumstances of 2026. Racism is not experienced equally. Class, gender and geography all matter. A hijab-wearing Muslim woman is more likely to be a victim of Islamophobia than a Muslim man. Those living in smaller, more isolated ethnic-minority communities are more vulnerable to racist attack. First-generation migrants have greater insecurity than the grandchildren of migrants. An effective anti-racist movement must reflect on these challenges and prioritise those most vulnerable to racist violence.

The good news is that we are starting to see a revival of this approach. A few months ago, I spoke alongside Grover at the launch of the Nottinghamshire Solidarity Network, which is taking a strategic approach to anti-racism by organising county-wide to ensure smaller ethnic-minority communities are not left isolated. A week later, I spoke at the launch of the Greater Manchester Workers’ and Tenants’ Association. Its members understand that the far right feeds on deprivation and despair in working-class communities, and they are seeking to organise on the basis of class in an attempt to offer a counter-narrative to that of division and hate.

All of these movements, past and present, understand that racism will not be defeated from above. It will only be defeated by us – ordinary citizens who refuse to look away.

Taj Ali is a journalist and historian and author of Come What May, We’re Here to Stay: the Story of South Asian Resistance in Britain

Burnham survived his first Trump meeting. His nice hair may have had something to do with it

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 11:54:08 GMT

The PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head?

Watching footage of Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly on Tuesday was like watching your child from behind a tree in the playground. Are they making friends? How normal do they seem relative to the average? How will they react when they come into contact with that hulking great child who seems to be running things? Burnham’s first face-to-face with Donald Trump was billed as a knife-edge encounter that, due to the latter’s capriciousness, could go either way. In the event, it was drama-free, leaving observers to ask: was it Burnham’s brilliance or simply the weather in Trump’s head?

To viewers at home, Burnham’s performance at the press conference looked like that of a man who had worked out his best approach was to go for the sheepish, slightly cheeky air of the junior partner. Burnham is 24 years younger than Trump, on top of everything else – which can afford a certain licence to the less powerful person in any exchange. At the last minute, the meeting had been moved behind closed doors and afterwards, in a windowless room at the UN, the two men appeared side by side, mirroring each other’s body language: just two guys, legs akimbo, shoulders hunched, hanging on a bench in the locker room.

It was intriguing to guess what Trump saw when he looked at the UK’s new prime minister. British people can’t always parse class or regional difference in Americans and one assumes Trump can’t distinguish Burnham’s accent from that of someone from Melbourne, or Torquay. Still, something in the British prime minister’s bearing clearly appealed to him. “Thank you, Mr President,” said Burnham after Trump praised this country as “special” and Burnham’s tone – “That’s wonderful. We really appreciate that. This relationship matters so much to us” – hit just the right note of warm condescension that probably struck the president as flattery.

Other factors in play: it seems ridiculous to mention, but knowing how superficial Trump is, it seems to me that Burnham’s extremely impressive coiffure for a man of his age – which appears to exist without augmentation – won’t have been missed by a US president who spends an awful lot of time on his hair.

There were also a couple of contextual factors that may have given Burnham an easier ride than some other, less fortunate world leaders. First, the run-up to the meeting had seen Trump on absolutely top chaotic form while addressing delegates at the UN, threatening the destruction of Iran and going on a whimsical detour to try to get the acronym SI (“superintelligence”) as opposed to AI off the ground. Perhaps, by lunchtime, he had burned himself out and was ready for a bit of quiet time.

We know Trump gets bored quicker than a toddler spoilt for toys and Burnham’s shiny newness will have, briefly, diverted him. The replacement of Keir Starmer in relatively brutal fashion also gave Trump an opportunity to do something he loves more than anything else in this world, which is to kick a person when they’re down. When asked about recent rockiness in US-UK relations, the president replied, “No, I think they’re up … well, they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.” In that moment, one saw a tiny endorphin rush of meanness light up his face.

And finally, I guess, the president is fresh out of friends at the moment, as the fight with Canada continues and he falls out with his European friend Giorgia Meloni, formerly known as the “Trump whisperer”. As a result, Burnham was lavished with the highest praise Trump can summon, namely: “I think he’s a natural businessperson.” An astute reader of weakness, he perhaps sensed in Burnham someone more sure of himself than Starmer was. And the prime minister passed Trump’s do-you-think-you’re-better-than-me? test, in which anyone who displays any kind of overt intellectual curiosity is instantly a threat to be vanquished. Even his name, Andy, gives regular-guy vibes that probably helped.

Burnham weathered all this with equanimity, although it was tempting to detect behind his poker face the shadow of a smirk while, surely, he thought to himself, “God, this guy”. “News is fake!” said Trump, and, in reference to the Chagos Islands, “they’re a very important piece of real estate!” Meanwhile, Burnham smiled slightly as if appeasing a lunatic. “He gets it,” said Trump and for once, one had to agree.

Ten of the best-value deals from this summer’s transfer window

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 11:25:10 GMT

From veteran strikers to exciting young talents, here are 10 signings who could prove to be bargains for their new teams

Even in this era of relentless transfer inflation, a fee of more than £20m does not usually represent a bargain. Roma’s move for the Porto playmaker Mora may be an exception, though. Now 19, he has been on the radar of Europe’s elite teams since starring for Porto’s B-team at 15, and Porto were braced for his €70m (£59.5m) release clause to be met in the summer of 2025. That didn’t happen and Mora then fell out of favour under the new head coach, Francesco Farioli. Roma swooped with an offer of €25m (£21.4m), plus a 50% sell-on fee which can be bought out. The potential move also intrigued Mora, who was eager to play under Gian Piero Gasperini. “He played a big part in my decision to come here because he likes players with my qualities, and I’m a fan of the way he wants his teams to play,” Mora said. The early signs are positive, with Mora netting his first Roma goal against Lecce as the Giallorossi made a flying start in Serie A.

Getting promoted to the Premier League is an expensive business. This summer, Ipswich, Coventry and Hull collectively spent £450m net on players. Amid such frantic investment, Hull’s move for the 24-year-old Sweden international Stroud looks like excellent business. The wide player was a standout for Mjällby as the small-town team won the Swedish title last year, earning a place in Graham Potter’s World Cup squad. Sergej Jakirovic identified him as a key squad addition after Hull’s playoff final success. “He’s a very good player; he’s very versatile,” the Hull manager said. “He can play full-back, wing-back, left-winger, and in the middle. He’s a runner too, so I think he will suit us very well.” The 24-year-old has been a pacy creative outlet for Jakirovic’s hard-working unit.

On the face it of, paying a nominal fee to sign a striker of Aubameyang’s class and experience is a no-brainer. Still, the former Arsenal and Dortmund player is 37 and has endured a nomadic career since leaving Barcelona. An unsuccessful stint with Chelsea has been followed by two seasons with Marseille, sandwiching a year in Saudi Arabia. Aubameyang’s goal return has still been impressive, with 44 across the last three campaigns, and he has reportedly accepted a greatly reduced salary to play regular La Liga football. Dépor’s ambitious project looks the perfect fit, with Aubameyang scoring five goals in seven league games.

The Bundesliga’s trio of promoted clubs, in sharp contrast to their English counterparts, spent a combined £7.2m net on signings. The second-tier champions, Schalke, secured some notable names on loan (including boyhood fan Robin Gosens) but the holding midfielder Tanaka was their most expensive permanent recruit, at €1m. The 24-year-old still represents something of a gamble, his only previous experience of German football coming since January with Fortuna, who were relegated to the third tier. Tanaka still caught the eye of Schalke’s director of football, Youri Mulder, who said: “His work rate and intensity fit our game really well.” On his Bundesliga debut, Tanaka’s battling qualities helped his team hold Bayern Munich to a goalless draw, and he could be key to whether Schalke stay clear of trouble.

Leeds have a clear recruitment model: sign reliable, experienced players with strong physical attributes, preferably from the Bundesliga. The Swiss centre-back Elvedi fits that mould perfectly. Daniel Farke might have anticipated an adjustment period for a player who had spent 11 years at Borussia Mönchengladbach. Instead, Elvedi has settled quickly alongside his fellow newcomer Tarik Muharemovic, mostly playing on the left of Farke’s back three. It’s a welcome reunion for the 29-year-old with his former Gladbach coach. “It was just one year but I loved him as a manager,” Elvedi has said of Farke. “I learned a lot from him and I will learn a lot now.” He is learning fast already.

Robin Roefs (NEC to Sunderland, £9.1m; pictured) The Dutch keeper’s commanding presence was key as Sunderland secured European football. Kept 10 clean sheets in 35 league games, with only three teams conceding fewer goals than the promoted Black Cats.

Ferran Jutglà (Club Brugge to Celta, £4.7m) Made a solid start at Celta with nine La Liga goals, but struggled to make an impact in Europe. Hit a purple patch in March and is now playing more regularly as a No 9 rather than out wide.

Ernest Poku (AZ to Leverkusen, £8.7m) Featured regularly in his first season at Leverkusen, but was allowed to join Besiktas on a loan-to-buy deal this summer. The winger has made a slow start in Turkey but scored in their Europa League win over Marseille.

Adrian Truffert (Rennes to Bournemouth, £11.4m) The left-back settled quickly in Bournemouth’s rebuilt defence, helping his side qualify for Europe. Called up by Zinedine Zidane for the Nations League and could win his second France cap, four years after making his debut.

Santiago Hidalgo (Independiente to Toulouse, £2.5m) Enjoyed a promising first season in France with nine goal involvements in Ligue 1. May need to find another goalscoring gear this term with Toulouse struggling early on.

Borna Sosa (Ajax to Crystal Palace, £3m) Played in 18 games for Palace last season but managed just 99 minutes in the Premier League as he struggled for consistency. Now on loan at Cologne, and looks unlikely to have a future at Selhurst Park.

Berke Ozer (Eyupspor to Lille, £3.9m) Kept a league-best 13 clean sheets in his first season, helping Lille finish third. Ozer has retained the No 1 spot despite the arrival of Paraguay World Cup hero Orlando Gill, and was voted fans’ player of the month in August.

Christian Ordoñéz (Vélez Sarsfield to Parma, £6.7m) One of six Argentinian players in the current Parma squad, Ordonez has admitted to being “surprised” at the step up in quality, but has featured regularly in a solid first season in Serie A.

Carlos Soler (PSG to Real Sociedad, £6.9m) Midfielder has enjoyed a much more pivotal role at Real Sociedad, scoring in the Copa del Rey final shootout victory over Atletico to help deliver a trophy.

Nikola Stulic (Charleroi to Lecce, £4.3m) Signed to replace namesake Nikola Krstovic at Lecce, the centre-forward had a middling first season, scoring four of his side’s 28 league goals.

• Read last year's list here

Paderborn have returned to the Bundesliga with a bang after shocking Wolfsburg in the promotion/relegation playoff, smashing their transfer record (which, admittedly, was only £700,000) to sign Vidovic and the striker Marvin Pieringer for €3m each. Vidovic is a former Bayern Munich academy talent and his return to Germany’s top flight is an intriguing prospect. He was brought through at Bayern by Julian Nagelsmann but the Croatian playmaker could not become a regular there. A successful loan in Zagreb led to another chance to impress with Mainz but Vidovic barely featured and Bayern cut the loan short. After moving back to Dinamo permanently, the Bundesliga looked a distant prospect until Paderborn pounced. “His sporting CV speaks for itself,” their sporting director, Sebastian Lange, said. The 22-year-old’s arrival is a risk for a club with limited means, but the potential ceiling spotted by Nagelsmann makes it one worth taking.

As the self-styled “league of talents”, Ligue 1 functions as a development pool for young players who are sold on for hefty fees. Strasbourg, a “partner club” to Chelsea, are closely tied to this model: four of their summer signings were drawn from the vast stock of spare players at Cobham, while Valentín Barco and Emmanuel Emegha went in the other direction. Reyna, despite being 23, feels like a different prospect. He was once a heavily hyped youngster who thrived with Jude Bellingham and Erling Haaland at Dortmund, but injuries and inconsistency have stalled his career. Reyna made only four league starts in his solitary season at Gladbach but has begun promisingly in France. He scored his first Strasbourg goal in the 6-2 rout of Troyes in early September; if he can stay fit and capitalise on this new start, it may not be long before he is linked with a move across the Channel.

An attacking left-back once touted as the next Nuno Mendes, Nazinho was called up to Sporting’s first team by Ruben Amorim but made only 11 appearances before drifting back into the reserves. An initial loan to Cercle Brugge in 2023 became permanent for €2m the following summer, and regular game time began to breed results. After recording four goals and eight assists last season, Nazinho was snapped up by Cercle’s partner club, Monaco. He has made an immediate impact, striking up a left-flank partnership with Stanis Idumbo as Filipe Luís’s side sit top of Ligue 1. Their Conference League campaign will offer Nazinho further chances to trust his attacking instincts, and potentially earn a first Portugal call-up.

Real Betis stole a march on several Premier League clubs with a move for the prolific forward Troy Parrott, who quickly showed his worth with a winner against Real Madrid. The Ireland international cost Betis €20m, though, and the fee would doubtless have been higher if Parrott were heading back to Spurs, rather than to Seville. García, a left-back, may be this summer’s real steal, sold for £3.2m plus 50% of any future sale as Madrid cleared out fringe players. At 27, he is approaching his prime and has plenty of big-match experience, featuring more than 100 times for Madrid and playing two full top-flight campaigns on loan at Rayo Vallecano. García was, perhaps unsurprisingly, linked with Fulham this summer; Álvaro Arbeloa may come to regret allowing Betis to swoop.

Everton experienced a traumatic transfer deadline day that left David Moyes with one senior striker and a squad desperately short of depth. They did at least wrap up a late deal for Maitland-Niles, a versatile addition at a decent price. The former Arsenal full-back’s arrival may not have soothed fans’ frustrations, but his late equaliser against Manchester United may already have repaid a decent chunk of his fee.
