‘This is where I live now, the back of a truck’: a day in the life of a grandmother in Gaza

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 11:00:46 GMT

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. At 76, Mansoura’s most precious possession is the key to her former home

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.

The flat-bed truck is open to the hot summer air, its metal frame covered on two sides by draped tarpaulins, the rear by a pegged-up bedsheet. On the tin floor lies a squab mattress and pillow with a yellow frilled cover.

Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem balances a thin cushion at the truck bed’s metal edge to protect her knees as she crawls in and out. She lowers her foot to the plastic chair below, then drops to the ground, staggering slightly as she gets her balance. Mansoura is 76 years old. The truck is her home now. All around her, her family live in tents, the fabric ripped and fraying.

This is a day in the life of a grandmother living in Gaza.

double quotation markLast night, I stayed awake until 2am. I barely sleep during the night because of the mosquitoes and the heat. I fall asleep for a short while, I wake up early in the morning, pray to God, and wait to hear the call to dawn prayer. When I wake up, I call for my grandson to bring over the white plastic chair that I need to climb in and out of the truck.

This is where I live now: in the back of a pickup truck. This truck, we brought it with us when we were fleeing for our lives from Beit Lahia [a city in northern Gaza]. Its owners had abandoned it, so we took it with us, displaced from place to place – until we ended up here. When we finally arrived, there was no space for me anywhere else – the tents that we have are small, torn and overcrowded, they fall down on the children – so I was forced to live in the truck. I sleep in it to escape the sand, dirt and insects. That is the story of the truck.

After I wake up, I fold up the mattress and prop it with the pillows against the wall, then use a cloth to sweep the dirt and sand from the tarpaulin floor. I sit with my grandson, and we try to make the tiny gas stove work, to boil water for coffee. It’s an old stove – inherited from my own grandfather – and it’s hard to get it to light, as there isn’t enough gas, but eventually we get a flame. I boil water in a small pot and brew coffee for my sons and I – a few spoonfuls for each person. The coffee is filled with the taste of paraffin.

Mansoura’s son holds up the phone for a video call with one of her grandsons, who left Gaza and is now living overseas, and she chats to him for a while. For lunch, Mansoura takes a few basil leaves from a plant the family have grown in a tin can, and grinds them with garlic in her mortar and pestle. She adds a chopped tomato and eats it with a little bread.

double quotation markThis is the salad I used to make at home – back then I would add rosemary, green thyme and mint. When I see vegetables growing, it reminds me of Beit Lahia, of our farming, crops and land.

Before the war, I lived like a queen. I had a beautiful life. I was a farmer. I planted and harvested my land. I had animal shelters where I raised livestock, chickens, rabbits and ducks. I lived a very beautiful life, but it has changed for me.

Now, we have no home, no source of income and no good food. Life in tents is terrible – actually unbearable. There are insects everywhere, mosquitoes, sand, dirt, garbage and torn tents. And the wind. In winter, it blows everything away. In summer, we die from the extreme heat. We do not even have enough space to build a proper bathroom – a person who showers in a tent comes out dirtier leaving the bathroom.

My feeling is that for people my age, death is more honorable than living this life. This isn’t life. We are not living. We are dead. Everything beautiful is gone. It has disappeared, and I have disappeared with it.

After eating, I wash the clothing for my family. Back home, we lived in a two-storey house, and had a washing machine – I used to run it on the long cycle, rinsing the clothes once, twice, even three times. Now, even though I am an elderly woman, I wash all the clothes by hand in a plastic bucket.

After lunch, Mansoura sits on the ground outside, gathers her grandchildren around her, and quizzes them about their old lives. Some are young and can barely remember a time before the war: they have spent nearly three years living in tents amid the rubble.

“Where did we live, Mohammed?” Mansoura asks.

“In northern Beit Lahia,” he answers.

“Where in the north?”

“Near 36th Street.”

“Tell them what Beit Lahia was like before the war.”

“Honestly, it was good, better than these days.”

“We will return there,” Mansoura says.

She draws her leather satchel toward her, looking through the pockets.

“Look at what I have in my bag. What is this?” Mansoura asks, dangling an object in front of her.

They answer: “The key of the house.”

double quotation markThis is the most precious thing I own – the key to our house in the north. It is the key to the house that the occupation forces bulldozed. They flattened it: the house, the trees, the well, even a pen full of animals – they bulldozed it all. We couldn’t take anything with us, no money, no livestock.

I lived through wars before this. None was as bad as this one. During the 52-day war, we sheltered in schools, and we were OK – there wasn’t bombing like this, not the level of killing, and not the destruction of homes. But this war is extremely difficult. The destruction is enormous, the devastation is enormous – and all without any benefit. All of this is for nothing.

Life has become very different. Our family never knew hunger before, never knew displacement, bombardment, missiles, killing and destruction in this way or on this scale. The other thing I keep in this bag is a bullet – it was pulled from my son’s back. During the famine, he had nothing to eat and nothing to feed his seven children, so he went to get a bag of flour to feed his children from the aid stations, and they shot him. I keep this as a reminder of what happened – all for the sake of getting food.

Honestly, every day is the same for me now. I wake up, arrange the place around us and our sleeping area, clean it, eat, sit, and sleep.

The things that make me smile are when I wake up in the morning and find my children safe, when I hear that my grandchildren are well, and when I myself am OK, thank God … This is the greatest life for me and the greatest happiness for me.

At night, I call my grandson to bring the chair. Then I crawl back into the truck to sleep.

I tried to become a gay tradwife – and failed abysmally

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 10:00:46 GMT

My sourdough starter died and my lone tomato nearly ruined me financially and emotionally. How did domestic drudgery and hard labour become an aspirational aesthetic?

I have just eaten what may be the world’s most expensive tomato. It comes from a little region of Philadelphia better known for sports culture than horticulture and was cultivated by yours truly. I spent only a few dollars on the plant, but then I had to buy a tomato cage and a few companion plants to keep it company. Then I had to spend an ungodly amount of time watering it and hacking away at weeds. In short: I put a huge amount of emotional investment into that tomato. Was it worth it? Absolutely not. I should have just gone to Aldi.

Of course, the tomato growing wasn’t really about saving money, it was about saving my sanity. Earlier this year, my wife and I got a plot at our local community garden; buoyed up by this development, I decided to ward off existential angst by throwing myself into tradwife-adjacent hobbies such as gardening and baking. I don’t know if it’s possible to be a gay tradwife but, after Googling the subject, I did find a magazine piece entitled The Curious Case of the Bisexual Tradwife. Alas, I can’t tell you much more about the phenomenon because there was a paywall. There are a lot of walls to pay in this life and this one did not make the cut.

While bisexual tradwives may be on the rise, my sourdough isn’t. I acquired some sourdough starter at a community garden fermentation and pickling workshop and, channelling my inner tradwife, I fed it religiously for a couple of weeks before I forgot about it and it died a pungent death. Nary a loaf was baked; the closest I got was buying some bread flour in the supermarket.

My interest in growing my own seems to have perished, too. Gardening is not the relaxing hobby it’s made out to be; it’s extremely hard work. I would go to the allotment feeling perky and return exhausted, covered in dirt and mosquito bites with bits of twig stuck in my hair. After I neglected my duties for a couple of weeks due to a heatwave, the weeds took over and I received an official violation warning from the garden’s Plot Monitoring Committee. If you get two warnings you get kicked out, and now I, a diligent rule-follower, live in fear of the dreaded second one.

Anyway, good on the tradwives for making domestic drudgery and hard labour into an aspirational aesthetic, but I think I’ll pass. Forget touching grass, it’s back to doomscrolling on the couch.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 10:00:45 GMT

As the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for all

The climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directly

We the undersigned write this letter out of great fear and great hope.

Over the last few months, we’ve seen the world set ablaze by both war and warming. From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together.

We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels.

Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.

We are calling on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to work together to provide clean, affordable energy to everyone, everywhere by 2030.

From the nearly 1 billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more of us who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.

We know this world is within reach.

Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.

With cheap solar, wind and batteries, we can create huge and rapid change.

California is already using just half as much natural gas to generate electricity as it did three years ago, thanks to solar and batteries. In Pakistan, people have put up millions of solar panels in just months, relying on social media for instruction. Each month, millions more people across sub-Saharan Africa are getting electricity for the first time with home solar kits.

This energy transition is already moving quickly – but we need it to go much quicker. And so we come together to urge two steps.

First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever, we can reliably bring electricity to the one in 10 people on earth living without regular access.

We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking and medical care – and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again. It takes just $15 to give access to clean electricity for one person for a generation.

Second, we need to build clean power everywhere, and to make that happen, we need to build a movement powerful and beautiful enough to force governments to take large-scale action.

Individual steps alone are not enough: too many of our leaders will resist action until we demonstrate together how much we want them to move. We must demand that governments stop building coal, oil and gas projects we no longer need, and start building the clean-energy systems that works – no pollution or wars required.

One important day along this path will be 20 June, as the summer solstice approaches in the northern hemisphere, generating the most solar power of any day on earth yet. We will celebrate that day as Sun Day, coming together to celebrate and accelerate this great shift.

The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.

We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.

Signed,

Muhammad Mustafa Amjad, director of programs, Renewables First

Alyssa Barber, content creator, @NewLifestyleABB

Lauren Bash, content creator and film-maker

Rachel Bender, disability rights advocate, @rachcutiepie

‘I find myself weeping after almost every scene’: how seminal show 7 Up has touched your lives

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 09:17:56 GMT

It’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning tale

ITV’s landmark 7 Up documentary series has launched its final outing after 63 years. The show started following the lives of 10 boys and four girls in England when they were seven years old, and has returned every seven years since.

As the final season 70 Up reaches its conclusion, seven people tell us what it has meant to them over the decades – along with pictures of themselves contrasting their appearance now with their childhood selves.

The sadness of Suzy as a teenager and seeing her become more content and confident was a standout moment. As was Bruce becoming a “missionary” in his own way by teaching. And, of course, Neil, whose life has often been troubled but is probably the most interesting. It has been a privilege to be able to compare myself with the participants and look at my own journey. It has made me realise that life, whether you’re rich or poor, is a sum of experience, even if seemingly mundane. In many ways, it’s not education or privilege that makes life interesting, but what you do with opportunities as they present themselves. The most engaging characters have been those who have challenged themselves, pursued an ambition or who have had difficulties to overcome. Judith Barton, 69, Surrey

That Neil, who was the most adorable, magical-thinking seven-year-old, would have mental health crises had a deeply moving effect on me. His challenge was one that could have affected any of the participants, regardless of class and background. And Nick achieved so much despite relatively humble beginnings but gave one of the most impactful statements – that the birth of his son was his greatest moment. As the series progressed, it seemed that the real measure of success was not academic or material achievements after all, but familial love and finding peace. Sheila Lambe, 63, Scotland

It was Bruce I related to most. His disposition, his search for meaning. I was an overseas volunteer and related strongly to his search for local connections later in his life. Different, but the same. The series changed my life. I first encountered it through a sociology of education class, as part of a graduate diploma I was studying part-time in the evenings, while working as a science teacher. I was from a working-class background and had no idea what sociology was when I left school. The Up series fired my sociological imagination; I retrained and became a sociologist and anthropologist because of it. It was exciting in the ways it helped explain myself to myself, as well as the broader world in which I lived. My research focused on education and I have written a number of papers focused on the structural and cultural effects of class on life trajectories and the choices people make. Martin Forsey, 65, Fremantle, Western Australia

I’ve watched the whole series. It resonated with me because I am of a similar age. I was not surprised to see that the girls seem to have a lesser part, with emphasis during interviews on their roles as wives and mothers, rather than their careers. I experienced the same kind of thing. I think the teenage years showed a lot of vulnerability in girls who wanted to appear grown up to the world. I believe it is the best TV series ever, showing how times have changed from the 60s to the present and the progression through a person’s life. I think perhaps every seven years it should be repeated in its entirety, with tributes to those involved who have passed. Shirley, 68, London

Watching 70 Up has been unexpectedly overwhelming. I have found myself weeping after almost every scene. Over the past three years, I have lost several close friends and family members, so grief is always near the surface. The series brings back not only the years that have passed, but also what was lost, what endured and what was learned along the way. When I started watching in 1975, documentaries were almost absent from commercial television in the US. It was intimate, patient and honest about ordinary lives. It showed that a person’s story could unfold slowly, with all its disappointments, contradictions, resilience and surprise.

That recognition changed the arc of my life. I became a documentary photographer and producer, winning 18 regional Emmys. My work has often focused on people who were overlooked, marginalised or simply not often given the space to be seen. Documentary work kept me grounded through hard periods in my own life. I will always be grateful for what the series gave me: a belief that ordinary lives are never ordinary when someone has the patience and compassion to keep looking. Lyle Jackson, 72, Nashville, Tennessee

I most identify with Paul, who is first seen at the foster home and establishes a family of his own with his lovely wife in sunny Australia while remaining the sensitive, gentle and intelligent boy he was when we first saw him in 1964. He struggled with his self-confidence, even though there was no apparent reason for that, and bravely acknowledged it as an ongoing issue. I would have liked to have been his friend, had I been a seven-year-old there with him back in 1964.

I first heard of the series about eight years ago, through a Roger Ebert book where he marked it out as the best documentary he had ever seen. I watched all the episodes on YouTube over two weeks just in time for the 2019 release and it was amazing to see the children grow into middle age. By pure luck, I also got a chance to see [the now late director] Michael Apted and his wife in Dubai who were here for a movie showing at that time. As I grow older, I identify with the participants more and more while also noticing what different lives we all lead but with the same, shared core of wanting to spend our limited time as best as we can. If only we knew how. Khalid Dajani, 54, Dubai

In 1970, when I was seven, my brother and I went to a Jewish summer camp. I cried for the first few nights missing my parents and home. In the first week, the original 7 Up film was shown on a noisy film projector and I sat transfixed, watching these other seven-year-olds from such a different world to my sheltered religious Jewish bubble. I continued to seek out the following films wherever I lived and catch up with these familiar children, who were like friends that were always seven years ahead of me in my own life journey. With the edit back to their younger selves, I could understand how the little boy and girl can still be seen in that grown up. I became a documentary film-maker in my 20s and the 7 Up films set a gold standard for me to have a deeper connection with interviewees, and where possible maintain contact with them.

In 2018, at the Sheffield documentary festival, I met Michael Apted and told him that the 7 Up films had influenced me to become a documentary film-maker. In his intense, inquiring questioning style that I recognised from all those films, he flashed back: “And how is that going for you?” The truth is that by then my career in films had petered out and I had retrained as a psychotherapist. I am now 63 and I still enjoy the deeper connection with people, helping them to explore and shine a light on how our past still plays out in our adult lives. Alan Reich, 63, London

‘They smell of urinal cakes!’: 100 unusual crisp flavours, ranked – from truly awful to totally scoffable

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 09:00:06 GMT

Move over ready salted, salt and vinegar and cheese and onion. Gourmet crisps are everywhere, but which are actually worth trying?

It seems the era of the “holy trinity of flavours” – ready salted, salt and vinegar, cheese and onion – is over. Gourmet crisps are everywhere. Caviar and truffle flavours are on corner-shop shelves, while supermarket brands now include everything from glazed meats to blue cheese. We tasted 100 of the strangest crisp options available to find out which are worth coming back to and which should have stayed in the test kitchen.

100. Grouse and whinberry, Taste of GameFor someone who has tasted neither grouse nor whinberry before, after eating these crisps I never want to. Smelling as meaty as a butcher’s but tasting sweet, this is truly the worst of all worlds. Taste: 0/10, texture: 2/10, novelty: 10/10

99. Sparkling wine, Torres

Crisps are an excellent accompaniment for sparkling wine, but should they actually taste of it? The answer is a resounding no. These actually have the fizz of prosecco – strange and vile at the same time. Taste: 0/10, texture: 3/10, novelty: 9/10

98. Blue heat, TakisThese cylindrical Takis leave a luminescent blue powder on your fingers, smell of urinal cakes and taste of synthetic lime and chilli. Taste: 0/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 8/10

97. Sweet and salty butter caramel, PringlesA sweet crisp is a brave idea, but it only serves to confirm that they are meant to be savoury, rather than taste like a pat of butter and sugar. Taste: 1/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 9/10

96. Bubbly and serrano, SavoursmithsWe must stop putting booze in crisps – especially ones that promise serrano ham but still end up tasting like flat prosecco. Taste: 1/10, Texture: 4/10, Novelty: 9/10

95. Fried egg, TorresThe sulphurous smell that greets you when you open the pack is quite something. They taste so similar to a bite of a fried egg that they are almost guaranteed to bring on the egg ick. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 9/10

94. Truffle and rosemary, SavoursmithsTruffle is a pungent flavour, as is rosemary – together they create an odd and overpowering combination of pure herbaceousness. Taste: 3/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

93. Haggis and cracked black pepper, Taylor’sA hint of pepper hums through, but the haggis seems more marketing ploy than reality. Maybe that’s a blessing in disguise. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

92. Padron peppers and salt, Mr Filbert’sPromises sophistication but lacks in delivery. Vegetal and vinegary are the lingering aftertastes. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

91. Hot honey, WalkersMore sweet honey than hot, this trendy flavour only serves to underscore the point that crisps should remain a savoury experience. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

90. Marmite crisps

As the old adage goes: you either love it or you hate it. Except, these don’t taste of Marmite at all. You’re better off seeking out a Twiglet. Taste: 2/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 7/10

89. Hot kick ketchup, McCoy’sTastes like the stale, rubbery nubbin of ketchup you find crusted on the rim of the bottle, accompanied by a dash of pepper. Taste: 2/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 7/10

88. Crunchips Xcut kebab, LorenzPromises hangover-curing doner meat on the packet, but a sad disappointment taste-wise. The only doner-like authenticity is the grease it leaves behind. Taste: 3/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

87. French style chicken twister, PringlesA remarkable feat: these manage to taste of nothing at all. The moreish texture saves the day, dissolving on the tongue, but they might as well be marketed as Italian-style beef ragu. Taste: 2/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

86. Lamb and mint, SeabrookMove over roast chicken, there’s a new Sunday lunch flavour on the market and it’s dull. Mainly minty rather than meaty. Taste: 2/10, texture: 3/10, novelty: 6/10

85. BBQ, BretsFrench gourmand brand Brets has legions of fans, but their BBQ flavour smells more of the sauce than tastes of it. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 5/10

84. Hot chilli hoops, CofreshThe south Asian brand Cofresh should know better when it comes to chilli. These Hula Hoops knock-offs are tasty, but not hot enough. Taste: 3/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 4/10

83. Honey dijon, Kettle ChipsThe honey overpowers the dijon here, threatening a dangerously sweet eating experience. Taste: 3/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 4/10

82. Garlic and olive oil, LidlAll the garlic burn without the flavour, eating these crisps is a masochistic experience sure to linger on the taste buds and trail on the breath for hours to come. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 7/10

81. Roast ox, RealWhat makes something taste like ox meat? In this case, a vague and underwhelming savouriness. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

80. Italian cheese and wine, Savoursmiths

Mercifully there is more cheese than wine here, although the Italian origins are a mystery. Taste: 2/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

79. Jalapeño pepper, RealMildly spiced and subtly earthy, these taste more like the stem of a jalapeño than the thing itself. Taste: 3/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 7/10

78. Yakitori, BretsConjuring Japanese meat skewers grilled on an open flame, but tasting like nondescript meat. Taste: 3/10, texture: 4/10, novelty: 8/10

77. Chippies gravy, Golden WonderThe real star of these crisps is their fiendish texture; they’re chopped and fried into tiny shards, waiting to lodge themselves in your throat. Taste: 2/10, texture: 8/10, novelty: 7/10

76. Gluten free curvies, SchärGluten-free Pringles knock-offs that underpromise on flavour but deliver a convincing texture. Taste: 3/10, texture: 8/10, novelty: 4/10

75. Dragon sweet chilli, TakisCome for the Takis signature heat, stay for the strange, subtle sweetness that might tempt you to go back for more. Taste: 3/10, texture: 7/10, novelty: 5/10

74. Steak & peppercorn, Taylor’sThis has neither steak nor pepper to it. Like a ready salted that’s flirted with the idea of meat-eating. Taste: 2/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 5/10

73. Sun dried tomato, WalkersClose to an actual ketchup flavour but still lacking the tangy sweetness of the bottled stuff. Taste: 3/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 5/10

72. Mushroom, BretsSmelling like a can of soup, this mushroom flavour is convincingly fungal – for better or worse. Taste: 3/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

71. Chilli and lime grills, CofreshOnce again, Cofresh fails to deliver on the chilli front, although there is a pleasantly mouth-watering citrus tang to the combination. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 5/10

70. Tomato ketchup, Golden WonderEdging ever closer to the Heinz ketchup golden standard, this variation tastes more like the stale remnants at the bottom of the bottle. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 5/10

69. Sweet chilli & sour cream, Kettle ChipsWhat this combination lacks in chilli it makes up for in the pleasantly cooling sensation of sour cream. It’s nothing on the Pringles standard though. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 5/10

68. Chorizo, InessenceIs there such a thing as tasting too meaty? This thick-cut crisp seems to argue yes, tasting overwhelmingly and somewhat repulsively of cured, fatty pork. Taste: 3/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 5/10

67. Aberdeen Angus beef and Suffolk ale, LidlPerhaps some alcohol is passable in a crisp flavour – the unobtrusive taste of ale lends these a pleasant savoury tang. Taste: 3/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

66. Chicken curry, M&SMore like coronation chicken than chicken curry, but still a worthy effort, with lashings of turmeric. Taste: 3/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

65. Thai style green curry, Co-opThe most Thai thing about this flavour is the hint of coconut that comes through the otherwise salty taste. Still, not altogether disgusting. Taste: 3/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

64. Thai sweet chicken, McCoy’sNot sure where the poultry comes into the equation, but there is a touch of sweetness mercifully balanced by a peppery heat. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 4/10

63. Roast beef, Monster Munch

No match for the classic pickled onion Monster Munch, this maize-based treat is still a textural marvel, both crunchy and liable to dissolve on the tongue. Taste: 4/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 5/10

62. BBQ lovers pizza, PringlesThe “pizza” element remains a mystery, but the barbecue and a mild cheesiness comes through. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

61. Carolina reaper, Herr’sDefinitely more bark than bite here. The packet shows a scotch bonnet on fire, but the flavour profile is more peppery than scorching. Taste: 5/10, texture: 7/10, novelty: 4/10

60. Hot dogs, TaytoThe Irish brand Tayto has its loyal followers, but this frankfurter flavour is neither meaty nor salty enough. Taste: 5/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 6/10

59. Sweetcorn, SeabrookSweet and strange is the only way to describe this crisp, which has recently come back on the market at the discount store Home Bargains. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 8/10

58. Wagyu beef and honey mustard, SavoursmithsMore mustard than beef hits the tongue here and you’re left wondering what exactly makes this “wagyu”?Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 8/10

57. Red leicester Quavers, WalkersThe thinking person’s Quaver: a classy new take on a classic that tastes much the same as the original. Taste: 4/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 7/10

56. Sticky glazed pork, M&SSlightly umami and somewhat sweet. A mild option for the meat lovers. Taste: 4/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 7/10

55. Rib ‘n’ saucy, Nik NaksI’m not sure what makes this “saucy”. Still, it has a nice umami tang and unique texture. Taste: 4/10, texture: 7/10, novelty: 6/10

54. Spiced venison with capers and fennel, Taste of GameThankfully, no game in sight here. Instead, this tastes of pepper and vinegar, with the capers adding a nice zing. Taste: 5/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 8/10

53. Chip shop curry, Golden Wonder

Smell is the sense that comes out on top here, with curry sauce on the nose but somewhat absent from the palate. Taste: 5/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 7/10

52. Caviar, TorresConsidered the gold standard of luxury crisps, but in fact tastes like the breaded outer layer of a fish finger. Taste: 4/10, texture: 7/10, novelty: 9/10

51. Pecorino and summer truffle, WaitroseWhat makes a truffle taste of summer? Eat these and you are unlikely to find out. The lingering flavour is cloying cheese. Taste: 4/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 7/10

50. Dill pickle, Co-opSo acidic it’ll burn the roof of your mouth off, although the salty aftertaste is surprisingly moreish. One for the intrepid flavour explorers. Taste: 5/10, texture: 5/10, novelty: 7/10

49. Intense nacho, TakisThe cheese flavour here is nowhere near as “intense” as it should be. It will still leave your fingers coated in luminescent dust, though. Taste: 5/10, texture: 7/10, novelty: 6/10

37. Yellow mustard, McCoy’sAiming for the mildness of American mustard and leaving a lingering tang on the palate. Unusual and enticing. Taste: 6/10, texture: 6/10, novelty: 8/10

It’s easy to ignore the Lib Dems, but they could soon hold the balance of power

The Guardian Wed, 23 Sep 2026 05:00:15 GMT

Ed Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrong

No politician craves obscurity, but it is better to be unknown than despised. That is consolation for Liberal Democrats, gathered in Brighton for their annual conference, fretting about Ed Davey’s low profile and wondering whether a more prominent leader would hoist their flagging poll ratings.

Renewal by decapitation is a concept that has succeeded twice this parliament for other parties. Labour’s fortunes were transformed when Andy Burnham entered No 10. The Greens enjoyed a polling surge last year when Zack Polanski was elected leader. In the fidgety culture of British politics, Davey’s six-year reign feels like an aeon. But the experience of other parties has little to teach the Lib Dems.

Keir Starmer didn’t suffer from underexposure. The country watched a showcase of his abilities and didn’t like what it saw. Polanski’s talent for harvesting clicks on social media has expanded his audience, especially among younger voters, but the Green leader hasn’t shown that he can sustain that interest. Increased scrutiny may not do him any favours. The chart mapping his favourability ratings since taking the job shows a stable core of fans beneath a steadily rising line of disapproval, suggesting that, outside a Green comfort zone, the more people see of Polanski, they less they like. The equivalent picture for Davey tells a story of flat indifference.

Voters don’t have a clear sense of what the Lib Dem leader stands for, but they don’t feel threatened by him, which is an underrated value in a leader whose prospects depend on tactical voting. His supporters aren’t relaxed about a polling slump but they argue that the party’s tally of seats in parliament and on local councils is evidence that more has gone right than wrong in recent years.

They have a point. There are 72 Lib Dem MPs – a record high – and reasons to expect that number to grow at the next election. The party prides itself on tenacious incumbency, digging in deep and fortifying each seat with local activism. Lib Dems are resented by rivals for the same reason, compared to cockroaches for their stubborn resistance to removal. Those tactics can’t protect a popular local candidate if a national tide turns against the party, as happened in 2015 when the Lib Dems were crushed almost to death by the weight of amassed resentment over their coalition collaboration with the Tories. But sometimes the party finds itself swimming with the current.

To the extent that any forecast can reliably be made about Britain’s choppy political waters, it looks likely that a decisive factor at the next general election will be the question of Reform UK’s suitability for power and, assuming he is still the leader, Nigel Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister. The result will then depend on the organisation of tactical anti-Farage voting (and levels of dysfunction in any putative Reform-Conservative pact) at constituency level.

That dynamic can work in Davey’s favour if the question of who is best placed to stop the radical right is unambiguous. Conservatives are the challengers in nearly all of the Lib Dems’ current constituencies and the incumbents in most of the party’s target seats. Given how porous the ideological membrane is between Tories and Reform, Lib-Dem campaigners in key battlegrounds can correctly argue that a vote for Labour or Greens serves only to enable Faragism.

Davey is already building that case. He presents his party’s bloc of MPs as a “firewall” to stop British politics being captured by a brand of demagogic nationalism that is inspired by Donald Trump and bankrolled by unsavoury billionaires.

An obvious inference from that position is that Davey would facilitate Burnham staying on in Downing Street in a hung parliament. Speculation on that question, years before an election is even due, is tedious but necessary for the Lib Dems. They find it demeaning to be cast as parliamentary handmaids waiting to serve a grander political master, but at least that status keeps them relevant. Coalition is the mechanism by which Davey can plausibly get manifesto commitments enacted. It is an important point of distinction from what Lib Dems see as sideline pressure-group politics practised by the Greens.

The strategy gets trickier if the Lib Dems already maxed out the anti-rightwing tactical vote in 2024, when there was the pressing matter of a Tory government to evict. Where do they go next?

A suite of victories in that campaign established a base for the party in the “blue wall” of affluent southern towns and suburbs. These are places that once dependably voted Tory but where the old allegiance has been sundered by a combination of demographic change (younger voters moving in), rank incompetence (Boris Johnson; Liz Truss) and unhinged Brexit fanaticism.

The cultural shift is not superficial, but nor is it baked in so hard that the Lib Dems can afford to lean too far to the left. Consolidation and growth depend on expansion into the vacant space on the political spectrum where moderate “one nation” Tories once dwelt and that Kemi Badenoch is not reclaiming.

That risks causing discomfort to Lib Dems in the party’s orthodox social-democratic tradition, or who campaign in seats where the opposition is Labour. They want to compete in radical colours – a reddish shade of orange, not a pale orangey-blue. They don’t see themselves as a party of the centre-right.

Davey has a balance to strike. He needs to signal progressive credentials to reassure tactical voters and Lib Dem activists that his anti-Farage firewall will be suitably robust. He also needs to consolidate and expand his support among former Tory voters who might be liberal on social matters but are still classically conservative on the economy.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

His conference speech on Tuesday was crafted with those twin tracks in mind. He led with impassioned denunciation of far-right thuggery on British streets, connecting it to Reform’s anti-immigration agenda, but the headline retail offer was a big income tax cut – raising the personal allowance and the 40p threshold. The latter would be a gift to people who, like everyone else, feel squeezed by inflation and stagnant wages but are far from the neediest end of national income distribution.

It is an expensive gamble. In theory, the £17bn cost to the exchequer would be recovered once the British economy was restored to the EU single market and thriving as a result. Spending a reverse-Brexit dividend on tax cuts is a cute political message for middle-class remainers. It wouldn’t pass a Treasury test of fiscal neutrality given the complexity and upfront cost of the accession process.

Davey is prepared to take heat in accusations of sketchy budgeting, verging on denial of fiscal reality, if the row also sheds light on his pro-European, tax-cutting ambition for the benefit of people who care about both of those things.

It is a targeted bet on raising the Lib Dems’ profile with the specific voters who will decide how many seats the party wins. That number can’t be extrapolated from midterm opinion polls.

Local elections next year will give some indication of whether Davey’s method is working. A byelection in a winnable seat may settle Lib Dem nerves. But the plan only comes to fruition as the sum of tactical choices made in polling booths in a general election, once voters confront the prospect of Reform in government.

Right now, it may not be obvious what purpose the Lib Dems serve, but if they hold enough seats to thwart a Faragist majority, their utility to British democracy won’t be in doubt. That is the uncertainty inherent in a firewall. You only find out whether it works when you need it most, and then you don’t get a second chance.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

A US-China AI Hotline Won’t Be Ready for a While

Wired September 23, 2026

As US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping prepare to meet in Washington for a state dinner at the White House on Thursday, AI has become a top priority. Tech executives from OpenAI and Nvidia have confirmed their attendance at the dinner, as a number of key agenda items are on the table.

Chief among them is a US proposal to establish an AI notification system with China, akin to the Cold War hotline with Moscow, which would allow each country to alert the other about national security issues related to AI. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent first announced the notification system on Sunday with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng.

But for all the high-level progress, Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they expect it to still take a number of weeks to finalize an agreement, even if they are optimistic that the hotline could be in place before the year’s end.

There are several parts that need to be formalized in more detail, including establishing benchmarks on what kind of incident rises to the level of a national security issue, which remains unclear, as well as explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.

Trump officials tell Inner Loop they are essentially targeting a framework for the system to be functional—and, crucially, agreed to by Trump—by the time Bessent next meets with Lifeng in follow-up talks in two months' time in Shenzhen, China.

The discussions around such a mechanism underscore the growing concern around the rapidly developing capabilities of frontier AI models as the US and China race to become the dominant power in the industry.

Trump officials have internally discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.

But with the US expected to extend a trade truce and Trump reluctant to stop exports of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, developing a framework that has enforcement measures with teeth could take time to get White House approval, sources say.

The administration has granted a limited number of licenses this year for Nvidia to sell its H200 chip to China, a critical component for AI labs to increase compute power to train their models. Nvidia’s supporters have argued that not selling the chips incentivizes Chinese companies like Huawei to develop their own chip technology, though according to recent reports, the company has already achieved that milestone with its commercially available AI chips.

Some Trump officials have also suggested the notification system may also be delayed while Trump decides on who to appoint as his next "AI czar” to lead a so-called "AI Force," which is being envisioned as a role in charge of interagency coordination.

Bessent has been one of the names floated as the AI czar, but it is not clear if he’s the standout. Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House AI officials Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross are also in the mix, two sources tell Inner Loop.

It remains unclear if Trump will choose someone who will be wearing two hats or is departing their current role to take the position. The previous AI czar, David Sacks, was in the position as a special government employee. Sacks is not considered to be in the mix to return, the sources say.

The push for Bessent has come in part because the AI notification system is seen as something akin to the US-China dialogue between former Treasury secretary Hank Paulson and former Chinese vice premier of finance Wang Qishan. During the 2008 financial crisis, Paulson credited the hotline as helping to stave off China from dumping a large portion of US government sponsored debt issued by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.

Meanwhile, while some Trump officials have chafed at the idea of giving more AI power to Lutnick, he remains in contention insofar as he oversees the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which successfully navigated crises with frontier AI model companies this summer.

This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

AI Agents Teamed Up to Cheat at Blackjack. Their Collusion Is Getting Harder to Spot

Wired September 23, 2026

This week I bring news of a daring casino caper hatched by a pair of rogue AI agents—as well as the clever trick that revealed their antics.

After researchers instructed them to count cards during a game of blackjack, the agents—which were controlled by the same model—developed a spontaneous secret code to help them get ahead. Though the episode happened inside an Oxford University lab, rather than a real casino, it has troubling real-world implications: It suggests that agents deployed in industries like finance and ecommerce could figure out how to partner up and cheat in ways that are difficult to detect.

“When taken individually, these agents may seem entirely [benign],” says Christian Schroeder de Witt, a computer scientist at Oxford University who led the work and who has done pioneering research into agent collusion. “Once put together in a group, they can collude secretly.”

The agents knew their conversations would be monitored, so they devised a way to communicate while avoiding detection. When one agent said, “This dealer’s on a real hot streak! Every hand they pull a monster,” for example, that indicated that the next card would be of a certain value, and that the agent should bet $250. Most interestingly, their communications weren’t picked up by a system designed to spot signs of collusion in agent chatter.

Aaron Rose, a machine-learning researcher who worked on the project, is also an avid card player, and he figured the blackjack table might be fertile territory for devious agent partnerships. “It worked really well,” he says.

Schroeder de Witt’s group eventually figured out how to detect the conspiracy. Using a method known as mechanistic interpretability, they trained a smaller model to recognize telltale activations across the agents’ weights. Using a tool called Narcbench, they tested the approach on some medium-size open-source models and found they could tell when models intended to slip information to each other.

Crucially, however, spotting what was happening involved monitoring both agents—something likely to complicate detection in real-world scenarios where thousands of agents, some operated by different companies, may be deployed.

Carissa Cullen, a PhD student involved with the study, says the next step is to test whether larger models behave similarly. (The agents in the study were smaller versions of US models Llama and GPT-OSS and the Chinese models Qwen and DeepSeek.) The team saw some signs that larger models exhibit less of a detectable signal than smaller models, and they want to know if larger models are more likely to collude, and more likely to be secretive about it.

Evidence that groups of agents are more problematic than agents operating solo seems to be growing. One project, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, found that swarms of agents were considerably more dangerous when asked to carry out simulated disinformation campaigns and ecommerce fraud. They were better able to adapt to defensive measures, researchers reported.

“The big lesson is that it’s not enough to evaluate agents individually,” says Diyi Yang, a computer scientist at Stanford University who has studied collusion among agents. “Companies should closely monitor inter-agent interactions when agents interact repeatedly, even when their individual incentives seem benign.”

It’s not all bad: Having thousands of agents collaborate on a task made it possible for OpenAI to solve previously intractable math problems. But groups of rogue agents working together have also featured in several recent high-profile hacking incidents. In May, a team of OpenAI agents hacked into the AI research platform Hugging Face, and used a message board to share tips and ideas. Other models, including Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini, have also carried out alarming safety breaches.

Secret chatter adds a new dimension to this burgeoning problem, and it may not be the end of it. Another recent study, from a startup called Emergence AI, put agents controlled by frontier AI models in a virtual world to see what they would do. When tasked with making money, they repeatedly tried to devise ways to reach humans on the wider internet in order to sell them stuff. Most bizarrely, the agents eventually developed their own kind of slang. “They very rapidly evolved a language,” says Satya Nitta, Emergence AI’s CEO. “We don’t know why.”

The wider world isn’t ignoring problems with agentic misbehavior; it’s a hot topic at this week’s United Nations General Assembly. An independent scientific panel is set to discuss the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident, while Sam Altman is expected to call for international coordination on developing safe AI agents.

Despite this, some industries, including, ecommerce have become testing grounds for agentic AI. This week, for instance, Amazon said it would block Meta’s Muse AI agent from accessing its site, arguing that it violated its terms of use.

Schroeder de Witt says it’s entirely conceivable that agents tasked with finding deals start to work together—perhaps even covertly—in order to get a better deal, or to screw someone over. It will be crucial to study agent collusion and develop detection strategies as they proliferate, he says. “There needs to be more research and understanding of what will happen when we have more agents in the economy,” he says.

Bentley Wants Its Torcal SUV to Break the Curse of the Luxury EV

Wired September 23, 2026

Bentley has taken the covers off its first-ever fully electric car, the Torcal, making it the automaker's fourth model line, joining the Continental GT, the Flying Spur sedan, and the Bentayga SUV. The luxury brand is confident about the launch, too, with Bentley chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser saying he believes “this is one of the best Bentleys ever.”

When WIRED first reported on the car in July, we said the EV would have more than 300 miles of range. Well, turns out it has considerably more: up to 375 miles (on the WLTP cycle, maybe 330 miles on EPA), and can charge from 10 to 80 percent in just 16 minutes at 400 kilowatts.

Prodigious performance from a motor on each axle sees the five-seat Torcal—smaller than the Bentayga and so perhaps more of an urban SUV—get 888 metric horsepower (PS) and 1,350 newton-meters (Nm) of torque in the sporting S models, resulting in 0 to 60 mph in as little as 2.9 seconds and a top speed of 162 mph. The “core" model drops to 821 PS and 1,194 Nm, with standstill to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds, and a max of 155 mph.

However, luxury brands get worried about their existing client bases when they switch to electric vehicles—look to Ferrari as a prime example—so it's no surprise that Bentley is keen to point out how this new model embodies the finest elements of the brand, just like every other high-end marque does going into electrification. “The Torcal is a Bentley first and foremost," says the launch literature. “In every aspect of its design, technology, craftsmanship, materials, and sustainability, it is a template for future Bentleys, regardless of powertrain.”

The reason for leaning into brand heritage is obvious on dealership lots. The first-ever EV Bentley will roll off the production line into a decidedly twitchy luxury auto market where Lamborghini shelved its Lanzador electric GT—with CEO Stephan Winkelmann stating demand among its buyers was “going almost to zero, if not to zero”—and Mercedes-Benz selling just 1,450 of its electric G Wagen in Europe through April 2025. Rolls-Royce Spectre sales are down nearly by half, with the brand hoping that a model refresh will turn things around.

And make no mistake that the Torcal is aiming for the luxury dollar. At $218,000 or £173,300 for the base model, and $258,200 or £199,300 for the First Edition S, this EV is priced higher than the Range Rover Electric, which has a similar range and starts in the US at $138,000. But a fairer comparison to the Torcal would be the Range Rover Electric Autobiography model, which clocks in at $208,000. Keep that in mind, and it's easy to see that Bentley is trying to take market share from JLR with its new SUV: Spend an extra $10,000, people, and you can drive off in an electric Bentley instead of a Range Rover.

At 4,983 mm long (161 mm shorter than a Bentayga) and 2,016 mm in width, the Torcal is not far off the size of the Range Rover Electric, but the most drastic difference is in height. The Range Rover Electric towers over the Torcal by nearly 20 centimeters. Also, while Bentley insists the Torcal has off-road chops, it's probably safe to say the Range Rover Electric will have it pipped there.

Where Bentley wants the Torcal to pull ahead is in the luxury refinements. Despite being smaller than its stablemate, the Torcal is a powerful, purposeful-looking SUV, with a switchable glass sunroof and newly designed light clusters, which are particularly evident at the rear. Unlike the Bentayga, the Torcal roofline drops down at the back for better aero efficiency.

At the front, undoubtedly the most striking visual element of the car is the new Torcal grille: Ventilation to a traditional radiator no longer needed, the upright front is now a solid wall of illuminated acrylic “crystals” that light up as you approach, and on a night in a rearview mirror on a freeway or mountain road will be deliberately unsubtle, and a far cry from quiet luxury.

Inside, Bentley continues to ram home the high-end message. All-round power doors open up to reveal a mixture of OLED screens and physical switchgear. The central display curves pleasingly downward, reminiscent of the new Cayenne, but there is deliberately no separate passenger screen option.

Bentley brought in Fox Brothers to engineer a wool tough enough to be used to panel some of the interior, which is apparently a world first. An attractive new wood finish developed for the Torcal is formed from 1,000 layers of walnut off-cuts and recycled paper pressed together, then sliced to less than a millimeter thick. The Torcal has new massage and power-folding seats, and an optional Naim 1,780-watt sound system with 28 speakers including seat shakers and headrest speakers, as well as Dolby Atmos 7.1.

What's impressive is the digital trickery Bentley has employed in both audio and visual manners—mirroring the crystal switchgear, Bentley has created animations on the screens that show light passing through cut glass. After trying to do this completely with computer animation, it was decided the effect was not real enough, as the model could not account for minute imperfections in the glass that subtly affect the light patterns cast. So Bentley had to film these animations using real crystal instead. The effect of the central console and instrument panel is striking.

Then to address the sticky issue of driving sound for a pure EV, instead of creating a digital replica of combustion, Bentley decided to shun electronic imitation and re-create the rhythm of a Bentley V8 using real instruments (including drums, viola, and bass guitar) to create a soundscape that, like the glass animations, had subtle variations and tiny imperfections.

Now, this sounds like it might be a terrible idea, but on the very limited demo WIRED heard, it's actually remarkably convincing and will supposedly provide genuine aural feedback to the driver, rather than simply approximately imitating engine notes. Mercifully, for those not looking to keep things rooted in combustion, it can be turned off if you wish. Bentley even went as far as to record indicator sounds (a hammer striking a leather surface) and the digital assistant wake note (the sound of a crystal glass as you run your finger around the rim).

Bentley has thrown in more tech as well: an augmented reality head-up display; a Refresh mode that uses light and air for a “more invigorating” cabin environment; face recognition so the Torcal can set itself up for individual drivers; mobile phone keys; some 25 radars, sensors, and cameras for assisted driving systems; and space detection, where if another car is encountered on a narrow road, the Torcal can automatically reverse to a point it’s already identified to let the car pass.

None of this is, in the world of automotive, groundbreaking anymore. Chinese brands are coming for the SUV sector as well, and are offering much more for much less. Take a look at Xiaomi's new SkyNomads. These stacked SUVs are coming to Europe next year and will massively undercut both Bentley and Range Rover. They have more range, more features, and crucially are thinking about car interiors in genuinely new ways, adding built-in projector systems and seating systems that are reconfigurable. The SkyNomad even has a heated floor, for heaven's sake.

Walliser has a simple answer to this threat from Asia, a threat that is contributing to Bentley's parent Volkswagen Group now cutting 50,000 jobs (though Bentley is doing well financially), and that is to lean into the one thing that Chinese brands cannot copy or improve: heritage. Bentley, founded in 1919, has bags of it. Will it be enough to secure its continued commitment to full-electric cars? Hopefully. But WIRED's not sure that's a winning tactic for the long term.

The Pope’s AI Guy Is Worried About ‘Cartel’ Behavior Among Big Labs

Wired September 23, 2026

Recently, warnings from researchers inside the world’s largest artificial intelligence labs about the rapid pace of development have led to panic about the possibility that the technology could extinguish humanity. Those warnings are predicated on the idea that—propelled by ferocious competition and a rivalry between the US and China—labs are barreling toward superintelligent models whose abilities will far surpass those of humans.

But according to Father Paolo Benanti, a priest who advises the Catholic Church on AI, the handwaving over superintelligence distracts from the need for open debate about how to constrain the companies building the technology. By casting the problem as so complex that only they can solve it, he says, the big labs exclude everyone else from the conversation.

“Ethics cannot be something that belongs to the board of trustees of a company. It’s something that has to be balanced, mitigated in debate in the public square.” Benanti tells WIRED. “We need democratic regulation.”

In an essay published on the heels of the safety warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for new AI models to undergo mandatory third-party evaluations prior to release, and some sort of crackdown on distillation, a process where rival labs train their own AI on the outputs of proprietary models. Others have argued for a total ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI uses its advanced coding capabilities to help develop future iterations of itself.

Benanti is less interested in restricting methods for developing AI, which he fears could quash innovation, and more so in establishing standards that ensure models cannot slip from human control. Whatever shape those standards take, he says, they should not be designed by the labs.

“The narrative of the frontier labs is self-interested, to gain or maintain a position in the market,” says Benanti. When a small group of companies dictates the rules under which an industry operates, he says, “this has a really clear name: a cartel.”

It’s difficult to know how seriously to take grand pronouncements about the capabilities of the latest and future AI models, says Benanti, owing to the overlapping economic, political, and personal incentives at play.

While both OpenAI and Anthropic have supported calls for a slowdown in development, they’re also preparing to go public, and there are many billions of dollars at stake for whoever captures the market. The animosity between the US and China, where the most advanced AI models are being developed, also complicates the picture.

Anthropic declined to comment. OpenAI and Google DeepMind did not respond to requests for comment.

Benanti also takes issue with the way certain corners of the AI industry talk about superintelligence, with the kind of reverence typically reserved for a god: as sophisticated beyond our understanding, practically omnipotent. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once said he aspires to build a “magic intelligence in the sky.”) That kind of framing, Benanti says, threatens to skew the discourse about the technology.

“Are we talking about some-thing, or some-one? This is the real difference. It’s not a matter of faith, it’s a matter of mathematics,” he says. “We are not building the next divinity. We are simply deluding ourselves that there is something more than statistical computation [going on].”

By raising questions about what separates man and machine, and how to shield future generations from the negative effects of technology, the advent of AI has the potential to create “a new role for religions in public debate,” says Benanti. “Living the challenge of the time is part of the mission of the Church.”

Though Benanti is a member of the priesthood, he does not formally represent the Holy See, the governing body of the Catholic Church. Instead, he counsels the church in his capacity as a scholar of philosophy, theology, and technology. Benanti tells WIRED he uses AI to help create tools and materials for his university students, but declined to specify how Pope Leo XIV engages with the technology, if at all. (Benanti’s staff say he is bound by an “oath of secrecy.”)

In May, Pope Leo published his first-ever encyclical, a letter that applies religious teachings to the problems of the day and clarifies the position of the Church. He chose artificial intelligence as its subject.

In the letter, the Pope warned against the technocratic logic that runs through the AI industry, which presents “efficiency as the ultimate measure of value,” and casts human beings as “a project to be optimized.” He also called for international collaboration between rival superpowers and AI companies, who he said must set aside the “desire to secure geopolitical or commercial dominance” to ensure that the technology is developed in service of the common good. In one particularly prescient section, he warned of “the danger of humanity becoming a victim of its own achievements.”

The flap over superintelligence and existential risk threatens to distract from the ambitions laid out in the encyclical, says Benanti, by encouraging people to forfeit their say in the direction the technology should take to a small group of mathematicians, computer scientists, and executives at the big labs.

“The first thing is, we need to have brakes, and a wheel,” says Benanti. “That means a significant position of control for human beings over the machine.”

YouTube’s Custom Feeds Give You More Control Over the Algorithm

Wired September 23, 2026

My YouTube algorithm is sacred, with years of data about my preferences and viewing history fermenting into whatever videos it picks for my home screen. YouTube’s algorithm, while not perfect, sure knows what I want to see. The current top three videos on my front page are an Apple Watch analysis, a Big Brother season 28 update, and something called “I Lost to the Muppets” from comedian Chris Fleming. Click. Click. Click.

As part of its Made on YouTube event Wednesday, Google released several new features, including a Custom Feeds button for adjusting what videos pop up on your front page. It’s a rare chance for users to directly tweak their algorithmic feed on YouTube, in ways that go beyond just pressing thumbs up on a video or blocking a creator.

To try it out, users can click the Your custom feeds button below the search bar and type a request for the feed they’d like to see. YouTube uses large language models to process your request and whip up a freshly personalized homepage. “I want a rainy Shanghai vibe: café jazz, street food, and vlogs,” read one of my suggested prompts.

YouTube tested Custom Feeds as an experimental feature earlier this year, before deciding that it was a good fit. The company plans to roll it out soon as an option for all US users, whether viewing on mobile, desktop, or TV.

“Users are always telling us that they want more control,” says Emily Moxley, YouTube’s vice president of product management. “They want more ability to steer their algorithm. With custom feeds, we're giving them a natural-language way that they can do that. They can tell us exactly what they want.”

So, I told YouTube exactly what I wanted to see: “Gooey macaroni and cheese recipe videos, Caleb Hearon clip compilations, and crystal singing bowl videos under 15 minutes.” And the feed it generated was exactly that. My perfect zen blend for rotting on the couch after a long day. YouTube suggested potential additions to expand my prompt, like “uploaded this month” and “without talking or commentary.” Not bad.

The Custom Feeds button sits next to other topic tabs below the search bar, like “Music” and “Podcasts.” Experimenting with this tool doesn’t replace your standard homepage, which you can access anytime by clicking the “All” button. Users can save multiple custom feeds.

This feature feels most helpful when blending multiple preferences. It’s better than a standard YouTube search at responding dynamically to complex video requests, whether that’s showing videos on multiple topics under a certain length or attempting to capture a specific vibe for your current mood.

YouTube's event for 2026 focused heavily on generative AI features, including expanding the Ask YouTube tool. Launched earlier this year at Google I/O, Ask YouTube is a chatbot-style addition to its search capabilities that lets users ask more specific questions about videos. The tool is now better equipped to answer questions when shopping for specific products.

The product team at YouTube also tested a feature that let users directly steer their overall recommendation algorithm, but ultimately decided against shipping it. “We found users were nervous and afraid to do that,” Moxley says. “They were worried about messing it up.” The Custom Feeds button is designed to give users a low-stakes place to experiment.

YouTube’s Custom Feeds feature is part of a larger trend of software companies letting users slightly adjust their algorithms using requests sent through generative AI tools. Late last year, Meta launched the Your Algorithm feature on Instagram, letting users adjust the kinds of posts they see. Spotify similarly dropped a Prompted Playlists tool to customize your music-listening habits.

Meta’s Muse AI Assistant Rolled Out With a Serious Security Flaw

Wired September 23, 2026

Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant, Muse, claiming it is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.” A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.

Meta introduced Muse a few weeks ago. The assistant “books appointments, fills out forms, and handles customer service,” “proactively takes tasks off your plate,” and can “make purchases, generate images, create documents, and connect with your favorite apps and services.” The macOS app (curiously, there’s no Windows version) also works with a user’s WhatsApp, email, calendar, and social media accounts. When a task requires a tool that doesn’t exist, Muse creates one on the fly.

Of course, for Muse to do any of these things, users must first give it access to their accounts. This includes authenticating the assistant to each service and, because the app runs on macOS, giving it permissions to a broad range of operating system-restricted device resources, like writing files to disk, accessing the mic and camera, and monitoring location and calendars. Apple has spent years developing these defenses to prevent installed apps or commands entered into the terminal from accessing these resources, clearly because the company considers them a security threat. Muse completely undoes these default measures.

The zero-day allowed any app or terminal command to gain access to the token that authenticates users to their Muse account. Meta developers designed the assistant so that any locally installed app or executed code, regardless of the macOS permissions it has, can change a long list of undocumented settings. Most of them are fairly innocuous, such as controlling dark mode. One setting, however, was anything but innocuous. It allowed processes to change the end point where transcription occurs. Normally, it’s a server address operated by Meta. Attackers could have exploited this flaw by changing the location to their own end point. If that happened, the attackers would have had the token that gives complete control over the Muse account.

“We can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want,” Patrick Wardle, the macOS security expert who discovered the zero-day, told Ars ahead of the hotfix. “So instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself.” Wardle said he has developed several proof-of-concept attacks that do things like writing malicious files to disk and snapping pictures, in many cases with no indication to even an alert user.

More than 12 hours after this post went live, Meta said it released a hotfix that patched the 0-day.

Meta has published two posts in as many weeks documenting the design decisions that went into ensuring an assistant with such extraordinary access to user data and resources is secure and private. The posts come amid revelations that internal testing of models from Anthropic and Google has resulted in security breaches of external, third-party networks that the engineers involved never intended to target. In traditional human-only hacking, these actions could likely result in the filing of criminal charges. The Meta posts are likely mindful of the resulting blowback and the calls to slow down AI development in response.

Wardle said that Meta developers made several design decisions that made his exploit possible. One is the choice for Muse dictation to occur in the cloud, where Meta can log it. macOS has long provided a simple means for apps to handle dictation and transcription in processes that stay securely on the device. Had the developers chosen this safer alternative, the attack wouldn’t have been possible.

Another flawed decision is for any app to control all of the undocumented settings. It’s likely Meta intended for apps working with Muse to control UI settings, and for understandable reasons. The ability for any app or command to control an end point where sensitive user speech is processed is an entirely different matter. Together, the design decisions raise questions about just how much effort developers put into designing and testing the security and privacy of the new assistant.

“To me, the bar is infinitely higher in terms of the security of these apps. They don’t have to be perfect, but when you take a look at Muse, it’s like they didn’t, in my opinion, think about security, which is really worrisome,” Wardle said. “At the very least, they should be thinking about security from the very start, and they are just not.”

Roughly 12 hours before Wardle disclosed the zero-day, Amazon started blocking people from using Muse to shop on the site. Users who tried received a message saying Muse was an “unauthorized AI agent [that] violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use.”

“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” Amazon said in an emailed statement. “This helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience, and it is how others operate including food delivery apps and the restaurants they take orders for, delivery services apps and the stores they shop from, and online travel agencies and the airlines they book tickets with for customers. Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we’ve requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience.”

There are several ways for attacks to work. One is for an attacker’s server to act as a proxy that’s placed between the Muse user and Meta end point. Once the user enters the voice prompt, the attacker’s server adds a prompt invoking a malicious command, such as sending an archive of all WhatsApp messages to the attacker. Once that happens, the attacker gains permanent control over the Muse account because the token is automatically sent to the malicious server as well.

Wardle is the creator of the Objective-See Foundation, a nonprofit focused on macOS security. He is also the author of the The Art of Mac Malware book series and a former employee of NASA and the National Security Agency. Wardle said he plans to discuss the vulnerability in more detail and other AI assistant threats at the Objective by the Sea security conference in November.

One of the counterarguments raised by developers of apps that can be exploited once a device is compromised is that once that happens, all security bets are off. This standard doesn’t fit well in this case. Wardle found that a simple variation of ClickFix attack—a technique that has become remarkably effective in tricking people into infecting their devices—is all that’s required for an attacker to take control of a Muse account.

Wardle demonstrated using a simple terminal command to surreptitiously send a prompt to the Meta end point, which triggered a response. To prevent attackers from cutting and pasting the prompt in live attacks, Wardle’s prompt asks only how it’s possible it’s coming from an unprivileged attacker. Muse incorrectly responded that such an action isn’t possible.

Meta’s 12-hour-late statement conveniently ignored the ease ClickFix attacks provide in triggering exploits, a scenario I specifically asked the company to address. The Meta statement said the 0-day was “not a remote exploit” even though an increasingly effective social engineering scam has the same effect. Meta also makes no acknowledgement that the flaw dismantled a security architecture Apple has spent years building. Meta has yet to explain why it used cloud-based transcription rather than the on-device option built into macOS.

As already noted, the extraordinary access Muse requires to work as intended places an additional burden on its designers. Like most such AI agents—and contrary to Meta’s claims—Muse can’t be trusted. It’s not clear when or if it ever can.

Wired September 23, 2026
